23280-the-shirley-letters-from-californi:
The Shirley Letters come from the California mines of 1851 and 1852. The text presented here sits within a larger historical volume, whose notes trace the first explorers' voyages along the coast. Those notes also cover the expeditions of Gálvez and Bucareli for settling California and founding its missions.

The volume adds a fresh index and a portrait, plus a Spanish map of the coast as known by 1791. Readers get gold-rush letters framed by deep Spanish colonial history. The mines are shown as only the newest chapter in a coast explored and claimed for centuries before.
arxiv-2510-00052:
Mallick and colleagues test whether the sound of breathing alone can screen for sleep apnea. The disorder where breathing repeatedly pauses in sleep, without the expensive overnight laboratory study that is the current standard. Using 18 audio files from the MIT-BIH Polysomnographic Database, they convert respiratory sounds into spectrograms and train a ResNet-based convolutional network. Deliberately optimizing for recall first so that almost no true apnea event is missed.

Oversampling the rare apnea segments and applying class weights counter the dataset's imbalance, and the model reaches 90.55 percent recall for apnea detection. At the deliberate cost of low precision and 36.42 percent overall accuracy in the reported results. The authors position the system as a cheap, device-independent pre-screening tool for homes and basic clinics. Where a false alarm can be resolved by confirmatory testing but a missed case cannot.
arxiv-2510-00452:
Dalal Alharthi of the University of Arizona wrote this 2025 paper on automating cloud forensic investigations with AI. After a cloud attack, investigators comb logs by hand, a slow and error-prone process. The proposed framework, called CIAF, uses a language model guided by a formal rulebook of forensic terms. Inputs are cleaned and standardized first, so log entries get read consistently.

The framework was tested on Microsoft Azure logs containing ransomware-related events. Simulated attacks measured how much the framework improved detection over the baseline. Precision, recall, and F1 all landed near ninety-three percent in the reported experiment. The modular design should adapt to other attack types beyond ransomware, the author argues. Standardized inputs also make findings easier to reproduce and defend later. The paper presents the framework as a foundation for AI-driven forensic workflows across cloud platforms.
arxiv-2510-00652:
Ouyang, Xiang, Wang, and Ding at Huawei's Singapore research centre present OTTER in this 2025 arXiv paper on multimodal tagging. Organizing personal and enterprise media needs labels, but a fixed category list cannot capture everything users care about, while fully free tagging drifts into inconsistency. OTTER unifies both worlds, pairing a curated taxonomy with an open layer of user-driven tags. The team built a large hierarchically organized dataset of images and text, labelled by vision-language models and refined by humans.

A multi-head attention architecture aligns visual and textual inputs with embeddings for both fixed and open-set labels. On two benchmarks, OTTER reached overall F1 scores of 0.81 and 0.75, ahead of the next-best systems. Its open-set tagging was near perfect, while predefined label quality stayed competitive with closed-set rivals.
arxiv-2510-00852:
Sotudeh and three co-authors test the Hadrosymmetric Twin Higgs model against cosmological data in this 2025 arXiv paper. Twin Higgs models solve the little hierarchy problem by adding a twin sector whose particles are neutral under ordinary forces. Unlike the mirror version, the hadrosymmetric variant copies only the quarks into the twin sector, adding no light twin photons or neutrinos. That restraint keeps it clear of limits on extra relativistic species, and colliders can barely see it.

The team implemented the sector in the CLASS code and fitted it with Markov Chain Monte Carlo runs. Against Planck cosmic microwave background data plus local Hubble measurements, the Hubble tension fell from over four sigma to about two and a half sigma. The matter clustering discrepancy eased at the same time. The authors argue cosmology may be the sharpest probe of this deliberately elusive model.
arxiv-2510-00952:
Farhadipour and six colleagues from the University of Zurich describe their team's entries to the NIST Speaker Recognition Evaluation of 2024 in this 2025 arXiv report. Speaker recognition systems decide whether two recordings share one speaker, a task that degrades with short clips, language mismatch, and poor audio. The Zurich team, called CL-UZH, entered both the fixed and open conditions of the challenge.

For fixed-condition audio trials they used an X-vector system built with the Kaldi toolkit, trained from scratch on the CTS superset data. Face recognition with FaceNet supplied the visual side for audio-visual and visual-only trials. For the open condition they submitted models pretrained on the large VoxBlink2 and VoxCeleb2 datasets. The report compares development and evaluation performance across these systems and conditions for other challenge participants.
arxiv-2510-01052:
Mahdipour Aghabagher and Momtazi at Amirkabir University of Technology build a hybrid dialogue state tracker for Persian chatbots, in this paper published in Computer Speech and Language. Dialogue state tracking keeps a running record of what a user wants during a multi-turn conversation. Pure rule-based trackers cannot adapt to free, human-like exchanges, which hurts languages with fewer ready-made tools. Persian is one such language, and the authors target it directly.

Their system combines rules with several learned parts, including BERT for slot filling and intent detection, XGBoost for intent validation, and a GPT model for state tracking itself. Online agents generate answers in real time on top of that state. Evaluated on a broad Persian multi-turn dialogue dataset, the hybrid clearly improved accuracy and coherence over existing Persian methods. The authors credit the mix of structure and learned flexibility.
arxiv-2510-01252:
Mahran and Simbeck trace how a language model's training books quietly become its social assumptions. Models absorb patterns from massive corpora, but evaluations rarely connect outputs back to sources. Sparse autoencoders offer a lens, splitting dense activations into readable features.

As a controlled case, the team trained a small GPT-style model on nineteenth-century novels by women. Features were probed against eleven social and moral categories. Gender and kinship formed a stable backbone, with associations entangling deeper in the network. The pipeline generalizes into an audit tool for any corpus's cultural fingerprint. Thirty-seven novels by ten authors form the deliberately narrow corpus. Marriage, class, and morality join gender among the probed themes. Depth entangles associations that early layers keep separate. Stable backbones suggest some themes organize the whole representation. Auditing data through models beats auditing outputs alone every time.
arxiv-2510-01352:
Blower and Malham solve the full noncommutative version of a classic hierarchy of wave equations. The KP hierarchy describes shallow-water and plasma waves through infinitely many coupled equations. Replacing ordinary multiplication with noncommutative operations produces a far harder system.

A linear integral equation carries the solution, with scattering data obeying the linearized hierarchy. Two routes confirm the match, one through classical dressing transformations. The second runs through an exotic nonassociative algebra tied to descent algebras of permutations. Working inside that stranger algebra, the final identity lands back in the ordinary associative world. Direct linearisation is the strategy that tames the infinite system. Gelfand-Levitan-Marchenko is the integral equation at the method's core. Semi-additive scattering data unlock the direct substitution route. Grafting products give the descent algebra its unusual multiplication. Completeness is the claim, the whole hierarchy at once.
arxiv-2510-01552:
Tang and co-authors automate the ranking of cyber threats with a language-model pipeline called Polar. Over eleven thousand new vulnerabilities appeared in a single recent year, far more than analysts can grade by hand. Older scoring tools miss context and drift as attacker behavior shifts.

Polar works in four stages, from triage through static and exploitation analysis to mitigation advice. It turns messy threat reports into structured severity scores and forecasts of exploitation chances. Evaluations on real-world threats showed better ranking accuracy than prior approaches. The explanations it writes also help analysts decide, rather than merely trust, each ranking. Structured outputs plug into existing ticketing and patch queues without reformatting. Disclosure details and standard attack mappings drove much of the accuracy gain. Hallucinations appeared in predictable spots and yielded to simple validation rules. Prioritization decides what gets patched tonight.
arxiv-2510-01852:
Ironmonger and Ruškuc build a general decision framework for pattern-avoidance questions in this 2025 combinatorics paper. They order structures by consecutive embedding, where neighbors in a small structure must stay neighbors in the larger one. An avoidance set collects all structures that dodge a finite list of forbidden patterns. Two questions matter: whether such a set is well quasi-ordered, and whether it is atomic.

Well quasi-ordering rules out infinite families of mutually incomparable structures. Atomicity asks whether the set splits into two strictly smaller avoidance sets. The authors extend recent methods into one framework that settles both questions at once. It applies across a wide range of structure types. Graphs, directed graphs, and collections of relations all fall inside its scope. The result turns case-by-case arguments into a reusable machine for consecutive orders.
arxiv-2510-01952:
Llosa Isenrich, Schesler, and Wu build simple groups with carefully prescribed finiteness behavior in this 2025 group theory paper. Finiteness properties grade how close a group comes to having a finite classifying space. Exotic examples separate those grades one rung at a time. Simple groups, which admit no proper normal subgroups, rarely cooperate with such fine control.

Starting from any finitely generated linear group over the rationals, they construct a simple group sharing its finiteness properties. The original group even sits inside the new one as a quasi-retract. One application is a simple group of type FP-infinity that is nevertheless not finitely presented. For every n, they also produce a simple group of type FP-n that is neither finitely presented nor of type FP-(n+1). The constructions arise as Röver-Nekrashevych groups. They answer a standing question of Zaremsky about what finiteness patterns simple groups can realize.
arxiv-2510-02052:
Bajnoková and eight co-authors catch a solar flare warming up minutes before it erupts in this 2025 astronomy paper. The event was a modest C1-class flare in September 2022. Geometry helped: the NuSTAR telescope saw it hidden behind the solar limb, while the STIX instrument viewed it face-on. That pairing let the team study faint coronal emission without the flare's glare.

NuSTAR detected nonthermal emission and plasma heated above ten million kelvin starting seven minutes before the flare. The signal implies electrons were already accelerating continuously in the corona during that quiet onset. Matching type III radio bursts from a ground array supported the same story. Model parameters stayed steady through the onset, pointing to one persistent process. STIX spectra of the main flare showed similar electron distributions with a higher low-energy cutoff. The onset may therefore be an early fingerprint of the flare's own acceleration engine.
arxiv-2510-02252:
Araújo, Ze, Xu, Wu, and Liu show that retargeting quality decides humanoid tracking success in this 2025 robotics paper. Humanoid robots learn to move by copying human motion mapped onto their bodies. That mapping leaves artifacts: sliding feet, self-penetration, and impossible poses. Learning policies then burn effort correcting bad references, amid heavy reward tuning.

The authors suppress that extra tuning and measure retargeting quality directly. Cleaner reference paths yield better tracking policies under the same learning setup. Sloppy retargeting caps what the policy can achieve, regardless of training time. The results reorder priorities for teleoperation pipelines. Effort belongs upstream, in the mapping stage, not in compensating rewards. Teams building humanoid datasets now have evidence for investing in conversion quality first.
arxiv-2510-02552:
Cruz-Garcia and co-authors simulate how cooling shapes eerily even patterns in superconductors. Their 2025 physics paper studies hyperuniform vortex arrangements. Hyperuniform matter suppresses density wobbles at large scales. Superconductor vortices can settle into that hidden order. Experiments saw finite size and disorder disturb the pattern. The team models vortices as layered elastic lines in three dimensions. Their cooling protocol mimics the real laboratory procedure. Slow cooling from liquid to solid mirrors the experiments. Finite thickness limits the even pattern in equilibrium already.

Cooling dynamics add a second, stronger limitation. Which effect dominates depends on cooling rate and thickness. Disorder slows the long waves that would heal the pattern. The results map a realistic route to synthetic hyperuniform materials. Host media thickness must enter design calculations early. Interpreting vortex images also becomes safer with this frame. Hidden order is fragile in specific, predictable ways.
arxiv-2510-02852:
Akbari-Moghaddam and co-authors rethink bed planning for intensive care units. Hospitals must guess future demand under deep uncertainty. Babies and patients arrive at uneven rates. Stays vary widely by case and by site. A common rule keeps average use under eighty-five percent. The authors show it can mislead planners badly. Units can meet the average target yet overflow on many days.

Their framework uses a queueing model with time-varying inputs. Arrival rates shift over time, and stay lengths come from real data. Statistical tools split the admission stream into trend and seasonal parts. They tested the method on years of Calgary newborn ICU data. Demand swings and stay-length spread drove the results. Plans based on plain averages fell short in surge periods. The same approach fits other intensive care settings. It gives planners clear, data-based support for hard capacity choices.
arxiv-2510-02952:
Rathod and co-authors trace how tissues change using spatial gene data. Spatial omics maps gene activity across a tissue slice. Slices arrive as snapshots at scattered times. The true path between snapshots must be inferred. Plain flow matching links snapshots by statistics alone. It can draw paths that biology would never allow. Their framework, ContextFlow, feeds prior knowledge into the flow.

Local tissue layout shapes one prior source. Ligand-receptor chatter between cells shapes another. Both feed a matrix that grades how plausible each link is. That matrix steers the transport plan behind the flow. The steered version was proven to respect the priors in its entropic form. Tests on three data sets followed. ContextFlow beat top flow matching rivals on accuracy scores. It also cut the number of implausible links sharply. Paths stayed coherent across time as well. The method should transfer to growth, healing, and disease studies.
arxiv-2510-03052:
Sortino and a large team watch hybrid light-matter waves move in a flat device. The device is a thin film of tungsten disulfide patterned as a metasurface. Its pattern traps light in near-bound states. Excitons in the film then merge with that trapped light. The hybrids are called exciton-polaritons.

The team mapped the polariton paths with momentum-resolved imaging. The effective mass flipped sign between the two in-plane axes. Pump-probe and multi-dimensional spectroscopy then timed the motion. Coherence lasted a bit over a hundred femtoseconds. Rabi oscillations, the beat of energy swapping, ran near forty-five femtoseconds a cycle. A three-state model fit the behavior best. It couples the light mode to both bright and dark excitons. Room-temperature coherence of this kind is a real step. Flat van der Waals devices may host future polariton circuits.
arxiv-2510-03252:
Kieu and co-authors translate between any two of many domains while training on only a star of pairs. Multi-domain translation usually demands fully aligned data tuples. Collecting those tuples grows impractical as domains multiply. Their universal variant asks for any pair among K domains. Only pairs touching one central domain are ever shown. A single diffusion model, the Diffusion Router, serves all directions.

Domain labels condition one shared noise predictor throughout. Indirect translations route through the central domain in two hops. A variational objective plus Tweedie refinement enables direct hops too. Three new large benchmarks tested the framework. It beat baselines on indirect and direct translation alike. Sampling cost dropped below rival approaches in the process. Novel pairings like sketch to segmentation map emerged unprompted by data. Such cross-domain leaps were impossible under older schemes.
arxiv-2510-03352:
Farahbakhsh and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on rebuilding damaged images with diffusion models plus side clues. Diffusion models can fill gaps and sharpen blur, but standard guidance can chase false rewards and create artifacts. Side information, when it exists, often goes unused by current pipelines. The authors add a search step at run time that steers sampling with the side clues. Their method balances trying new paths against refining good ones.

The search plugs into many existing reconstruction systems with little change. Tests covered box inpainting, super resolution, and several kinds of deblurring, including motion and blind cases. The guided search improved both quality and measured scores across those tasks. It also beat gradient based guidance rivals in the reported comparisons. Gains grew largest when the damage was severe and the base problem was hardest to pin down. Reliable rebuilding matters for medical scans, photos, and sensor data alike.
arxiv-2510-03452:
Davis and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper cleaning up microscope images from a variant of structured illumination imaging. Projecting patterned light onto a sample reveals detail and slices away out of focus blur. A two phase version halves the capture time but leaves residual artifacts that filters cannot remove. No clean reference images exist to train a network on. The team built synthetic training pairs, stamping artifact patterns onto synthetic images, and trained encoder decoder networks on them.

Both networks improved clarity on real images from pool boiling experiments. The denoising autoencoder suppressed structured line artifacts. The U-Net handled uneven illumination better and preserved bubble edges. Artifact type, not habit, should decide which network a lab deploys. Synthetic training sidesteps the ground truth problem that blocks supervised denoising in many imaging methods. Faster optical sectioning matters for watching living or moving samples, where captures blur the dynamics.
arxiv-2510-03552:
Ghosh and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on whether cold gas clouds can survive inside hot galactic winds that also churn with turbulence. Galaxy winds mix cold dense gas with a hot thin medium, and older simulations treated wind and turbulence separately. Their 3D simulations drive both at once across a range of turbulence strengths. Survival turns on one race: mixed gas must cool faster than a slightly shortened destruction time. When that holds, clouds live despite the extra churn.

In the survival regime, turbulence stretched clouds and grew their surface area. Cold mass then grew up to ten times faster than in calm winds, and entrainment into the flow sped up sharply. Instead of thin tails, turbulence smeared cold gas sideways over wide areas. That spread changes the absorption signatures telescopes should see. The results help astronomers read real galaxy outflows, where wind and turbulence always arrive together.
arxiv-2510-03652:
San and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper exploring whether parametric X-ray radiation could treat tumors that contain amounts of sulfur. Tumor tissues concentrate sulfur atoms above healthy levels. Parametric X-rays form a beam in both energy and angle when electrons pass through a crystal. Tuned to a resonance, the beam is absorbed by sulfur, ionizing those atoms and damaging the cancer cells. Healthy tissue, with little sulfur and off resonance, should receive less dose.

The authors' estimates support the concept for sulfur tumors. Selectivity comes from the beam's spread plus the resonant absorption, not from aiming. The total dose falls well below what conventional X-ray tubes or accelerators deliver for the effect. Parametric sources run at electron energies typical of medical accelerators, tens of megaelectronvolts, rather than the gigaelectronvolt scale of synchrotrons. A compact source is the prize. Much validation remains before clinics could test the idea.
arxiv-2510-03752:
Chatterjee, Mu, and Vasudevan present a 2025 arXiv paper building public key encryption whose security rests on the MinRank problem over random instances. MinRank asks for a low rank combination of matrices, and cryptanalysis suggest it is hard, with no quantum speedup. That suits post quantum cryptography. Encryption schemes from rank problems needed structured instances built around decodable codes, a crutch that can leak weakness. This construction works from uniformly random instances, matching the decoding hardness of random rank metric codes.

The key enabler is a notion of duality for rank metric codes, developed in the paper. Removing the structure requirement matters because structured assumptions are where cryptosystems break. A scheme resting on the problem inherits the confidence of the cryptanalytic record. Public key encryption is the primitive in the post quantum migration, so each foundation counts. The construction gives rank metric code theory a tool that may serve designs.
arxiv-2510-04052:
Farkiani, Liu, and Crowley present this 2025 arXiv paper on closing a security gap between service meshes and the networks beneath them. Service meshes enforce application-level policies for microservice traffic, but raw IP-level flows answer to separate network rules. Keeping both layers consistent across different infrastructures takes coordination that often fails. Studies show most Kubernetes clusters enforce no network policies at all.

The authors integrate Layer 3 network policy enforcement directly into the service mesh. Their design builds an overlay network and routes traffic through chosen enforcement points. A default-deny stance with authorization keys blocks anything not explicitly allowed. Developers can then define policies from Layer 3 through Layer 7 in one place, portable across infrastructures. A prototype on Kubernetes and Istio added under a millisecond of latency. The work gives platform teams one consistent enforcement story instead of two drifting ones.
arxiv-2510-04352:
Villagrán presents this 2025 arXiv paper on how declining political trust changes public tolerance for violence by protesters and police alike. Research on protest tactics usually emphasizes movement demands and organization, while context receives less attention. Earlier structural studies linked perceived injustice by authorities to acceptance of violent protest methods. This article tests political trust, another form of authority legitimacy, using longitudinal Chilean data from 2016 to 2019 spanning the Social Outbreak.

Three modeling approaches, fixed effects, cross-lagged, and multilevel, point the same way. As political trust fell, acceptance of police violence weakened. Simultaneously, tolerance toward protesters' violent tactics increased. The dual shift helps explain why demonstrations have radicalized in many low-trust states recently. Eroding trust raises resistance to state force while lowering condemnation of radical repertoires. Rebuilding institutional credibility becomes, on this account, part of violence prevention rather than a separate governance goal.
arxiv-2510-04452:
Jenny Liang and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on tools for prototyping AI interface agents. Agents that act on user commands are hard to design, since their behavior unfolds step by step. Designers without AI training have valuable views on that behavior, yet lack ways to test ideas. The team first interviewed twelve people with varied agent experience. From those talks, they listed what a prototyping tool must support.

The study named five core activities in agent prototyping and six capabilities a tool should offer. The team built those ideas into a design probe called AgentBuilder. Fourteen people then used AgentBuilder in a live prototyping study. Their work confirmed the design requirements and showed how developers actually shape agent behavior. The study surfaced needs that interviews alone had missed. The paper gives tool builders a tested checklist for agent design software.
arxiv-2510-04652:
Ines Akaichi and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on tracking duties that come with using shared data. When data crosses between organizations, the receiver owes duties: delete it by a date, report its use, or pass limits downstream. Those duties change state over time as they are met, broken, or allowed to expire. The team extends a policy framework called GUCON so duties carry time inside the model. Their tools are the star forms of the RDF and SPARQL web data standards.

The extension states temporal duties in a formal way, with start times and deadlines as first class parts. A component named the Obligation State Manager watches usage traces in a temporal knowledge graph. It updates each duty state as events arrive and flags duties that drift toward breach. The authors built a prototype and evaluated the model and software. A state machine gives auditors a language for compliance.
arxiv-2510-04852:
Victor May and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a benchmark for AI agents that migrate Java code. Enterprises hold vast Java estates built on old versions, and upgrades are slow, risky work. Language model agents promise to automate the move, but nobody had graded them on real projects. FreshBrew collects projects that build on Java 8 yet fail on Java 17. High test coverage was required, so success can be checked honestly.

The suite holds two hundred twenty eight real repositories. An agent passes only through three gates in order. The project must compile, then pass its original tests, then keep its test coverage nearly intact. Those gates block the reward hacking of deleting tests to look successful. The best model tried, Gemini 2.5 Flash, migrated just over half of the projects. Rule based tools served as the comparison baseline. The failures clustered in instructive places, which the authors catalog for builders.
arxiv-2510-05152:
Jingtong Su and four co-authors show that one character can flip AI leaderboard rankings in this 2025 arXiv paper. Evaluations steer models with demonstration examples inside the prompt. Nobody standardized the character separating those examples: comma, newline, hash, or pipe. The authors suspected this tiny formatting choice was not harmless.

Across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, MMLU scores swung by up to 23 points either way with delimiter choice. By picking the separator, one could put any tested model in the lead. The brittleness persisted across topics and did not fade with scale. Probing attention heads showed good delimiters steer attention toward key tokens. Naming the delimiter explicitly in the prompt improved robustness. The paper closes with practical recommendations for which separators work best.
arxiv-2510-05452:
Plumridge and colleagues work on simulating how radiation moves through matter. Such models matter for nuclear reactors, supernova studies, and medical and energy research. A standard method expands the flow in spherical harmonics, but sharp changes create false wiggles in the answer. A filter can smooth those wiggles, yet picking the right filter strength is hard.

The team lets a neural network choose the filter strength from local conditions at each point. Training uses an optimization setup built in PyTorch, with no need for the true solution. Work was based at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Across their test suite, the learned filter made the base method much more accurate. It beat a fixed-strength filter in most two-dimensional cases, though the fixed filter won some one-dimensional tests. The approach gives modelers a practical way to control error at low extra cost.
arxiv-2510-05552:
Phan and Khisti revisit two linked problems in information theory with a sampling twist. Channel simulation sends a noisy version of data through few bits. Distributed matching asks two parties with shared randomness to pick the same output. Their 2025 paper attacks both with ensemble rejection sampling.

For channel simulation, their scheme reaches a near-optimal coding rate. Standard rejection sampling also achieves that rate, even for continuous alphabets. The main result is a distributed matching lemma for the ensemble method. Its matching probability comes close to the known Poisson matching benchmark. Experiments on Gaussian sources and MNIST images validate the compression gains. Channel simulation underlies tasks from model compression to federated learning. The work extends an earlier importance matching lemma from the same group. A matching lemma this strong gives distributed coders a sharper tool.
arxiv-2510-05952:
Van Drunen and Vrijenhoek argue that public datasets bottleneck diversity-aware news recommendation. News recommenders increasingly decide what individuals see online. Normative scholarship wants recommenders serving democracy through diversity, not just engagement. Their 2025 analysis asks what data such systems would actually need.

Current public datasets mostly support optimizing short-term engagement. Data on article formats, styles, and viewpoints are largely missing. Audience characteristics needed for diversity designs are likewise absent. The theory-practice gap in recommender research traces substantially to data. The authors then examine European law's possible remedies. Existing data access measures fail to deliver the needed access. Structural researcher access is the legal reform direction proposed. Public service media could play a more active technological role instead. Exposure to new perspectives is the democratic function at stake. Engagement metrics alone cannot certify a recommender as diversity-aware.
arxiv-2510-06052:
Lu and co-authors make reasoning models think hard only where it counts in a 2025 machine learning paper. Long chains of thought solve tough problems, but most steps are routine arithmetic or simple rewriting. Treating every step at full length wastes time and money.

Their framework, MixReasoning, watches the model's uncertainty token by token as it writes. When uncertainty spikes at a decision point, the system expands a short window into detailed reasoning. When the path turns routine again, it settles back into a concise mode powered by a small adapter. Tests on GSM8K, MATH-500, and AIME show shorter reasoning traces with no loss of accuracy. Accuracy often improved, since shorter traces leave less room for verbosity-driven mistakes.
arxiv-2510-06552:
Tarek Naous, Philippe Laban, Wei Xu, and Jennifer Neville look at the other side of chatbot conversations. Their 2025 paper notes that most language models are trained to act as polished assistants. Real users write messier turns, change their minds, and spread a request across several messages. Testing assistants against fake users therefore needs simulators that behave like real people.

The team shows that assistant models make poor user simulators. Surprisingly, better assistants turn out to be worse simulators of users. So the authors train purpose-built user language models on real user messages instead. These models match human behavior more closely across their tests. They produce more varied turns, split intent across messages, and end conversations more naturally. The authors also release an eight-billion-parameter user model for other researchers. Assistants tested against these realistic users perform worse, which exposes weaknesses that easy simulations had hidden.
arxiv-2510-06652:
Shangjian Yin and four co-authors ask whether a language model can train itself to follow human preferences. Their 2025 paper tackles a cost problem in alignment. Human feedback is expensive, and feedback from other AI systems still needs costly prompts, answers, and external judges. Their framework, called SAO, removes those outside inputs.

Under SAO, the model plays varied personas to invent its own prompts and responses. It then judges those pairs itself and learns from its own preferences. Tests show clear gains on chat benchmarks such as AlpacaEval 2.0. Performance on objective tasks, like question answering and math, stayed strong at the same time. Bigger self-made datasets and repeated rounds improved the results further. The work offers a practical route to alignment for teams without annotation budgets. It also raises a sharp question about how far self-judgment can safely go.
arxiv-2510-06752:
Yijun Wang leads a team examining gas flowing out of a bright active galaxy called 3C 59. Their 2025 paper is a pilot study of warm absorbers, which are streams of ionized gas leaving the galaxy's center. Jets and outflows both shape how host galaxies form stars. How the two relate remains unclear, and 3C 59 shows both at once.

The team fitted the galaxy's spectrum from near-infrared light through hard X-rays. Data came from several instruments, including the XMM-Newton space observatory. Careful modeling separated the glowing disk, the hot corona, and the absorbing gas. They found two distinct warm absorber layers with different ionization levels. Adding each layer improved the spectral fit by a large margin. A possible third layer helped too little to keep. The broader aim is a reliable fitting routine for larger samples. That routine can later test how jets and outflows interact across many galaxies.
arxiv-2510-06952:
Bing Li leads a team showing how generated 3D objects can hide from the laser scanners of self-driving cars. Their 2025 paper studies adversarial attacks on LiDAR detectors, which autonomous vehicles trust to spot pedestrians. Earlier attacks tweaked point data directly and rarely made objects vanish fully. They were also hard to build in the physical world.

The team first ran a systematic study inside the CARLA driving simulator. Changing a single pedestrian's shape or brightness did not fool detectors reliably. Combining several objects into one composition fooled most detectors much more strongly. Placement mattered too, especially occlusions around the lower body. Their generator, Phy3DAdvGen, uses text prompts to build such evasive human-object compositions. Prompts steer where objects sit, keeping the visual footprint small. Tests in simulation and in physical setups fooled leading detectors consistently. The results expose a realistic blind spot that safety testing must now cover.
arxiv-2510-07452:
Hughes and co-authors introduce Patch, a defense that edits the exact circuits inside a language model that leak private data. Their 2025 paper starts from a privacy hazard: models memorize names, emails, and other personal details from training text, and adversaries can extract them. Broad defenses like differential privacy blunt the leakage but badly damage usefulness. Circuit discovery tools can locate the internal pathways responsible for reciting personal information. Patch ablates the most important links in those pathways. The pathways turn out to be shared across many types of personal data, the study finds.

Editing them cut the recall of leaked information by up to sixty-five percent while preserving model quality better than rival defenses. Stacking Patch on top of differential privacy drove residual leakage nearly to zero. Leakage circuits persisted even after other defenses were applied, explaining why those defenses plateau.
arxiv-2510-07752:
He and nine coauthors wrote this 2025 computer graphics paper on rebuilding moving 3D scenes from video. Color video at low frame rates leaves motion between frames uncertain. A pixel's match in the next frame becomes guesswork, and blur makes it worse. Event cameras attack the problem from the other side. They record brightness changes at speed but carry no color. The authors fuse the two sources into one reconstruction system.

Their framework, DEGS, lets event motion cues guide the scene's deformation. A tuning step adapts an event flow estimator to each scene. A geometry-aware method links event motion to the scene's Gaussian elements. Splitting motion into parts and adding pseudo-labels between frames steadies the fit. Across synthetic and real scenes, DEGS beat image-only and event-based rivals. The gains showed most clearly in fast motion with blur, where events supply what color frames miss.
arxiv-2510-07952:
Fabj and four coauthors wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on black hole mergers in AGN disks. Such disks pair up stellar-mass black holes and drive them to merge. Folklore says gas should spin the holes up and align their orbits with the disk. Aligned mergers would show positive effective spin in the data. The authors test that story with post-Newtonian simulations of binary-single encounters plus a gas alignment model.

Quasi-circular binaries do align before merging, as the standard picture says. Eccentric binaries inspiral too fast for gas torques to finish the job. Their tilts survive, and effective spin spreads around zero. The divide sits at an in-band eccentricity of about one tenth. This creates a correlation between eccentricity and effective spin for the disk channel. It may explain massive events whose spins look misaligned. Alignment timescales, not just disk physics, decide the signature.
arxiv-2510-08152:
Khasanova and five coauthors at Dialpad wrote this 2025 paper teaching small language models to follow instructions in business conversations without forgetting their general skills. Large models are too expensive to run for every meeting summary or call analysis. Small models follow instructions poorly outside their training. Ordinary fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting. The authors' method, DACIP-RC, continues pre-training through reading comprehension instead. The model answers generated questions about real conversation transcripts.

Forty-one hand-written meta-prompts automatically produced over twenty-five million training instances. The approach significantly improved zero-shot performance across business tasks, from meeting summarization to call purpose identification. The authors describe the work as the first instruction pre-training on business conversational data. The lesson for industry is concrete: proprietary transcripts can adapt a cheap model to a company's own tasks.
arxiv-2510-08352:
Nikos Theodoridis and co-authors test small vision-language models on traffic scenes in a 2025 arXiv paper. These models read both images and text, and car makers hope to use them in self-driving systems. Cars must spot hazards at long range, not just nearby, yet on-board hardware cannot run huge models. The team built a benchmark that isolates pure perception from reasoning.

Their benchmark, DTPQA, asks only perception questions about traffic scenes, each tagged with object distance. Questions cover near objects up to twenty meters and far ones beyond thirty meters. Several leading small models were evaluated against human answers. Despite the simple questions, the best small model reached only about sixty percent accuracy. Humans scored about eighty-five percent on the same questions. The gap shows small models remain shortsighted for safety-critical driving tasks.
arxiv-2510-08852:
Luthra, Mishra, and Galanti ask whether two training methods that look alike on paper also learn alike inside, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Contrastive learning trains vision models without labels by pulling matching images together and pushing others apart. A supervised cousin uses labels for a similar push-and-pull. Earlier theory showed their training goals nearly coincide when classes are many. Whether the learned features stay twins throughout training was open.

Training both methods from the same start, with the same data order and image tweaks, the authors prove their internal representations stay close. The guarantee sharpens with more classes and with a softer similarity scale, and it depends on batch size in a stated way. The weights themselves, by contrast, can drift apart without bound over time. Experiments confirm the split picture, and the supervised cousin tracks the label-free method more closely than other supervised goals.
arxiv-2510-09052:
Xu proves a pair of conjectured identities about a family of infinite series, in this 2025 arXiv paper in number theory. The series are called Apéry-like, after a famous series used to prove that a certain constant is irrational. They blend central binomial coefficients, which count lattice paths, with layered harmonic sums. Genčev and Rucki had recently conjectured exact evaluations for several of them, and Xu settles those conjectures.

He gives two independent proofs, both powered by hypergeometric functions, the master family containing most classical series. Along the way he establishes broader identities that contain the conjectured ones as special cases. A second thread uses iterated integrals to show that a class of mixed multiple values reduces to these same series plus a known zeta pattern. That reduction yields explicit formulas for the mixed values in terms of ordinary zeta values.
arxiv-2510-09252:
Vogl and co-authors measure how squeezing a silicon crystal shifts the light absorbed by donor atoms, refining numbers silicon quantum computers will be designed around, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Donors such as phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony are leading qubit candidates in pure silicon. Their bound exciton state, an electron-hole pair clinging to the donor, sets and reads out spins. The team studied that optical transition under tuned uniaxial stress along two crystal axes, across a wide range of magnetic fields.

From the spectra they extracted donor-specific deformation potentials, constants linking strain to energy shifts. One, the uniaxial electron deformation potential, came out much larger than values for other silicon states, and depended clearly on the donor species. That points to unusual sensitivity to strain and to the donor's core. The hole's shear constant varied with magnetic field too, hinting at richer strain coupling than standard theory describes.
arxiv-2510-09352:
Andreas Granath, Daniel Appelö, and Siyang Wang propose a faster solver for the Helmholtz equation in a 2025 arXiv paper. That equation describes how waves settle into a steady pattern, and it appears in acoustics, optics, and medical imaging. Solving it on fine grids is expensive, so the team looks for a way to store the solution in compressed form.

Their method builds on WaveHoltz, which filters a related wave equation over time to extract the steady solution. They discretise the wave problem with high-order finite differences and keep the solution in low-rank form, as a compressed matrix in two dimensions and as a tensor train in three. Step truncation and a low-rank acceleration scheme keep the size under control. Tests on free-space and half-space problems, with steady and piecewise wave speeds, show the scheme converges and works well.
arxiv-2510-09652:
Patrick Achenbach and a large collaboration of co-authors present a white paper for a new facility at Jefferson Lab in a 2025 arXiv paper. When an intense electron beam strikes a dump, a block that absorbs it, the interactions create secondary beams of muons and neutrinos, and possibly of light dark matter particles. Such beams could serve experiments that the main accelerator programme cannot.

Searches for light dark matter with the approved Beam Dump eXperiment are already driving construction of a new underground vault. The white paper argues the vault could grow into a broader Beamdump Facility with minimal extra installation. It summarises a workshop on secondary beams held at the lab. Several muon physics applications and neutrino detector technologies suited to Jefferson Lab are highlighted. A possible secondary neutron beam is noted but deferred to a future edition of the document.
arxiv-2510-09752:
Sai Krishna Reddy Mudhiganti, Juanyan Wang, Ruo Yang, and Manali Sharma demonstrate Patentformer in a 2025 arXiv paper, an AI platform that drafts patent applications. Drafting a patent demands an experienced attorney who understands both the law and the invention's technology, and who can write in a formal legal style. That dependence on scarce expertise makes drafting slow and costly.

Patentformer is designed to support attorneys rather than replace them. It rapidly produces high-quality draft applications that adhere to legal writing standards. The paper presents the system as a demonstration of AI-assisted automated patent drafting. By automating the first pass, the platform aims to let attorneys spend their expertise on judgement and refinement. The authors frame the tool as an example of specialised professional work being accelerated by models trained for a narrow, demanding genre of writing.
arxiv-2510-09952:
Topcuoglu, Kaan Onarlioglu, Steven Sprecher, and Engin Kirda defend web apps against discrepancy attacks in this 2025 arXiv paper on web security. Modern web apps route traffic through layers of proxy services. Because HTTP is complex and vendors make different design choices, two proxies may read the same request in different ways.

Attackers exploit that gap for web cache poisoning and request smuggling, which can poison stored pages or sneak hidden requests past checks. The authors propose HTTP request synchronization, forcing the layers to agree on one reading of each request. When every proxy parses the request the same way, the mismatch the attacks rely on disappears. The defense aims at the root cause rather than each attack variant.
arxiv-2510-10152:
Wan, Mingwen Shao, Renlong Wu, and Wangmeng Zuo present Color3D in this 2025 arXiv paper on 3D computer vision. Color3D colorizes static and dynamic 3D scenes from monochrome input. It gives users guided control over the colors while keeping them consistent across views and over time.

Older methods handle only static scenes and enforce consistency by averaging color choices, which dulls richness and removes user control. Color3D instead uses a personalized colorizer that preserves diverse, vivid color while still agreeing between viewpoints. The balance matters for film, games, and heritage digitization, where black-and-white captures need plausible color that does not flicker as the camera moves. The framework aims for both artistry and stability.
arxiv-2510-10352:
Amaresh Sahu studies how osmotic forces change lipid membrane fluctuations in this 2025 arXiv paper in soft matter physics. Lipid bilayers form the walls of cells. Hydrodynamic models often treat the membrane as impermeable to the surrounding fluid, which holds dissolved solutes.

Real membranes leak, and that permeability creates osmotic forces, flows driven by solute imbalance, whose effects on membrane flickering are poorly understood. Sahu works out how those forces modify the fluctuations. Membrane fluctuation spectra are a standard tool for measuring bending stiffness in experiments. If osmosis shifts the spectra, past stiffness measurements may need a second look, and cell mechanics models gain a missing ingredient.
arxiv-2510-10452:
Utsav Maskey, Mark Dras, and Usman Naseem study why chatbots refuse harmless requests when they search documents before answering, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Safety training makes models decline risky requests, but aggressive filters also block benign ones, a problem called over-refusal. In retrieval augmented generation, the fetched context can tip the balance. The team built RagRefuse, a benchmark spanning medical, chemical, and open domains, with benign and harmful queries paired with controlled contaminated contexts.

Their analysis shows that context layout, contamination, the domain, and the density of harmful text can all trigger refusals of benign queries. The effects vary with each model's alignment choices. To counter this, they propose SafeRAG-Steering, an intervention that nudges the model's internal embeddings toward regions linked to safe, non-refusing outputs at answer time. In their tests it cut over-refusals in contaminated pipelines while keeping legitimate refusals of truly harmful requests intact.
arxiv-2510-11052:
Qinglin Zhu and nine co-authors fix two flaws in how diffusion style language models write text, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Unlike autoregressive models, which generate word by word, diffusion models draft in parallel. But they discard the predicted distributions for unfinished tokens at each step, losing information, and they commit to local choices too early without a global view. Their Latent Refinement Decoding keeps unfinished positions as mixtures of predicted tokens and the mask embedding, so beliefs stay soft and globally consistent.

A predictive feedback loop then finalizes confident tokens while uncertain ones keep iterating. The team tracks how beliefs shift between rounds, as a signal for when to stop. Across coding and reasoning benchmarks the method improved accuracy: HumanEval rose 6.3 points and MATH500 rose 3.8 points among the reported gains. It also delivered speedups of up to 10.6 times over standard decoding in their experiments.
arxiv-2510-11152:
Solving the Navier-Stokes equations of fluid flow on fine grids is slow and memory-hungry, especially on a single graphics card. Jiale Meng, Shuqi Tang, Steven M. Wise, and Zhenlin Guo build a solver for this problem in a 2025 arXiv numerical methods paper. Their matrix-free multigrid solver runs on a GPU in MATLAB and uses the Full Approximation Storage scheme on staggered finite difference grids.

A new smoother design removes the branching that slows standard red-black iteration, and the transfer operators between grids are also GPU-accelerated. On the heat equation, the solver ran 61 times faster than one CPU core in two dimensions and 46 times faster in three dimensions on an RTX 4090 card. A memory-efficient redesign cut the stored variables to eight, letting full Navier-Stokes runs at the largest tested grid fit on one card where classical implementations run out of memory.
arxiv-2510-11352:
FRB 20121102A was the first repeating fast radio burst found and the first pinpointed to milliarcsecond precision. M. P. Snelders and a large collaboration revisit it thirteen years after discovery in this 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. The source sits in a magneto-ionic environment inside a dwarf galaxy about a billion parsecs away, and it is accompanied by a persistent radio source.

Using the European VLBI Network, the team re-localized the burst source and the persistent source, confirming they are co-located and improving results by about a factor of four. Their transverse offset is constrained to roughly twelve parsecs. The persistent source remains compact after a decade. They also report eighteen bursts from the Nançay Radio Telescope. With published data, these show the dispersion measure has dropped by about 25 units over five years. The local plasma contribution has fallen by more than fifteen percent.
arxiv-2510-11452:
Two rivals fighting on many fronts at once, from armies to advertisers, face a spillover problem: effort spent on one battle can help in neighboring ones. Marcin Dziubiński, Sanjeev Goyal, and Junjie Zhou model that situation in this 2025 arXiv economics paper. Each player has their own network of spillovers linking the battlefields, so a resource allocation plays out differently on the two sides' network architectures.

The authors prove there is a unique equilibrium with a clean form. A player's relative chance of winning a battle is the product of the battlefield's centrality ratio in the two networks and the ratio of relative effort costs. They then study network design, characterizing the architectures that maximize total effort and those that maximize total utility. Finally they solve the fuller game in which players choose both their networks and their efforts.
arxiv-2510-11652:
Contest benchmarks for math and code are saturating, while real academic research problems, the kind in top journals, remain nearly untouched by evaluation. The OPPO AI Agent Team introduces AcadReason to close that gap in this 2025 arXiv paper. The benchmark holds fifty expert-annotated problems across five high-reasoning domains: computer science, economics, law, mathematics, and philosophy. All were drawn from recent top-tier publications and put through rigorous quality control, so each is both hard and answerable.

The team systematically evaluated more than ten mainstream language models and agent systems. The results were sobering: most models scored below twenty points, and even the cutting-edge GPT-5 reached only sixteen. Agents did better, but none exceeded forty points. The authors read this as a measured capability gap between today's systems and the demands of super-intelligent academic research tasks. AcadReason is offered as a rigorous yardstick for that frontier.
arxiv-2510-11752:
Zhiyu Wang and six co-authors present PLASMA, a deep learning tool for comparing the local shapes of proteins. Proteins do their work through small structural motifs, such as active sites where chemistry happens. Finding and matching these substructures across proteins is key to tracing evolution and designing new proteins. Older methods handle the task poorly. This 2025 arXiv paper recasts the matching problem as optimal transport, the mathematics of moving mass at least cost.

PLASMA uses differentiable Sinkhorn iterations, a fast algorithm for transport problems, to align residues one-to-one between two structures. For each pair it outputs a clear alignment matrix and one interpretable similarity score. Wide-ranging tests and three biological case studies show the alignments are accurate yet lightweight. The team also offers PLASMA-PF, a variant that needs no training data at all. That variant gives labs an option when training examples are unavailable.
arxiv-2510-11852:
Saroj Basnet and four colleagues test how well open-source vision-language models understand sarcasm in social media posts. Sarcasm in memes lives in the clash between picture and caption, so a model has to read both together. The team's 2025 arXiv paper evaluates seven leading open models, including BLIP2, LLaVA, PaliGemma, and Qwen-VL. They use three benchmark datasets named Muse, MMSD2.0, and SarcNet.

The models were prompted with zero, one, or a few worked examples. At simple yes-or-no sarcasm detection they achieved moderate success. Their explanations lagged badly, though. When asked to explain why a post is sarcastic, the models could not reliably pinpoint the visual-textual mismatch that creates the joke. High-quality explanations, the authors find, still require task-specific fine-tuning. The study gives developers a clear map of what free models can and cannot do with ironic content today.
arxiv-2510-11952:
Priyanka Dey and five colleagues personalize language models without harvesting piles of human feedback. Standard personalization leans on costly annotations or interaction logs and still misses who the user deeply is. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces GRAVITY, a framework that synthesizes preference data from rich user profiles. The profiles draw on Hofstede's cultural dimensions, Schwartz's basic values, the World Values Survey, and the Big Five personality traits.

From each profile, GRAVITY fabricates pairs of responses, one aligned with the user's values and traits, one not, to teach the model taste. The team tested the method by generating book descriptions for four hundred Amazon users across the United States, Brazil, Japan, and India. Profile-grounded synthetic data beat prompt conditioning, standard fine-tuning, and naive synthetic pairs. Preference gains ran over four percent above the baselines. In user studies, people preferred GRAVITY's outputs over eighty-six percent of the time.
arxiv-2510-12152:
Chaiwon Kim, Jongyeong Lee, and Min-hwan Oh split the bandit problem's two jobs between two different arms. In a decoupled multi-armed bandit, each round the learner explores one arm, seeing its loss for free, and exploits another, paying its loss unseen. Their 2025 arXiv paper designs a Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader policy using Pareto perturbations.

The policy earns the best of both worlds. In stochastic environments it achieves constant regret, beating even the standard bandit's optimal rate, because exploration costs nothing here. In adversarial environments its regret is minimax optimal. Practicality matches theory: unlike the previous best-of-both-worlds policy, it needs no convex optimization step, and unlike typical perturbed-leader methods, no resampling. The result runs about twenty times faster than its predecessor while performing better empirically in both regimes. Experiments also show naive hybrids, pure exploration bolted onto standard exploitation, fall short.
arxiv-2510-12552:
El Maalouly and Lakis design algorithms for matching problems with quotas, parameterized by how repetitive the input graph is, in a 2025 arXiv computer science paper. Exact matching asks whether a perfect matching uses a set number of red edges in a graph with red and blue edges. It is a famous test case for whether randomness is truly needed.

They focus on the equivalent top k perfect matching problem, maximizing the combined weight of the k heaviest edges in the matching. The inputs are blown up graphs, where vertices were replaced by cliques or sets. Their fixed parameter algorithm runs in time governed by k and the neighborhood diversity, a measure of how few neighborhood types exist. They extend it to an approximation scheme with softer dependence. For prototypes of bounded bandwidth they give a recursive subexponential algorithm. The same separator ideas adapt the method back to exact matching.
arxiv-2510-12952:
Papireddygari and co-authors study the efficiency of a prediction market maker in this 2025 arXiv paper. Automated market makers quote buy and sell prices in combinatorial prediction markets, where the number of possible securities grows doubly exponentially and markets would otherwise be too thin to trade. The classic logarithmic market maker is hard to price and its worst-case loss grows with the number of outcomes.

The constant log utility market maker keeps worst-case loss fixed and can even add outcomes on the fly. Simpler versions underpin major decentralized finance protocols. Still, the authors prove that pricing its securities is computationally hard in a strong counting sense. To make it practical, they give a randomized approximation algorithm that works with high probability. It is built on an oracle they show can be implemented efficiently for interval securities, the kind used in financial options.
arxiv-2510-13052:
Ul Abrar, Michelusi, and Larsson study optimization on streaming data in this 2025 arXiv paper. Classical optimization assumes a fixed objective. Systems learning from live data must chase a moving target: at each step the goal is a weighted average of losses over all samples seen so far. Earlier time-varying optimization work used generic formulations that ignored this streaming origin.

The authors analyze two weighting strategies, uniform weights treating every sample equally, and discounted weights whose influence decays geometrically with age. For gradient descent updates they derive tight bounds on the tracking error, the gap between the current parameters and the time-varying optimum. Uniform weighting drives that error to zero at a steady decay rate. Discounted weighting leaves a nonzero error floor. That floor is set by the discount factor and the number of updates per step. Numerical simulations confirmed the theory.
arxiv-2510-13152:
Chen and Shen map how long galaxies take to grow bars in this 2025 arXiv paper. Bars, the elongated stellar structures crossing many disk galaxies, form through a spontaneous instability that classical swing-amplification theory describes only in rough terms. A recent empirical finding, the Fujii relation, says the formation timescale depends exponentially on the disk's mass fraction, but only a limited parameter space was explored.

The authors test the relation across disk mass fraction, the Toomre Q stability parameter, and disk scale height. The Fujii relation held for reasonable stability and thickness values. The timescale also grew roughly linearly with both Q and scale height, so hotter or thicker disks form bars more slowly. Combining all three dependencies into one relation, they estimate bar formation times in pure stellar disks. The times run from a few hundred million years to beyond the age of the universe in extreme cases.
arxiv-2510-13452:
Engstrøm's doctoral thesis, posted on arXiv in 2025, examines near-infrared hyperspectral imaging for food analysis. The thesis, from the University of Copenhagen with industry partner FOSS, runs four studies. Hyperspectral imaging records both pictures and detailed light spectra for each point. That mix lets models judge chemical content and visible traits together.

Across the studies, joint spatial-spectral analysis with convolutional networks beat purely spatial or purely spectral models for mixed traits. Adding a first layer for spectral folding sharply improved chemical predictions from images. For average chemical content, though, classic partial least squares modelling performed just as well. One study trained models on bulk average reference values plus many image patches. It classified uniform samples accurately and regressed varied ones well, after small corrections. Another study mapped fat content across pork bellies from bulk averages alone.
arxiv-2510-13652:
Qu and co-authors present EditCast3D, a pipeline that spreads a single edited image across a whole 3D scene. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles 3D editing, where foundation image models are powerful but costly and closed. Plugging them into older iterative editing loops is impractical at dataset scale. Editing each view separately also invites clashing interpretations of the prompt.

EditCast3D instead edits only the first frame with any image editing model. A video generation model then propagates that edit through the remaining views. Propagation alone leaves views too inconsistent for clean 3D reconstruction, though. A view selection step picks out consistent, reconstruction-friendly views for the final build. Reconstruction is feedforward, skipping expensive refinement passes. On common 3D editing datasets, the pipeline beat leading baselines on editing quality while staying highly efficient, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-13852:
Banyas, Sharma, Simmons, and Vispute benchmark whether language models give different demographics factually different answers. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces ConsistencyAI, an independent test built without any model provider's involvement. The same questions get asked while the prompt adopts one hundred different personas. If facts shift with the persona, consistency fails by definition.

Each model answers requests for five facts across fifteen topics, repeated across all personas. Responses become sentence embeddings, and cross-persona similarity yields a consistency score. Scores ranged from 0.9065 at the top to 0.7896 at the bottom across the nineteen models tested, with Grok-3 ranked most consistent overall, the authors report. Lightweight models clustered at the inconsistent end of the table. Topic mattered too: job market answers diverged most, while G7 leader facts held steadiest. Code and an interactive demo accompany the release.
arxiv-2510-13952:
William McClymont, Aaron Smith, and Sandro Tacchella present a major upgrade to COLT, a computer code that models the glowing gas in galaxies, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Nebular emission, light from ionized gas clouds, is a key probe of how galaxies grow, and new telescope data from JWST have made interpretation, not data collection, the bottleneck.

The update adds a thermal equilibrium solver that computes gas temperatures by balancing heating from starlight against many cooling processes, from atomic line emission to Compton scattering. A speed-based limit prevents unrealistic over-cooling in diffuse halo gas. Applied to a simulated nearby galaxy, the solver reduced excess lukewarm gas and resolved warm ionized and cold neutral phases more cleanly. Applied to high-redshift simulations, COLT reproduced observed emission-line ratios, supporting its use across cosmic time.
arxiv-2510-14152:
Gabriele Ilha and a collaboration test whether radio jets drive the outflows seen in quasars at cosmic noon, the era when galaxy growth peaked, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Active galactic nuclei, feeding black holes, push gas out of their galaxies. At low redshift, radio jets stir the interstellar gas and drive outflows. Whether the same holds two billion years after the Big Bang was unclear.

The study uses Very Large Array radio observations of three quasars with ionized outflows from the SUPER survey. The resolution matches infrared data. Two quasars showed extended radio structure. In one, the structure suggests a jet running from the nucleus to galaxy-wide scales. In all three, radio emission and ionized gas span comparable scales. Their orientations differ by less than thirty degrees where structure exists. The authors conclude radio jets could drive outflows at cosmic noon too.
arxiv-2510-14652:
Chen and colleagues report, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a case of particles being accelerated locally inside a structure formed when solar eruptions collide. On March 23, 2024, two eruptions left the same active region of the Sun in succession. The faster one's shock overtook the earlier eruption and trapped it in the sheath ahead of the main body, forming what the authors call an ICME-in-sheath structure.

Using data from the Solar Orbiter and Wind spacecraft, the team found both electrons and ions accelerated inside the trapped region. Suprathermal electrons were enhanced at its boundary, where strong flow shear and magnetic changes suggest local acceleration. Energetic electrons showed a long-lasting enhancement with a spectrum much like that in the main eruption, hinting at a shared solar origin. Heavy ion ratios inside the structure resembled flare particles, suggesting remnants of flares stayed confined within it.
arxiv-2510-14852:
Danawe and Tol design, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a material that treats sound-like elastic waves differently depending on which way they travel. Their metamaterial is a layered piezoelectric structure converting strain to electric fields and back. With inversion symmetry broken, the fields couple to motion, an electro-momentum effect akin to Willis coupling. Shunt circuits on the layers, with a resistor, an inductor, and strain-proportional feedback, let the team tune stiffness and damping by frequency.

Dynamic homogenization exposes the material's effective behavior, including both couplings. The design hosts exceptional points, settings where scattering modes merge and the wave response becomes extremely lopsided. Near them, the material achieves zero reflection and perfect absorption in one direction at once: waves from one side are completely absorbed, while waves from the other side are totally reflected. The authors offer it as a compact, reconfigurable platform for directional wave control.
arxiv-2510-15052:
Zimmermann, Hashemi, Busch, Blanco-Redondo, and Perez-Leija introduce, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a photonic filter built on loss itself. In science and engineering, dissipation is routinely used to turn incoherent waves into a pure coherent output. Topological states, robust modes protected by a material's global structure, had not been given the same treatment. The authors apply the filtering principle to them.

Their non-Hermitian filter, non-Hermitian because it includes gain and loss, isolates one desired state from an input. It works regardless of the input's coherence properties: feed it a messy mixture and the chosen state emerges. The design carves out a dissipation-free topological subspace. Inside it, the wanted states live untouched by the loss that removes everything else. Their topological protection is enhanced there. The authors present the filter as a simple tool for state selection, aimed at integrated photonics.
arxiv-2510-15552:
Jinliang Liu builds a retrieval system that answers questions needing several chained facts, in this solo 2025 arXiv paper. Language models hallucinate and stumble on such multi-hop questions, so grounding them in a knowledge graph helps. Existing graph retrieval, though, leans on flat embeddings and wanders down noisy paths, which muddies the evidence the model receives.

His framework, ParallaxRAG, splits both the query and the graph's facts into multiple views before matching them. The design leans on an observation about attention heads inside the model. Different heads specialize in different relation types at different reasoning stages, effectively covering different hops of the chain. Enforcing diversity among the starting points while pruning weakly related paths yields cleaner subgraphs for the model to reason over. On two standard multi-hop benchmarks, WebQSP and CWQ, the system reached competitive retrieval and answer accuracy.
arxiv-2511-00652:
Ali Khalid and six co-authors compress self-driving car data by exploiting nostalgia: cars drive the same streets every day. A vehicle can generate terabytes of sensor data daily, much of it LiDAR point clouds headed for cloud storage and later training or forensics. Their system, DejaView, finds redundancy not just between neighboring frames but across days and months of repeated routes.

The core is a diff operation that stores each point cloud compactly as a delta against 3D data captured in the past. On two months of LiDAR data, the end-to-end system compressed point clouds by a factor of two hundred ten, with reconstruction error of only fifteen centimeters. Network and storage bills shrink accordingly, a reminder that the best compression looks backward.
arxiv-2511-00852:
Lajos Diosi writes a short comment disputing a recent claim in Nature by Aziz and Howl. The claim held that classical, unquantized gravity can entangle quantized matter when matter is described by quantum field theory. Diosi argues the claim fails, in a note whose arguments were corrected to work in the Heisenberg picture.

His objection is direct. The earlier result was derived about, in the interaction picture, and he shows it conflicts with an exact, non-perturbative derivation that rules the claimed entanglement out from the start. The note is brief, but it bears on a live question: whether gravity must itself be quantum to create entanglement between masses.
arxiv-2511-00952:
Marijn van Dijk, Harrison Nicholls, and Tim Lichtenberg model the earliest Earth, just after the giant impact that formed the Moon. The planet then had a global magma ocean under a thick, volatile rich atmosphere. Earlier studies used idealized, oxidizing chemistry and often left out heating from tides raised by the young Moon.

Using the PROTEUS simulation framework, they vary tidal power, interior chemistry, and volatile content. The feedback between tidal heating and greenhouse forcing stretches magma ocean lifetimes from about thirty million years to about five hundred million. Long epochs of global radiative balance commonly appear in between. Under oxidizing conditions, late water vapor release strengthens the greenhouse effect, keeping melt and heating alive longer.
arxiv-2511-01052:
Yeawon Lee, Christopher Yang, Chia-Hsuan Chang, and Grace Lu-Yao use large language models to read cancer stage information out of free text pathology reports. Staging drives prognosis and treatment, but extracting the pathologic TNM stage from unstructured reports usually needs large hand labeled data sets, which limits how far older methods scale.

They test two knowledge elicitation methods. One prompts the model repeatedly to induce staging rules from unlabeled reports, keeping them in long term memory. The other extracts rules from guidelines in one pass, then applies them without repeated retrieval. On breast cancer reports from the TCGA collection, the memory based method beat the retrieval based one under zero shot chain of thought prompting, and both aim at interpretable, rule based staging.
arxiv-2511-01352:
Lucie Flek and colleagues present MiniFool, an adversarial attack algorithm built for the classifiers particle physics actually uses. Neural networks in particle and astroparticle physics sort events into classes, and knowing how easily small, physically plausible changes flip a decision is a robustness question with real stakes.

MiniFool minimizes a cost function combining a chi squared style test statistic, which scores how likely a perturbation is given the experimental uncertainties, with the deviation from the attacker's target score. The method began with the search for astrophysical tau neutrinos at IceCube. The paper also applies it to handwritten digit images and to open data from the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. Scaling the attack by the uncertainty level quantifies how robust each classification is.
arxiv-2511-01952:
Jinhua Yin and seven colleagues devise the first purely black-box membership inference attack on large vision-language models. Such attacks test whether a specific item was in a model's training data, a live privacy question for models trained on vast scraped corpora. Earlier attacks needed internal likelihoods, which mainstream models do not expose; only generated text comes out.

Their method probes the model's memory of private semantic details embedded in a suspect image, details unlikely to be inferable from general world knowledge, and calibrates the probe with prior knowledge. Across four vision-language models and three datasets, the attack identified training data effectively using outputs alone, performing comparably to gray-box and white-box methods that peek inside. Further analysis probes its robustness against adversarial manipulation by a defensive model owner.
arxiv-2511-02452:
Junghee Pyeon, Davide Cacciarelli, and Kamran Paynabar hunt for a specific kind of trouble in industrial prediction models. The trouble is local concept drift, where the relationship between inputs and outputs quietly changes in one region. Labels, the ground truth needed to notice, are scarce and expensive. Most drift detectors assume a global shift and plentiful supervision, which makes them poor fits for regression problems with patchy, local change and a tight labelling budget.

Their adaptive sampling framework splits effort between exploring residuals for signs of drift and exploiting the regions already suspected. Meanwhile, an exponentially weighted moving average monitor watches the stream for change. The design aims to spend labels where they teach the most. On synthetic benchmarks and a case study from electricity markets, the method outperformed alternatives on both label efficiency and detection accuracy, according to the authors.
arxiv-2511-02552:
Marco Mattuschka, Daniel Walter, Max von Danwitz, and Alexander Popp build the math for locating a contamination source from a handful of sensors, fast enough to guide an escape. Their model predicts how an airborne contaminant spreads by advection and diffusion, and the inverse problem works backwards from scarce readings to the release. Because the data underdetermine the answer, the unknown sources are modelled as a spread over space and found with variational regularisation that favours sparse solutions.

A problem-specific method alternates between greedily moving candidate points and tuning their intensities, approximating the sparse minimiser efficiently. Two- and three-dimensional tests, with instant and continuous releases, beat methods based on usual squared-error regularisation. A final test imports real building geometry from OpenStreetMap, showing the method in the kind of cluttered domain where protection decisions are actually made.
arxiv-2511-02652:
Vision transformers chop each image into fixed square patches, ignoring what the picture shows. Marius Aasan and four colleagues offer a smarter way to cut up images in a 2025 paper. Their tokenizer adapts to image content down to single pixels, yet it can still slot into existing models, even ones already trained.

The method picks its splits by a layered model selection rule guided by information criteria. It performs well both at labeling whole images and at dense tasks that mark each pixel. It can even turn raster pictures into vector shapes right away. For teams with trained models on hand, the design promises finer image handling without starting training from scratch.
arxiv-2511-02752:
Amit Misra and four colleagues ask whether weak language support slows the spread of AI in some countries. Frontier language models perform poorly on low-resource languages because training data is scarce. In a 2025 paper, the team tests whether that gap cuts the value people get from AI and so holds back adoption.

Using a weighted regression, they separate the language effect from income, education, and other social factors. Countries whose main languages are low-resource had a share of AI users about 20 percent lower than their baseline would suggest. The authors read this as proof that language access is a real, independent barrier. Closing it, they argue, is part of making AI growth fair across the world.
arxiv-2511-03152:
Srishti Yadav, Jasmina Gajcin, Erik Miehling, and Elizabeth Daly ask whose view of risk should count when an AI system is judged. A doctor, a patient, and a regulator may rate the same medical AI very differently. Their 2025 framework uses language models as judges grounded in each stakeholder's stance, drawing on the Risk Atlas Nexus and an explanation method called GloVE to produce readable, stakeholder-specific policies.

Three real cases, medical AI, self-driving cars, and fraud detection, show the method at work. An interactive visualization then lays out where and why stakeholder views clash.
