The team finds that perspective strongly shapes both risk ratings and conflict patterns. Their pitch is governance-facing: risk tools should show their disagreements, not average them away.
arxiv-2511-03252:
Taiyo Fukai, Keisuke Kawata, Mizuki Komura, and Takahiro Toriyabe measure how far apart the pay men and women ask for is in public job referral records. Large official data let them see wish wages across a wide pay range, not just among top earners. They split the gap by age, by the region people hope to work in, and by the job people hope to get.

Choice of occupation explained the largest share among the three factors studied. Still, the part left unexplained by all three was larger than any single factor's share. Extra checks across groups and assumptions probed that leftover gap further. The study shows that sorting into different jobs drives much of the ask gap, while a sizable share remains beyond those measures.
arxiv-2511-03452:
Jordan Roulleau-Pasdeloup finds an explicit spending rule for households that save and borrow under a hard limit. The classic problem, with income shocks and wealth earning a fixed interest rate, has long lacked a global closed-form answer. In continuous time, the zero-rate case yields an exact rule built on the Lambert W function.

For small positive rates, a closed-form approximation holds across the whole wealth range. From those rules come exact expressions for how spending responds to assets and to lasting income. The cross effect between the two is strictly positive, so each response strengthens the other. Explicit rules let economists check numerical solvers and read household behavior directly off a formula.
arxiv-2511-03552:
Jonathan R Dunkley asks whether Fisher information is merely able to mimic quantum mechanics or actually forced by basic physical demands. The classic Madelung picture rewrites quantum motion as flow of a density with a phase. Dunkley starts from modest axioms: locality, probability conservation, symmetry under shifts and rotations, reversibility, and convex regularity.

Inside the broad class those axioms allow, the bracket linking density and phase is pinned to the canonical one. A gauge-aware change of variables then merges density and phase into one complex field. Only one density functional survives the filters to yield a reversible completion, the familiar quantum form. The result strengthens the case that quantum structure follows from information geometry plus plain physical principles.
arxiv-2511-20152:
Hadzic, Thaler, Bogensperger, Joham, and Urschler restore damaged images with a mask-guided flow method. Their 2025 paper introduces Restora-Flow for image restoration. Flow matching generates images faster than diffusion models. Degraded photos need repair that respects surviving pixels. Masks mark exactly which regions are damaged or missing.

Restora-Flow needs no training of its own. A degradation mask steers the flow sampling process. Trajectory correction enforces consistency with the degraded input. The sampler keeps steering back toward measured data. Inpainting, super-resolution, and denoising tasks were tested. Both natural photos and medical images served as data. Perceptual quality beat diffusion and flow baselines. Processing time dropped compared with those rivals too. No extra hyperparameters beyond standard step counts appear. Over-smoothed results, a common flaw, were avoided. The method treats restoration as a guided generation problem. Non-mask degradations are the next target.
arxiv-2511-20352:
Chatterjee, Muntaha, Blondel, and colleagues simulate fission gas bubbling inside nuclear fuel. Their 2025 paper models UO2 microstructure in three dimensions. Reactor fuel pellets trap xenon and krypton gases. Bubbles swell the fuel and eventually leak gas out. Grain boundaries host the intergranular bubble networks.

A hybrid code couples cluster dynamics with phase-field modeling. Xolotl handles atoms inside grains; MARMOT moves the boundaries. Ten-grain and hundred-grain structures were simulated for months. Temperatures of 1200 and 1600 kelvin were compared. At the lower temperature almost nothing evolves. At 1600 kelvin bubbles flatten and merge into networks. Grain boundaries migrate until bubbles pin them. Fewer starting bubbles means more boundary sweeping. Gas arrival at interfaces then spikes transiently. Free surfaces drain nearby bubbles into denuded zones. Boundary coverage saturates below fifty percent. Results match White's classic coalescence trend. Engineering release models gain mechanistic grounding.
arxiv-2511-20652:
Karen Jia-Hui Li and colleagues report in 2025 on the first randomised controlled trial, the gold-standard test in medicine, of large language models used for nutrition advice. Do features that shine in lab tests still help when real people use a diet chatbot every day? The team added two features to a rule-based chatbot: one rephrased messages for variety, and one gave nutritional counselling from a fine-tuned model.

Inside the seven-week trial, 81 participants used three versions of the chatbot, from the plain rule-based system up to the full version carrying both new features. The researchers tracked what people ate, their emotional well-being, and how often they opened the chatbot. The added features scored well in lab checks but brought no consistent gains in the real trial. The authors say health chatbots should be tested with real users before anyone trusts lab results alone.
arxiv-2511-20752:
Daniel A. Boyea, James W. Johnson, and David H. Weinberg trace in 2025 where the Milky Way's carbon was forged. Carbon is the Universe's second most abundant metal, yet its sources are disputed. Massive stars explode as core-collapse supernovae, while ageing giant-branch stars shed carbon gently, and astronomers argue over the split. The team ran chemical evolution models against abundances for 154 subgiant stars from the APOGEE survey.

The data show the carbon to magnesium ratio rising gently with metallicity, yet giant-branch production should fall as metallicity climbs. Reconciling the two forces one conclusion: supernova yields must rise with metallicity, matching models of massive stars that include rotation. A second trend pins the giant branch share of carbon at solar metallicity to between 10 and 40 percent. Shifting giant branch yields toward longer lived, lower mass stars improved the fit, hinting that stellar predictions or the iron production rate need revision.
arxiv-2511-20852:
Ava K. Tse, Olivia M. Markowich, and Trung V. Phan settle in 2025 which force laws make a spherical shell impersonate a point mass. Newton's shell theorem says a uniform shell attracts outsiders as if its mass sat at the centre, for the inverse-square law and few relatives. Gurzadyan's theorem, from 1985, characterised all such potentials in flat three-dimensional space. Tse and colleagues generalise the classification.

Working on constant-curvature spaces, sphere, Euclidean, and hyperbolic, in any dimension, and on topologies like the torus, they tie the spherical property to spherical means and their Euler-Poisson-Darboux identity. Any potential whose shell average obeys it yields the full family of laws. Their results reproduce the known flat-space findings and collapse to Gurzadyan's theorem when the shell's rescaling factor is one. The shell trick is thus no curiosity of flat three dimensions, but a feature of curved geometries.
arxiv-2511-21052:
P. Djorwé and colleagues propose in 2025 a scheme for weaving several entangled links inside an optomechanical device, two coupled mechanical resonators driven by one polarised light field. A polariser splits the drive into vertical and horizontal modes. Left alone, the system hides a dark mode, a combination that decouples from the light and blocks entanglement. Twisting the polarisation angle breaks that dark mode and opens multiple paths of bipartite entanglement between light and mechanics.

Switching on phonon hopping between the resonators adds a second control knob, the coupling's modulation phase. Breaking the dark mode with both knobs yields bipartite and tripartite entanglement together. At a fine-tuned angle of pi over 4, the device produces twin entangled states, degenerate pairs prized for quantum networks. Entanglement in the broken regime survives heat far better, up to two orders of magnitude more robust against thermal fluctuations than in the unbroken regime.
arxiv-2511-21152:
Computational chemists Radu Talmazan and Christophe Chipot argue in 2025 that chemical reactions should be mapped as moving processes, not frozen paths. Static calculations trace one route over an energy landscape at zero temperature, yet real reactions wobble, branch, and switch channels. Their workflow pairs a neural network trained to find the committor, the point of no return in a reaction, with a machine-learned atomic potential built at high accuracy.

Talmazan and Chipot test the method on two reactions. A nucleophilic substitution, the SNAr reaction, proves concerted, meaning it runs in one step, and its true barrier comes out lower than static estimates suggested. The isomerization of protonated isobutanol reveals three competing channels with similar barriers: the known concerted route plus two stepwise paths, carried by water and methyl transfer, that pass through previously undescribed intermediates. Barrier heights matched high-level quantum benchmarks closely.
arxiv-2511-21352:
Janis Geise, Sebastian Spinner, Richard Semaan, and Andre Weiner tackle a data deluge in computational fluid dynamics in 2025. Modern flow simulations produce so much volume data that storing and analyzing it, not computing it, becomes the bottleneck. Their improved Sparse Spatial Sampling algorithm shrinks time-dependent simulation data by building one fixed octree grid, a nested set of boxes refined only where a user-chosen metric says the flow matters.

Geise and his coauthors test the method on three demanding cases: transonic flow past tandem airfoils, turbulent flow around a circular cylinder, and flow over an aircraft half-model at high speed. The sampling cut mesh cell counts by 35 to 98 percent across the cases. A singular value check confirmed negligible information loss, with the dominant flow dynamics preserved. Many datasets became light enough to post-process on a local workstation instead of a supercomputer.
arxiv-2511-21552:
Roi Bar-Zur, Aviv Tamar, and Ittay Eyal redesign blockchain rules to starve selfish miners of profit, in 2025. Selfish mining, secretly hoarding blocks to outpace honest miners, gets worse under adverse conditions. Those include network rushing advantages, block rewards that vary with content, called miner extractable value, and petty miners who accept bribes. The previous best defense, Colordag, ignored those conditions and was proven secure only at impractical latency.

Their protocol, MAD-DAG, rests on a mutual-assured-destruction ledger rule: when two equal-length chains compete, both chains' contents are discarded, destroying the selfish miner's prize. Bar-Zur and his coauthors model a rational attacker as a Markov decision process, with reward rules deliberately generous to the attacker, yielding honest upper bounds on attack profit. Under bribery and high reward variability, MAD-DAG's security threshold runs from 11 to 31 percent of mining power, where Colordag and Bitcoin collapse to zero.
arxiv-2511-21852:
Sahu and colleagues study how to attach algebra to regions of spacetime picked out by gravity. In holography, an entanglement wedge is the bulk region tied to part of a boundary system. Bousso and Penington recently extended the idea to general spacetimes, far beyond the best-studied cases. The team asks what algebraic structure, if any, sits behind each such wedge.

They postulate a map that assigns an algebra to every generalized wedge. The map is chosen so that basic facts about wedges read as natural facts about algebras. They also propose a generalized Ryu-Takayanagi formula. It links the gravitational entropy of a wedge to an entropy computed inside its algebra. If the link holds, key entropy rules for wedges would follow from standard entropy rules for algebras. Those rules include monotonicity and strong subadditivity, two checks any sound theory must pass.
arxiv-2511-22252:
Fromion, Robert, and Zaherddine, applied probabilists, analyze how a cell rations its protein-making machinery when food runs short. Their chemical reaction network model has three species types that assemble into working complexes, consume an incoming resource flow, and emit product. The regulation under study sequesters one species whenever the resource flow drops, preventing idle complexes from piling up. The biology behind it is the stringent response, the emergency program bacteria use to survive starvation, a key gene-expression control.

Scaling analysis uncovers three asymptotic regimes, each with an averaging principle making fast dynamics look like infinite-server queues. One regime, optimal sequestration, had apparently never been identified: resource inflow is low, yet the network's state stays acceptable in unused macromolecules, demonstrating the mechanism's remarkable efficiency. The proofs combine coupling arguments, path estimates, and stability of planar dynamical systems.
arxiv-2511-22552:
Baumeler, Tselentis, and Wolf extend Bell-style tests from separated parties to parties who can communicate. Bell inequalities bound what non-communicating observers can achieve. The authors derive analogous bounds for any number of communicating parties whose signalling is restricted by an assumed causal structure, covering fixed, definite, and bi-causal order. Each bound is a graphical game: a directed graph over the parties is drawn, an edge is chosen at random, and the parties must communicate along it.

Remarkably, all the derived inequalities are simple. For definite causal order, every game is specified by a graph family they call kefalopoda digraphs. Correlations satisfying all these inequalities are dubbed weakly causal. Deciding whether given correlations are weakly causal takes only polynomial time in the number of parties, making the causal test computationally practical rather than a search over all possible orders.
arxiv-2511-22652:
Metni and many co-authors review how generative machine learning is changing the hunt for new crystals. Materials discovery once ran on experiments, theory, and simulation. Data-driven methods now let researchers not just screen known candidates but generate entirely new crystal structures. The review surveys how crystals are represented for such models, catalogues the generative architectures used for structure prediction and de novo design, and weighs each approach's strengths and limitations.

Beyond the models, the authors give experimentalists practical guidance: how to evaluate generated structures, and which software tools to adopt. Emerging frontiers get their own treatment, including modelling disorder and defects, integrating generation with advanced characterisation, and building synthetic feasibility, whether a proposed crystal can actually be made, in as a constraint. The review addresses two audiences, experimental scientists choosing models and machine learning specialists learning what makes inverse materials design different.
arxiv-2511-22852:
Pala and a large collaboration present NuclearConfectionery, open-source software simulating atomic nuclei colliding at near light speed. Relativistic heavy-ion collisions create quark-gluon plasma, and modelling them end to end, from impact through hydrodynamic expansion to final hadrons, takes a chain of specialised codes. The core is ccake 2.0, a smoothed-particle hydrodynamics solver substantially upgraded for this release.

The solver evolves energy, momentum, and three conserved charges together, using a four-dimensional equation of state, spanning energies from RHIC's Beam Energy Scan to the LHC. A particlization module enforces global charge conservation on the freeze-out surface before handing particles to a hadronic afterburner; source terms couple jets into the fluid. Users can choose among three equations of motion, run on GPUs via Kokkos and Cabana, and validate against benchmarks including BSQ Gubser flow.
arxiv-2511-23152:
Huh and Jeong supply the missing theory for HyperCube, a neural model that discovers symmetry groups and their unitary representations from raw data by factorizing an operator-valued tensor. Earlier work showed the model is biased toward groups, but not why. Their analysis splits its training objective into two parts, one regulating the scale of the factors and one penalizing directional misalignment between them.

On the special set where the misalignment penalty vanishes, they prove feasible solutions exist exclusively for group-like operations. The scale term pushes solutions toward full-rank unitary representations rather than the low-rank shortcuts typical of deep learning. Assuming their Collinearity Dominance Conjecture, which the evidence supports, the global minimum is achieved exactly by the unitary regular representation. Every non-group operation scores strictly worse, which formally quantifies, in effect, the model's pull toward associative group structure.
arxiv-2512-00152:
Confinement, the force that keeps quarks locked inside particles, remains hard to characterize from first principles. Pavel Popov and co-authors study simpler stand-in theories in a 2025 study of dihedral lattice gauge theories. These discrete models let theorists probe confinement with group theory and numerical analysis.

The authors show that the physical effects of confinement in these theories are closely tied to a central subgroup of the symmetry group. Their title points to color screening and gluelumps, states where color charge is shielded. Understanding such toy models guides work on real quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force. Dihedral groups are the symmetry groups of regular polygons, simple enough to compute with.
arxiv-2512-00552:
A language model can produce a correct answer with broken reasoning and still look competent. Subramanyam Sahoo and co-authors ask how smaller reasoning models pretend to reason with mathematical fidelity in 2025. Evaluation by answer accuracy alone can mask fundamental failures in logical computation.

Their diagnostic framework separates genuine reasoning from pattern matching along four axes: forward-backward consistency, transitivity coverage, counterfactual sensitivity, and perturbation robustness. A case study applies the framework to a small Qwen model. Such diagnostics matter because schools and businesses increasingly trust model reasoning that may only imitate the real thing. Four axes are harder to game than one accuracy number, which is the point. For schools that use such tools, the gain is a stern test. Right replies with false steps are caught, so trust is earned by the work, not by the score.
arxiv-2512-00752:
Shawn Li and a team from universities and Adobe Research study editing scientific charts with AI in a 2025 paper. Generative models edit photos impressively well. Charts look like images, but they are not just arrangements of pixels. A chart encodes structured data under a set of drawing rules, called a graphical grammar.

Changing a bar or a label without touching the data behind it breaks that link. The authors lay out the challenges that follow from this mismatch. Tools that edit charts must respect the data and grammar, not just the pixels. Their analysis points toward chart editors that keep numbers honest.
arxiv-2512-00952:
Audrius Alkauskas, Chris Van de Walle, Lukas Razinkovas, and Ronald Ulbricht study diamond defects in a 2025 paper. Nitrogen-vacancy centers are flaws in diamond where a nitrogen atom sits beside a missing carbon. They serve as quantum sensors and qubits, and their charge state decides how well they work.

Charge states can flip as electrons tunnel in and out, so ensembles of centers drift toward some balance over time. The authors examine that equilibration and the role of electron tunneling in reaching it. The lessons reach beyond diamond, to defects and impurities in wide-bandgap materials generally. Stable charge means steadier quantum devices.
arxiv-2512-01352:
In-Jae Lee and co-authors build a way to box objects in three dimensions with no hand labels. Self-driving cars need those boxes for safety. Hand labels cost a lot, and cars must spot objects they were never taught. Most past tools box all objects the same way.

Past tools also miss the state of each object, like open or shut. They need many rounds of self-training to clean up boxes. The new tool, OpenBox, aims for sharp boxes in one pass. It takes the state of each object into account. Cleaner boxes cut cost and risk for car firms.
arxiv-2512-02052:
Gauge theories, including Yang-Mills theory and general relativity, are the backbone of modern physics, and their roots lie in symmetry. B. Sazdović's 2025 article rebuilds that connection, starting from Poincaré invariance, the symmetry of flat spacetime, and two foundational tools from earlier work.

One tool is a set of principle field equations that yield the motion of free fields with any spin and helicity. The other is the Fock-Ivanenko covariant derivative, which handles how fields change under local transformations. From these ingredients the article derives the gauge theories themselves, showing familiar structures growing out of symmetry principles rather than being imposed by hand.
arxiv-2512-02252:
In a radio network with no central control, nodes need short labels so messages can be gathered and broadcast efficiently. Adam Gańczorz and Tomasz Jurdziński study in 2025 two basic tasks: k-broadcasting, spreading messages from several sources to everyone, and k-gathering, collecting messages at one sink.

They seek labeling schemes of optimal length, where the labels assigned to nodes carry the routing information, plus fast algorithms that use them. In k-broadcasting, messages from the sources must reach all nodes; in k-gathering, they converge on a designated sink. Short labels and quick protocols are precious in radio networks, where spectrum and energy are both scarce.
arxiv-2512-02952:
Md Sohag Mia and Muhammad Abdullah Adnan estimate the layout of any room with one transformer model. Indoor layout estimation recovers walls, floors, and structure from an image. Their Layout Anything adapts the universal segmentation design of OneFormer to geometric structure prediction.

Two additions tailor the model: topology aware data augmentation that respects Manhattan world structure, and differentiable geometric losses. Those losses enforce planar consistency and sharp boundaries during training. One universal model for all rooms could serve renovation apps, robot navigation, and virtual staging tools. One tool for all rooms beats ten tools for ten room types. That edge counts when a crew must scan a whole block of flats in one day of work.
arxiv-2512-03052:
Zeqiang Lai and seven co-authors present LATTICE, a framework for high fidelity 3D generation that can scale. Two dimensional image synthesis rides on fixed grids and mature transformer designs. Three dimensional generation must predict spatial structure and detailed surfaces from scratch, a harder joint problem.

That gap keeps 3D output behind 2D in quality and scale. LATTICE aims to close it, making detailed 3D assets cheap to produce in volume. Democratized 3D generation would serve games, film, shopping, and design, where custom models are now slow and costly to commission. Scale with grade is the pair that counts. One with no mate is a demo, but the pair at once is a trade that shops can build a line on.
arxiv-2512-03352:
Some four-manifolds carry spheres with special geometric traits. Vsevolod Shevchishin and Gleb Smirnov prove a result about them in this 2025 work. They study closed, oriented four-manifolds with a bounded positive index.

Inside such a manifold sit disjoint embedded spheres of a stated type. The authors prove a metric exists where each sphere's dual is an anti-self-dual harmonic form. Their result extends an earlier one for a different sphere type. Such theorems link topology and geometry in four dimensions, a famously hard area. Anti-self-dual forms link to instantons, tying the result to gauge theory as well.
arxiv-2512-03452:
Chemotaxis systems model how cells chase chemical signals. Jingyuan Hu, Zhongjian Wang, Jack Xin, and Zhiwen Zhang present a fast simulation method in this 2025 work. They target the three-dimensional Keller-Segel system, a classic chemotaxis model.

Their particle-field method blends particle dynamics with spectral field solvers. Particle-in-cell acceleration and fast Fourier transforms keep it efficient. They also give error analysis for the method. Fast, accurate tools help model bacterial colonies, immune cells, and other systems that move toward signals. Error analysis matters as much as speed, since biologists must trust the simulated patterns.
arxiv-2512-03552:
Two star clusters travel together through the Galaxy. D. Bisht and a large team analyze the pair NGC 146 and King 14 in this 2025 work. They ask whether the pair is bound together or merely co-moving.

Using data from Gaia, Pan-STARRS, WISE, and TESS, they study light, motion, and dynamics. They identify hundreds of high-probability members for each cluster. Their evidence points to a co-moving but unbound pair, as the title states. Such pairs reveal how clusters form and dissolve over time. Member counts in the hundreds give the pair's shared motion a firm statistical base, well beyond earlier small-sample claims about the system.
arxiv-2512-03852:
Rain, snow, and fog degrade the traffic camera images that intelligent transport systems depend on. Liwen Pan and colleagues attack that restoration problem in a 2025 computer vision preprint. Most existing methods model only the spatial layout of pixels, they note, while ignoring frequency information. Their framework, Frequency-Aware Mamba, brings frequency guidance into a sequence model built for long-range dependencies.

Two components do the heavy lifting. A dual-branch extraction block scans the image adaptively in two-dimensional frequency space, adjusting its path to the texture of each sub-band. A prior-guided block then rebuilds fine detail by learning from wavelet-based high-frequency residuals. An adaptive scanning mechanism lets the Mamba architecture sweep different frequency subgraphs in turn. Extensive experiments, the authors report, show the design restores weather-damaged traffic images efficiently and with precise detail, outperforming approaches that stay in the spatial domain alone.
arxiv-2512-04052:
When the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, economic hardship pushed a generation of Russian physicists abroad in one of the century's great scientific migrations. Vladimir Shiltsev, himself part of that world, surveys the exodus in a 2025 history of physics article. Earlier emigration in the nineteen seventies and eighties was a trickle; the post-Cold War wave became a genuine brain drain.

Europe and the United States absorbed specialists in accelerator, nuclear, and high-energy physics, from seniors to fresh postdocs. Many emigres rose to lead major experiments and theory efforts. They matched or surpassed what they had achieved at home. Shiltsev weighs both sides: the damage to Russia's research infrastructure, and the diaspora's lasting contributions to global collaborations and discoveries. The article treats the migration as a defining feature of the field's modern era.
arxiv-2512-04452:
Xin Kai Lee, Ali Ramadhan, Andre Souza, and co-authors built NORi, a model of the ocean's top mixing layer that weds physics rules with neural networks. The boundary layer, stirred by wind and waves, drives how heat and gases pass between air and sea. Classic closures capture much of that churn through the Richardson number, which weighs buoyancy against shear. What they miss is entrainment, the gulp of deep water at the layer's base. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets that gap.

Neural ordinary differential equations learn the entrainment term while the physics closure handles the rest. Training used large-eddy simulations, scored on time-integrated outcomes rather than noisy instant fluxes. NORi conserves tracers by design and uses realistic water thermodynamics. In tests it predicted boundary layer behavior with strong accuracy. Better mixing models feed straight into weather and climate forecasts.
arxiv-2512-05052:
Xander Peetroons and a large team of co-authors report precise control of a single electron-spin qubit built in a factory-made silicon device. The quantum dot holding the electron was fabricated on an industrial wafer line of the kind used for ordinary chips, using a silicon-on-insulator wafer. Making qubits in such a process matters because it points toward building quantum hardware with the tools of mass production rather than one-off laboratory craft.

The team drives the spin with electron spin resonance and reaches a brisk operating rhythm while shielding the spin from the magnetic chatter of nearby silicon atoms. Tracking the qubit's frequency and correcting for drift stretches its useful coherence, and randomized testing puts the average accuracy of single-qubit operations above ninety-nine percent. The results show that factory-made silicon qubits can reach fidelities once reserved for bespoke devices.
arxiv-2512-05152:
Kun Wang, Donglin Di, Tonghua Su, and Lei Fan present EFDiT, a diffusion transformer tuned for fine-grained image generation. It makes pictures that differ in small details, like bird species or car models. Class-based generators handle categories well, but at fine-grained scale they tangle the meanings of parent and child classes and lose the features that tell classes apart. The result is images that look plausible yet miss the point.

The team's answer has three parts. A tiered embedder feeds the model information from both the broad class and the subclass, untangling the two. A sharpening stage, built from enhancement and degradation models, sharpens detail as features are formed. And an attention mechanism, called ProAttention, keeps the transformer affordable. On benchmarks the method beats state-of-the-art fine-tuning approaches, offering a route to detailed, controllable generation in domains where differences carry the meaning.
arxiv-2512-05252:
Simone Betteti and four co-authors rebuild the theory of neural network stability for circuits that mix excitation and inhibition. Energy-based models explain neural computation well, but they assume symmetric links — a premise real excitatory-inhibitory networks violate, since one neuron's push is not matched in kind. Without symmetry, the energy landscape that held the theory up is gone, leaving such dynamics adrift.

The authors extend the energy framework to asymmetric firing-rate networks and uncover a game at the core: each neuron behaves like an agent trimming its own energy. Solid stability results from network theory let them study how activity is kept in balance in excitatory-inhibitory circuits. Going back to models — Wilson-Cowan dynamics and lateral inhibition — they show how cortical columns built from inhibition microcircuits can act as contrast enhancers, sharpening differences around them. The work bridges energy and game views of the brain.
arxiv-2512-05752:
Buyan Li and Jie Xiao continue a set of notes recasting classical Lie theory through root categories. Chevalley groups are the group counterparts of semisimple Lie algebras, built uniformly from root data. The authors use root categories to define the compact real forms of complex semisimple Lie algebras. They also define their maximal compact subgroups.

The notes then bring in a second machine: Lusztig's modified quantum group and its canonical basis. From that side come the reductive group and its coordinate ring, including its tensor product decomposition. By combining the two structures, the authors show how the classical theory of compact Lie groups can be recovered in full. In particular, the Peter-Weyl and Plancherel theorems both reappear. The value is unification: old pillars of representation theory stand up again inside a modern, categorical frame.
arxiv-2512-05952: Mark Powell's paper is a short result in four dimensional topology. Its objects are spanning discs: collections of discs in the four sphere, attached along the trivial 2-link, two unlinked rings. Two such collections can look really different. Powell proves that the gap is an effect of dimension. Pushed into five dimensions, any two collections become smoothly isotopic, each deforming into the other with the boundary fixed. Results like this map where the strangeness of dimension four begins.
arxiv-2512-06152:
Po-Jui Chen and Piers Coleman explain a ghost pattern seen in a superconducting flake: pairs that ripple. Microscopy recently found pair density modulation in such flakes, a state bulk crystals do not show. Landau theory is the tool. The modulation is a hybrid of two order parameters with opposite parities.

At the surface, broken glide symmetry lets nematic order stabilize the state. Opposite parities favor site based pairing, pointing at Hund's coupling. A magnetic field should strengthen the modulation, then bring a reentrant triplet phase. A surface ripple carries evidence about the whole family.
arxiv-2512-06252:
Homayoon Farrahi and Rupam Mahmood ask what happens when a learning agent never gets a reset. In most training setups, a robot task is cut into short episodes, and the scene is set back to a clean start again and again. Real machines get no such favors, so skills learned with resets may fail to carry over.

The authors adapt a well known learning method, Soft Actor Critic, so it can keep learning in one long run. With small changes to the reward, the long run version matched or beat the episode version on test tasks. One task, though, exposed a snag: without resets of the robot body, the agent explored too little and learned slowly or not at all. Adding ways to spur wider search helped on more tasks, even a real robot vision task. The study maps what resets quietly do for learning.
arxiv-2512-06752:
Chang Liu and five co authors give protein structure networks a sense of scale. Proteins work through hierarchy: small folds join into domains, and distant parts sway each other through long range effects. Standard geometric networks pass messages between neighboring atoms, which traps them at the local scale and misses that hierarchy. The authors argue the architecture itself should mirror the biology.

Their Geometric Graph U-Nets coarsen the protein graph step by step, learn at each scale, then refine back down, like a U-Net for graphs. They prove this design can express patterns that standard geometric networks cannot. On the task of classifying protein folds, the U-Nets beat both invariant and equivariant rivals by a clear margin, catching the global shapes that define a fold. The work offers a principled base for learning the multi scale structure of biomolecules.
arxiv-2512-06852:
Manideep Reddy Chinthareddy addresses a storage headache in managed cloud databases that cap the size of any single stored item. Services such as DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Firestore all impose such caps, yet many applications must keep larger objects close at hand across several regions. The usual fix stores the big object elsewhere and leaves a pointer behind. That split, Chinthareddy argues, invites delays and race problems when regions update at once.

The proposed pattern instead chops each large object into ordered pieces that live inside the database itself, beside its descriptive data. A working version built on DynamoDB global tables anchors the design. Evidence from a live production system, handling heavy hourly traffic, shows the pattern removes cross-system lag risks. For objects of about a megabyte, the slowest regional updates also reached consistency faster, since data and metadata now travel together.
arxiv-2512-06952:
Mirco A Mannucci and Corey Thuro build a type system that certifies, before a program runs, how much it will cost. Running time, memory, blockchain gas, and other measures all fit one scheme: each term in a typed program carries a bound drawn from an abstract ladder of resources. A graded modality, a marker that tracks how values may be used, comes with laws that keep the accounting honest.

Their central theorem covers simple typed programs without recursion. If a finished term is assigned a bound under a given budget, its true running cost provably stays within that bound. The authors also build a model of the system from syntax itself, inside a standard mathematical universe, and show it is the canonical one. A worked example follows binary search written in the Lean proof assistant, with the bound proofs kept separate from the native recursion.
arxiv-2512-07152:
Brian Collier, Jérémy Toulisse, and Richard Wentworth build a joint arena for Higgs bundles, objects that bundle geometry and field data on a curved surface. Usually the surface is held fixed; here its shape is allowed to wander through its deformation space at the same time. The resulting joint moduli space carries rich structure and respects the surface's large-scale symmetries, the mapping class group that reshuffles the surface without tearing it.

Four characters turn out to be secretly linked: a foliation that tracks deformations keeping a certain monodromy fixed. A natural pairing descended from a classic symplectic form, a holomorphic lift of motions in the deformation space, and an energy function for special maps between spaces.
arxiv-2512-07452:
Clarisse Bardiot and seven co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on theatre history and language models. Heritage collections hold vast stacks of theatre programmes. Their tangled layouts and thin records leave them hard to search or study at scale.

The team lays out a workflow that turns such programmes into structured data. Vision-language models first read and transcribe both born-digital and scanned pages. Their extraction proves highly accurate in the team's tests. A reasoning model, trained with rewards for form and meaning, then adds semantic labels. It writes the results as linked data that fits existing knowledge graphs. A custom Linked Art extension holds the structure together. Their test case is the programme archive of the Festival d'Avignon. The work points toward theatre history that computers can query and explain.
arxiv-2512-07852:
Erhan Güler and Magdalena Toda wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on minimal surfaces in four dimensions. A minimal surface is one that cannot shrink its area locally, like a soap film. The Henneberg surface is a classic example of the family, with only one side in effect.

The authors build a higher-order clan of Henneberg-type surfaces. Their tool is a generalized form of the Weierstrass-Enneper representation in four-dimensional space. From it they derive concrete formulas for the whole family. The surfaces' normal vector fields and Gauss curvature are worked out in detail. Two normal directions appear because the surfaces live in four dimensions. Projecting those forms down to three dimensions yields pictures. Those pictures reveal the shapes the formulas describe in the abstract. A second, simpler form of the representation also falls out of the work. A matching algebraic function rounds out the family.
arxiv-2512-07952:
Anna R. Gallazzi and Stefano Zibetti wrote this 2025 astronomy paper, with Arjen van der Wel and eleven co-authors. The LEGA-C survey gathered deep spectra of galaxies seen as they were long ago. Their starlight encodes when those galaxies formed their stars and with what chemistry.

The team measures ages and metal content for hundreds of massive galaxies. Absorption features and broad photometry are read against a library of model spectra. Bayesian inference turns those readings into light-weighted ages and metallicities. Systematic errors get careful mapping. Scaling relations then link age and metal content to galaxy mass. The downsizing pattern known nearby was already in place back then. Older, heavier systems sit above younger ones in a bimodal age split. Metal content rises steeply with mass, then flattens at the top end. Velocity dispersion sharpens the age transition more than mass alone does.
arxiv-2512-08152:
Tetsufumi Tanamoto and Keiji Ono, physicists in Japan, posted a simulation study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is reading out silicon spin qubits built into a gate all around transistor, a transistor whose gate wraps the channel on all sides. Their logical qubit is made of two physical qubits, and each spin arrangement reshapes the charge in the device.

Because the charge pattern changes the transistor electrostatics, the current through the device depends on the qubit state. The authors compute current voltage behavior for three dimensional models of the combined structure with industry style device simulation tools. They then run circuit simulations to test whether a standard CMOS readout circuit can amplify the weak qubit signals. With the applied voltage controlled dynamically in a well designed circuit, a conventional sense amplifier detected the readout effectively. The work links device physics to circuit design for future silicon quantum chips.
arxiv-2512-08252:
Sohom Bhattacharya and Subhabrata Sen, statisticians, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about causal inference when treatments interfere with each other. In network data, one person treatment can affect another outcome, breaking the assumptions of standard causal methods. They work in a chain graph framework developed earlier for exactly this setting.

Their first result is a warning: with no extra assumptions on the graph, even evaluating a treatment effect is computationally hard. They then add structure, either a dense interaction graph or random Gaussian interactions. In both cases the treatment effect settles to a clear limit as the population grows, and they give fast algorithms that estimate it consistently. The algorithms stay reliable under estimated parameters, and they work even in cold regimes where the usual sampling methods crawl. Dense graph results lean on regularity partitions, while the Gaussian case borrows from spin glass theory.
arxiv-2512-08652:
Ulrich Bauer and coauthors present faster methods to convert multi parameter filtrations into free chain complexes. In such filtrations, each simplex can enter in several steps along a staircase. Examples arise in degree Rips filtrations and in models of the multicover filtration, both used in topological data analysis.

The conversion, called a free resolution, keeps the same homology and is a first step for later processing. The first algorithm builds resolutions for path graphs and joins them with extra maps. It runs well in practice but can grow large in the worst case. The second algorithm keeps paths short, giving near linear time and output size. Tests show that precomputing a resolution speeds up finding a minimal presentation of homology. A curious finding is that a minimal complex can be larger to describe than a non minimal one.
arxiv-2512-08752:
Gowri Nair, Amlan Chakraborty, Luca Amendola, and Subinoy Das revisit limits on total neutrino mass using new data on cosmic expansion. Limits on neutrino mass depend strongly on what is assumed about dark energy, because the two effects can mimic each other. Recent analyses used a two parameter form for dark energy, which may be too narrow.

The authors use a more flexible four parameter form and run a full sampling analysis with data from Planck, the latest DESI baryon acoustic data, and supernova data. Adding the new DESI data tightens limits on the transition behavior of dark energy. The neutrino mass bound is looser than in the standard model, yet tighter than the bound found in the two parameter DESI analysis. Reconstructed dark energy history shows no strong sign of phantom crossing at mid redshift, and a modest improvement in fit over the standard model.
arxiv-2512-08852:
Hadi Salloum and coauthors present a faster way to run the Goemans Williamson random rounding method for binary tuning problems. That method is a classic method for quadratic problems with binary variables, but its standard loose form is a semidefinite program that is costly to solve. Reducing that cost while keeping solution quality is the central goal.

Instead of solving the full loose form, the authors use a difference of convex tuning method to roughly match its solution . The new trial vectors feed the usual random rounding step to produce high quality binary solutions. A further step minimizes expected cost directly over low rank matrix surfaces to improve quality. Benchmarks include real world problems such as inverse motion, and comparisons cover leading solvers including quantum inspired methods. The method shows strong closeness quality alongside large gains in work speed for large cases.
arxiv-2512-08952:
Filippo Cenacchi, Deborah Richards, and Longbing Cao present a simulation first approach to train humanoid robots for mental health screening interviews. Testing humanoids with real users is slow, wears the hardware, and limits iteration and diversity. Screening for depression and trauma conditions demands skill in timing, voice, backchannels, and attention to faces and speech.

The team turns interview data into hundreds of virtual patients in a game engine, with synchronized speech, gaze, face, and body pose, plus standard clinical questionnaires. A perception fusion policy loop decides what and when to speak, when to backchannel, and how to avoid interruptions, under a safety shield. Training uses counterfactual replay and an uncertainty aware turn manager. Among three controllers compared, a custom delayed deterministic method performs best, with near complete coverage and steadier pace. Results are simulation only, with the physical humanoid as the transfer target.
arxiv-2512-09452:
Kehao Zhang reports, for the STAR Collaboration, a search for strange dibaryons, hypothetical bound states of two baryons containing strange quarks. Dibaryons would reveal how the strong force works beyond ordinary hadrons. Strange dibaryons are especially prized because they probe the poorly known forces between hyperons and nucleons, and between two hyperons.

The analysis uses collisions of ruthenium and zirconium nuclei recorded by the STAR detector at an energy of two hundred giga-electronvolts per nucleon pair. Zhang measures correlation functions between protons and two kinds of strange baryons, the Xi and the Omega, which encode how strongly each pair attracts or repels. Fitting those correlations with the Lednicky-Lyuboshitz formalism yields scattering parameters. The paper discusses what those parameters imply for two candidate bound states, the H dibaryon and the N-Omega system, long-sought objects in the study of the strong interaction.
arxiv-2512-09752:
Michele Botti and Lorenzo Mascotto prove new trace inequalities for functions that are smooth only piece by piece. Trace inequalities link values inside a region to values on its boundary. They are basic tools for showing that partial differential equations with natural boundary conditions stay stable. They also help prove that numerical solutions move toward the exact solution as a mesh is refined or the accuracy is raised.

The setting matters because methods such as Crouzeix-Raviart and discontinuous Galerkin use functions that are only piecewise continuous, so standard trace inequalities do not apply. The new results hold on fairly general meshes built from many sided pieces, even with very small facets. They avoid finite dimensional shortcuts used in earlier proofs. They also cover a wider range of integrability settings, both the maximal cases and those below them.
arxiv-2512-09852:
Juan Calles, Gabriella Contardo, Jorge Noreña, Jacky H. T. Yip, and Gary Shiu hunt for traces of primordial non-Gaussianity using topology. Non-Gaussianity describes how the early universe's density pattern deviated from a pure random Gaussian field. The team built a new simulation suite with more than twenty thousand halo catalogs. The suite varies two shapes of non-Gaussianity, called local and equilateral, alongside basic cosmological parameters.

They compare topological descriptors against the standard power spectrum and bispectrum, asking which best constrains the signal and how the answer depends on halo mass. Simple statistics of the topological features performed best for the equilateral shape. Heavy halos carried the signal, while light halos mostly added noise. Mappings learned on fast simulations transferred imperfectly to an independent suite.
arxiv-2512-09952:
Hyeeun Jang describes a learner centered teaching routine developed across undergraduate mathematics classes from fall 2022 to spring 2025. The routine has four steps. Class opens with a question. A short mini lecture then explains meaning rather than procedure. Students next work in structured small groups. The session ends with a brief exit check, sometimes aided by quick visuals. Jang used it mainly in elementary statistics.

The evidence is deliberately local and practical: teaching notes, one minute exit checks, informal student comments and surveys, and conference feedback. Across courses, Jang saw less passive lecturing and more visible participation. Students spent closing time explaining their reasoning out loud. The limits are stated plainly: one instructor, and no controlled comparisons. Next steps are better prompts for different student groups and simpler visuals. The paper offers the routine and its timing as a template other instructors can adapt.
arxiv-2512-10152:
Tiago Brogueira and Mário Figueiredo rethink causal discovery between two variables through a wider symmetry lens. The standard assumption for such data is that samples are independent and identically distributed. The authors argue the right frame is exchangeability, the weaker condition that sample order does not matter, which strictly generalizes the usual assumption. Building on a recent causal de Finetti theorem, they propose a hierarchical model that is exchangeable by design. In it, uncertainty about the causal mechanism and about the latent variable distribution are both captured more honestly.

They build a synthetic dataset mimicking their model's generation process, and it mirrors the real benchmark's statistical and causal structure better than earlier synthetic sets. A neural method trained only on that synthetic data then competes with leading methods on the real benchmark.
arxiv-2512-10452:
Yang Yang and co-authors study code search when a query mixes plain words with a code snippet, and the code being hunted may be written in a different programming language. Programmers rely on such hybrid search daily. Yet the authors' survey of current code models found three recurring faults: shallow grasp of meaning, clumsy merging of the two query halves, and weak carry-over across languages.

Their framework, UniCoR, learns one shared representation for code that is meant to be steady in meaning, cooperative across query types, and blind to language. Contrastive training aligns code with code, words with code, and words with words, while a second module lines up the feature patterns of different languages. On both study and large-scale benchmarks, UniCoR beat every baseline and held up well on cross-language hunts.
arxiv-2512-10552:
Vladimir Belykh, Nikita Barabash, and Anastasia Suroegina work toward a rigorous picture of the Lorenz and Chen attractors. These are two famous chaotic systems. Their shared traits and deep differences have resisted full proof for decades. Rather than attack each system separately, they reduce both families to one universal normal form and study that.

For the normal form they prove there are infinitely many homoclinic orbits, loops that leave an equilibrium and return to it, sorted by how many times each winds around the symmetry axis. Those winding features pass down to the attractors of Chen-type systems, where they produce the twisted look that sets Chen attractors apart from Lorenz ones. The result turns a long-observed visual difference into a theorem. And gives a cleaner target for finishing the rigorous description of both families.
arxiv-2512-11052:
Joe Suk and Samory Kpotufe study anomaly detection on data that arrives as a single, changing stream. The classic tool, a one class support vector machine, is heavy to run and misses many anomalies when the data distribution drifts over time. Their new method, SONAR, solves the same problem with a fast gradient based approach and strong regularisation.

They prove error guarantees for SONAR that beat those known for the classic method, for both false alarms and missed anomalies. Under gentle distribution shifts, the method keeps learning well over a long lifetime. For harsher, adversarial changes, they embed it in an ensemble with change point detection to adapt phase by phase. Tests on synthetic and real datasets support the theory.
arxiv-2512-11452:
Kenenisa Dame and fellow authors improve the spotting of harmful drug side effects after medicines reach the market by letting an ontology of adverse events guide the statistics. Medical trials miss many adverse drug reactions, so regulators mine spontaneous report databases for suspicious drug event links. Events that resemble each other biologically produce correlated counts, and most pairs never occur, creating excess zeros that naive models mishandle.

Their model folds an adverse event ontology into a zero inflated count model, using similarity between events to disentangle real associations. Significance is judged by a permutation procedure that preserves correlations within each report. Model runs and a real regional drug safety database showed steady gains over a standard shrinkage method. The authors also explore data thinning, a technique that splits data into independent training and validation parts without discarding drug event pairs, and compare splitting strategies for honest testing.
arxiv-2512-11852:
Muhammad Jawad Bashir, Shagufta Henna, and Eoghan Furey add explanations to AI control of smart greenhouses. Connected greenhouse robots tune heat, light, and air on their own, but the forecasting models behind them act as black boxes. Farmers and regulators need to see why a setting was chosen.

The team uses a Temporal Fusion Transformer to set actuators, then explains its calls three ways: built in importance, LIME, and SHAP. The model hit 95 percent accuracy on a skewed test set. Explanations show how temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide, light, and outdoor weather each push decisions. Clear reasons should help growers fine tune settings and trust the system with crops.
arxiv-2512-12052:
Gorkem Kadir Solun and Ugur Dogrusoz give an algorithm for threading a chain of sequences through a pangenome graph. Pangenomes pack many related genomes into one graph, capturing variation that a single reference misses. Such graphs already help read mapping, variant finding, and genotyping.

The task here is functional: given a chain of sequences, find all maximal paths in the graph whose vertex segments align with the chain, allowing gaps up to a user set limit. Maximal paths matter because they mark the longest consistent placements of the chain. The algorithm serves comparative genomics workflows that need to locate ordered sequence patterns inside a whole population graph at once.
arxiv-2512-12152:
Shangyou Zhang continues his finite element work in a second 2025 paper. Finite elements are small blocks that help computers solve equations for heat, stress, and flow. Here he builds C1 Pk elements on rectangular meshes for k of 4 or more, adding special bubble functions inside each block.

He adds 5 bubbles when k is 4, 7 when k is 5, and 8 for all larger k. He then proves three things: each element has a unique solution, it stays smooth across edges, and its error is near the best possible. Numerical tests run for k from 4 through 8.
arxiv-2512-12252:
Kyosuke Nishishita, Atsuki Sato, and Yusuke Matsui present an optimized learned Count-Min Sketch in a 2025 paper. Count-Min Sketch is a compact tool that estimates how often items appear in a large set. A learned version adds a machine learning model to cut error, but it builds slowly and lacks firm error guarantees.

Their version splits the input range and gives each part its own sketch. Settings for each sketch come from formulas, and cut points are chosen by dynamic programming. That cuts trial and error tuning, speeds building, and adds theoretical guarantees. Tests show faster builds, lower bad error rates, and accuracy matching the learned version.
arxiv-2512-12352:
Mohamed Chaouch and Thanasis Stengos study the link between happiness and sustainability across countries in a 2025 paper. They use survey based well-being scores and the Sustainable Development Goals Index for 126 nations in 2022. Past work found a positive link, but mostly with straight line methods that hide uneven patterns across groups.

Graphical Lasso, a network estimation method, found a direct link after controls for governance, income, and life expectancy, with partial correlation about 0.21. A quantile method showed the link flips sign: positive for unhappy but sustainable nations, negative for happy but unsustainable ones. The authors call the link modest and context bound.
arxiv-2512-12952:
Krishna Srikar Durbha and co-authors work on bitrate ladders, the sets of quality levels a streaming service prepares for each video. Tailoring a ladder to each shot of a video saves bandwidth and improves viewing. But building the ideal ladder by trying every option is very costly.

Their method predicts quality scores for compressed video with a learned model, using measures taken from the source video and from the compression step itself. They test it on a large video corpus against leading prior methods and the fixed ladder. They also check how ladders built for one encoding setting transfer to others, a key cost question for services.
arxiv-2512-13052:
Bruno Cessac and co-authors present Macular, a simulation platform for the retina and the primary visual system. Users build a three-dimensional scene of layered cells, where each layer is a cell type from retina or visual cortex. Inputs are arbitrary videos.

Through a graphical interface, users can use built-in cells and synapses or define their own with equations typed as text. Macular then generates and compiles the needed C++ code on its own. Users can watch cell activity and tune parameters without programming. The platform ships with published example scenarios, including a retino-cortical model, and supports tests of altered states such as pathology or drug effects.
arxiv-2512-13252:
Chi-Hsien Tai and Wen-Yu Wen investigate a time-crystalline phase in a single-band holographic superconductor. A time crystal is a state whose pattern repeats in time, breaking time-translation symmetry. Their model uses the holographic duality that maps a gravity theory to a strongly coupled material.

Adding a nonlinear coupling between gauge and scalar fields plus external driving, they derive coupled equations for plasma and Higgs-like modes. Multi-scale analysis shows a resonance with subharmonic growth, the sign of broken time symmetry. Numerical study of quasinormal modes confirms the transition into the time-crystalline phase. The setup offers a tool for studying strongly coupled time crystals.
arxiv-2512-13552:
Hour Kaing and co-authors introduce PrahokBART, a compact model trained from scratch to generate text in Khmer. Big multilingual models often ignore Khmer traits such as word breaks and text norms. The team built curated Khmer and English corpora and added word segmentation and normalization steps to fix that gap.

They test the model on machine translation, text summarization, and headline generation. On all three tasks, PrahokBART beats mBART50, a strong multilingual model. Their checks also show how each language module helps and how well the model handles spaces. Space use matters a lot for natural Khmer text, so the result points to value in language-specific training.
arxiv-2512-13852:
Jelena Losic proposes a graph neural network design that stays robust when a graph's structure is perturbed. Graph networks are the standard tool for learning from graph data, but small edge changes can break them. Her framework adds topological features and stability rules to harden the model.

The method extracts multi-scale features with persistent homology, encodes them as persistence images, and feeds them to a GIN architecture. Stability constraints inspired by Hiraoka and Kusano tie the parts together. Across six data sets from biochemical, social, and collaboration networks, accuracy stayed competitive. Performance fell only 0 to 4% on most data sets under edge perturbation, far better than baseline stability.
arxiv-2512-14252:
Kelly Davis introduces Goedel Poetry in a 2025 paper on automated theorem proving, a long standing challenge for artificial intelligence. The system uses specialized language models that write proofs in Lean4, a formal proof language checked by computer.

Hard theorems are split recursively into simpler propositions that together imply the original claim. A multi agent setup coordinates formalization, proof generation, and that splitting. Without splitting, the system reaches a 90.4 percent pass rate on miniF2F, a standard benchmark. With splitting, the rate improves significantly, though the abstract gives no exact figure. A key tool is an extension of the Kimina Lean Server that parses proof syntax trees. The code is open source on PyPI.
arxiv-2512-15052:
Hongbo Wang and two coauthors fit multimodal AI models with what they call safety glasses. Big models that read images and text inherit toxic signals from messy pretraining data, and hostile prompts can coax out plainly toxic replies. Late, bolt on detox methods are opaque and often miss these attacks.

Their method, SGM, works inside the model at the level of single neurons. It finds neurons tied to toxicity and softly suppresses them, weighted by expertise, with no retraining of the model's parameters. On open source multimodal models, average harmful output rates fell from 45.0 percent to 4.5 percent, while fluency and reasoning held up. A stronger combined version, SGM*, stacks SGM with older detox tools. The team also built a multimodal toxicity test set, MM-TOXIC-QA, and released an interpretable, low cost defense.
arxiv-2512-15752:
Molla Basir Ahamed, Sujoy Majumder, and Nabadwip Sarkar extend Bohr type inequalities to several complex variables in a 2025 paper, dated December 11. The classical Bohr inequality bounds the sum of a bounded analytic function's coefficients on the unit disk. Its multidimensional analogues for the polydisk were less complete.

The authors prove a sharp improvement of the Bohr inequality for bounded holomorphic mappings in the polydisk. Two further sharp versions replace the constant term with the absolute value of the function, or with its square. They also extend known results on the modulus of a derivative, replacing it with the radial derivative in several variables. Every result is shown to be sharp.
arxiv-2512-16152:
Bhal Chandra Joshi, Aris Karastergiou, and Marta Burgay introduce a special journal issue in this 2025 arXiv paper. The topic is pulsar science with the SKA Observatory, a pair of giant radio telescopes on two continents, known as SKA-Low and SKA-Mid. Pulsars are spinning neutron stars that sweep radio beams across the sky like lighthouses.

The authors outline what makes the SKA special for this work: huge sensitivity, wide frequency coverage, and many simultaneous beams. They then preview the issue's eleven articles, each covering a different corner of pulsar research, and show how the topics connect. The paper serves as a map for readers, framing why the SKA could transform radio astronomy in general and pulsar studies in particular.
arxiv-2512-16452:
A Talha Yalta and A Yasemin Yalta propose a governance tool in a 2025 preprint on arXiv. AI rules like the European Union's AI Act now demand proof about training data. Institutions must justify the data used in automated decisions. Existing governance offers few practical methods, though. Choosing, weighting, and explaining data inputs is still hard.

Their Smart Data Portfolio framework treats data categories as assets. Each asset brings returns but also carries risk. Two quantities define the trade-off. One is Informational Return, and the other is Governance-Adjusted Risk. Together they trace a Governance-Efficient Frontier of attainable data mixes. Regulators shape that frontier with risk caps, allowed categories, and weight bands. Those tools turn fairness, privacy, and provenance duties into measurable limits. A sector example shows different services needing different portfolios under one structure.
arxiv-2512-16852:
Kevin N. Ortiz Ceballos, Yvette Cendes, and Edo Berger report the first targeted radio hunt for star-planet interaction in two exoplanet systems, TOI-540 and SPECULOOS-3. Both host close-in planets around active stars, prime ground for magnetic links that could glow in radio.

Deep multi-epoch runs with the Very Large Array and MeerKAT found no signal. Limits reach below 7.5 microjanskys at 4 to 8 gigahertz for SPECULOOS-3, and 30 to 80 microjanskys at lower tones for TOI-540. For SPECULOOS-3 b, most of its orbit is cleared of visible interaction. Modeling shows the hunts could have caught such glow even for a planetary field near 1 gauss, if beamed our way.
arxiv-2512-17052:
Bhrij Patel and coauthors present Dynamic Tool Dependency Retrieval, a light method that picks external tools for on-device language model agents. Static retrievers choose tools from the first query alone, missing how multi-step plans grow and shift context.

DTDR conditions on both the first query and the unfolding tool plan. It learns tool dependency patterns from past function-calling demos, so retrieval adapts as the plan evolves. Across data sets and model backbones, DTDR beat top static retrievers on retrieval precision, task accuracy, and compute cost. Gains in function-calling success ran from 23 percent to 104 percent, proof that plan-aware retrieval cuts the noise of irrelevant tools.
arxiv-2512-17152:
Nan Zhou and coauthors present PhysFire-WM, a physics-informed world model that forecasts how fires spread. Fine fire forecasts aid emergency response, and infrared images plus fire masks give thermal and boundary clues, but mask-only models miss much of the dynamics.

Their model internalizes combustion dynamics by encoding priors from a physical simulator, fixing the physical slips of plain video world models. A cross-task training plan shares parameters and coordinates gradients between thermal radiation and boundary tasks, easing the thin signal of masks. On a fine multimodal fire data set, forecasts beat rivals in accuracy, and ablations credit both the physics priors and the joint training.
arxiv-2512-17252:
Aashwin Mishra, Daniel Ratner, and Quynh Nguyen describe nanoXPEEM, a sharper way to image flat materials and buried layers. Their base tool, XPEEM, uses soft X-rays to map which elements sit where, and how deep they lie. Lens flaws and charge effects blur those maps, and no lens setup can fully fix the blur.

Instead of new lenses, the team trains a deep learning model with a spatial attention step to clean the images after capture. The cleaned maps reach 48 nanometer detail across a field 232 micrometers wide, a record for this energy range. Clearer maps of this kind help researchers design thin materials for real devices.
arxiv-2512-17352:
Ivan Kralj and four co-authors trim the chatter between roadside computers that forecast traffic together. Their forecast models read streams from sensors spread over a city, split across small edge servers called cloudlets. Neighboring servers keep resending each other the same sensor data, which wastes bandwidth and slows the whole system down.

Their fix prunes the shared data on the fly, cutting what recent performance shows is not helping, while guarding the links that matter. They also coin a new score, SEPA, that grades how fast a model reacts to sudden jams and clear-ups. On two large California traffic data sets, pruning kept forecasts sharp while sending far less data. The new score revealed links that plain error scores had undervalued.
arxiv-2512-17652:
S V Demidov, D S Gorbunov, and A L Polonski correct a claim that nuclear reactors should glow with dark photons far more brightly than thought. Dark photons are hypothetical cousins of light that could let reactors leak a dark sector signal. A 2024 paper argued photon scattering inside a reactor boosts their production tenfold, which would sharpen reactor-based searches a great deal.

Redoing the math and checking it with detailed GEANT simulations, the trio finds a boost, but a far smaller one. Scattering does make extra dark photons, just not ten times as many. The resulting shift in the limit on photon-dark photon mixing stays below 30 percent across all masses. They also flag that the original reactor photon spectrum needs an update.
arxiv-2512-17752:
Jan Philip Wahle and three co-authors release ABCDE, a giant labeled trove of everyday writing for researchers who study feelings and minds through language. Psychologists and social scientists often need text pre-tagged for emotion words, body talk, thinking words, and writer traits such as age. The tagging tools exist, but finding and running them defeats many non-programmers.

ABCDE does the tagging once, at scale: over 400 million short texts from social media, blogs, books, and AI sources, each annotated across five feature families named in its title. A sociologist can now ask how emotion words shift with age without building a single model. The set is built to serve fields from political science to the digital humanities.
arxiv-2512-17852:
Mengkun Chen, Sanidhya Tripathi, and James Tunnell work on Raman spectroscopy, a laser method that reads the chemical makeup of tissue without labels or damage. In real tissue the useful signal is faint, and a bright glow called fluorescence often buries it. Their paper builds a way to clean up such noisy spectra.

The team modeled each major noise source, then used that model to create realistic fake spectra for training. A two stage neural network learned to remove both random detector noise and the fluorescence background. Tests on simulated human skin spectra suggest the approach could make tissue scans faster and more accurate.
arxiv-2512-17952:
Hanyu Li and Xiaotie Deng ask whether AI agents would trade with each other even when they share the same beliefs. Classic theory says trade needs differing views, so agents who agree should sit still. Their model gives each agent a fixed budget of computing power, and power caps how complex a plan it can run.

The twist is that calm appears only when the agents' power differs by a small amount. Agents with equal power may never settle, and their endless small adjustments act like trade. Letting agents hide some power makes balance even harder to reach. Markets of AI agents, the authors warn, may stay restless for reasons old theory missed.
arxiv-2512-18052:
Menglong Zhao leads an eleven author team modeling a tricky edge effect in the DIII-D fusion device. In negative triangularity plasmas, the exhaust region, called the divertor, must cool and detach from full contact to protect the walls. They run the 2D edge code UEDGE to map when that detachment sets in.

Scans in plasma density match the measured drop in target current. Pointing the magnetic field forward needed about 40 percent more density to detach than the reverse way, and deep detachment never arrived in reverse. Against standard shapes, the negative form needs densities at or above a known cap, thanks to a shorter path to the target and weaker sideways drift.
arxiv-2512-18352:
Fengzhu Zeng leads a seven author team catching rumors early, when posts are still few. The hard part is timing: call too soon and the call may be wrong, call late and the rumor has spread. Big language models judge claims well but read time poorly and cost a lot to run on a live feed.

Their split design gives the clock to a small trained agent that picks the moment to decide, while the large model, left untrained, judges the claim itself. Across four real data sets the pairing beat past early detection methods on both accuracy and earliness, and it lifted every large model it was paired with. Only the small agent needs training.
arxiv-2512-18852:
Khairul Alam and Banani Roy study how scientific workflow systems, the software pipelines researchers use to run analyses, handle their bug reports on GitHub. Fast, reliable issue handling keeps these tools trustworthy, but nobody had measured what speeds it up. Their study, posted to arXiv in December 2025, analyzes 21,116 issues across a collection of workflow projects.

They find 68.91 percent of issues get closed, half of them within 18.09 days, though speed varies widely between systems. Projects follow structured management habits, and two simple practices stand out: labeling issues and assigning them to someone both go with faster resolution. The authors close with recommendations for developers who maintain workflow repositories. For open-source science software, the message is that triage discipline, not just coding effort, sets the pace of repair.
arxiv-2512-18952:
Kang-Min Hu, Min Namkung, and Hyang-Tag Lim review how to run the variational quantum eigensolver, VQE, on light. VQE is a leading algorithm for today's noisy quantum machines, estimating ground-state energies for chemistry and materials problems without deep circuits. Photonic hardware brings room-temperature operation, low decoherence, and several degrees of freedom per photon. Their review, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in Nano Convergence, lays out the photonic path.

They first explain the VQE framework and its variational energy procedure. Then they show how photonic systems implement each step, addressing a wide range of problems with either many qubit states or a single high-dimensional qudit state. Because qudits pack more information per particle, photonic VQE suits scalable, high-dimensional computation. The review serves as a design guide for groups building chemistry solvers on optical chips.
arxiv-2512-19152:
Jakub Martinka, Mikołaj Martyka, Biman Medhi, and Jiří Pittner present a flexible surface-hopping framework inside the MLatom software. Surface hopping simulates molecules that jump between energy surfaces after absorbing light, a core process in photochemistry. Their setup hosts Tully's fewest-switches method and a time-dependent Baeck-An variant.

Three examples show the workflow, from computing energies and couplings to following many trajectories at once. Custom user models can cut compute time and serve as fair tests for machine learning models. In their comparison, a Landau-Zener style scheme beat the Baeck-An variant. Analysis tools for single paths and whole ensembles round out the package.
arxiv-2512-19452:
Qiang Wen, Mingshuai Xu, and Haocheng Zhong rebuild holographic tensor networks as exact tilings of anti-de Sitter space. Tensor networks are the standard toy models of the AdS/CFT correspondence. Yet their discrete meshes match smooth gravity only roughly. A recent thread construction, based on partial entanglement entropy, tiles the space perfectly.

The authors place a quantum state on each vertex of that thread network and build three models. One is factorized, made of paired states. One uses perfect tensors, in the HaPPY style. One is random. Each reproduces the exact Ryu-Takayanagi entropy formula, a key holographic check. Geometry and network finally share the same skeleton.
arxiv-2512-19652:
Serat Saad and Yuan-Sen Ting use pairs of far-apart stars to stress-test a rival to dark matter. The rival is modified Newtonian dynamics, called MOND. Wide pairs drift in such weak gravity that MOND says their motion should break Newton's rules. Gaia's speed data are too coarse for the tiny gaps at stake. Past tests had to rely on motion across the sky alone.

The pair built a way to read speed gaps from sharp spectra. It reached a precision of eight to fifteen meters per second. They applied it to 85 wide pairs from the C3PO survey. They kept 57 firmly bound pairs and fit their orbits with a Bayesian model. The fits clash with MOND's accepted acceleration scale. Two standard forms of the theory are ruled out at mild to moderate strength. The team notes that how the outside field is handled may shift these claims.
arxiv-2512-19752:
Nicholas Laws and Elaine Petro simulate what happens when propellant hits a spacecraft thruster. Electrospray thrusters are compact and use fuel well. They suit small satellites. But ground tests are muddied by extra species and by neutral products that tools miss. The team runs mixed quantum and classical dynamics. They crash the ionic-liquid fuel EMI-BF4 into gold surfaces. Impact energies run from ten to one hundred electron volts.

Three regimes show up as energy rises. At low energy, ions split apart. At mid energy, a window opens where charges cancel out. At high energy, bonds break into many light pieces. Heavy fragments bend less, and light ones scatter wide. Short-lived states peak near fifty electron volts. A key warning stands out. Charged debris still forms even when the ion plume is fully blocked.
arxiv-2512-19852:
Rahul Shrestha leads an eight-author team shrinking atomic vapor gear onto photonic chips. Alkali vapors that meet nanophotonic guides promise scalable quantum tech. But glass cells, distilled metals, and epoxy seals fight mass production. Stray rubidium also harms the photonics. Their device joins silicon nitride circuits with tiny borosilicate cells. Pill-type rubidium sources sit inside. Anodic bonding seals the stack for good.

Good runs hinged on firing the source in short, low-power pulses. That frees a controlled dose of vapor on demand, with less harm done. A laser aimed back along the guide then wiped out rubidium-caused losses. That let the team do spectroscopy through the guide itself. Vapor density could be tuned by pulse length, duty cycle, and heat. The result is a compact platform that can be manufactured at scale.
arxiv-2512-20252:
Longqing Ge, Qingdong Cai, Yonghao Zhang, and Tianbai Xiao simulate gas flows around solid bodies without fitting the grid to the body's shape. Their tool is an immersed boundary method built on the discrete velocity model of the Boltzmann equation. A Maxwell model of gas-surface interaction shapes the particle distributions in ghost cells near the surface.

Two improvements anchor the work. A compact upwind-weighted interpolation keeps the scheme stable for awkward geometries without wide stencils or normal projections. A cut-cell correction in velocity space repairs quadrature errors caused by surface discontinuities. Analysis confirms second-order accuracy and stability in both spaces. Numerical tests match body-fitted solvers while keeping the simplicity of a Cartesian grid.
arxiv-2512-20352:
