The United States should take an active part in restoring the Tangier zone and in running it in the interim.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1052:
Britain's delegation presented this note to the conference on August 1, 1945. A file notation says Stalin asked for time to study it. The note recalls a standing pledge. British and American commanders are supplying their Berlin zones with food and coal. The rates are 40,000 tons of food a month and 2,400 tons of coal a day. The pledge runs for thirty days from July 15.

Until a deal sets the Soviet deliveries owed under the reparations agreement, the Control Council should act at once. It should draft a six-month import program for Greater Berlin. The program would cover the food, coal, and fuel needed to lift the whole city's people to an agreed standard. The Soviet government would furnish those amounts as an advance delivery.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1152:
One day after its last paper, the American team tabled another proposal, dated 30 July 1945. Back-to-back papers in the final days show a team racing the clock. The summit would close on 2 August, and every unsettled line was being fought over.

Late proposals traded the last gains and closed the last gaps. Some won their points; others were dropped to save the deal as a whole. This paper is one more American move in that endgame. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it lets readers follow the drafting of the final protocol almost hour by hour.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1252:
A second Hurley message to the President and the Secretary of State bears the date 26 July 1945. Two dispatches in a day from the China post show a file moving fast. The ambassador split his subjects across them as events demanded.

That day the Allied terms to Japan went out from Potsdam. China would feel their effects at once, in its war and in its politics. Hurley's twin reports belong to that charged moment. This one is the day's companion piece, and together the pair shows an envoy working at full stretch on the summit's most crowded day.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1352:
Ambassador John Winant cabled the acting secretary of state from London on 18 July 1945. Winant had served in Britain through most of the war and knew its leaders well. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

London's reading of events carried special weight in Washington, and Winant was trusted to give it plainly. His cable arrived as the Potsdam talks got under way, when British views on Germany and the Soviets mattered hour by hour. For readers, the message is a window on the alliance at work. One capital telling another what it sees, in the middle of a summit that would set Europe's shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-152:
The United States delegation issued this memorandum on July 31, 1945, as the conference worked toward its final text. Memoranda on the last day served the closing push. They carried checks, fixes, and last views between the team's offices. The paper entered the second Potsdam volume of the official Foreign Relations series.

A final-day memo shows staff discipline under strain. Writers had no time for polish, so they wrote plain. That plainness helps readers now: the memo states needs and facts without a gloss. It belongs to the inner record of how the American side finished its largest wartime conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-52:
Combined Chiefs of Staff minutes record the approval of their 197th meeting's conclusions, from July 20, 1945. The top secret record is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Two amendments to the record are set out in the part printed here.

One amendment concerns command in the Southwest Pacific and Southeast Asia. It now records that the British chiefs would seek the agreement of three governments to the new set-up. Those governments are Australia, New Zealand, and the Netherlands. A second amendment quotes General Marshall's condition for accepting the directive. The British chiefs, he said, must be responsible for winning that approval. Those governments had been parties to the original arrangements, so their consent was owed. The chiefs then turned to the long-running debate on basic objectives, strategy, and policies.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d752:
George Kennan, the American chargé in Moscow, wrote to the Acting Secretary of State on July 17, 1945. Document 752 opens the volume's Moscow thread. Kennan was already known for hard, clear views of Soviet aims. With Harriman at Potsdam, Kennan held the embassy. His letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A Kennan dispatch rewards attention. He wrote to be read, in prose that cut through routine. Readers get the view from inside the Soviet capital as the summit opened. The document also shows the odd split of that week: the ambassador bargained with Stalin in Germany while his deputy watched Stalin's capital.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d852:
The United States delegation tabled this proposal on July 17, 1945, the opening day at Potsdam. Document 852 stands among the volume's first-day texts. The American team led with paper from the start. Its drafts framed the talks' early shape. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Opening proposals from the same day can be read as a set. Together they show the breadth of the American agenda. Readers can sort which topics the team pressed first. The document also shows summit craft: table early, table in writing, and make the others react. Potsdam's two weeks of argument grew from first-day texts like this one.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d952:
American drafters prepared two rival conference statements in this undated working paper, filed with the July 25, 1945 papers. One draft fits agreement on reparations; the other fits failure. Both were written ahead of the Potsdam outcome, so the delegation could move fast either way.

The agreement draft favors quick deliveries of existing capital equipment to cut Germany's war potential. The Soviet Union would also draw equipment from the Ruhr, while sending food and raw materials west. The failure draft lets each occupying power take interim reparations from its own zone. Both drafts stress shrinking the metals, machinery, and chemical industries, and helping lands ruined by German attack.
gao-gaoreports-b-297452: SERAPH took its January 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing. The process stays the same for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-297552: Computers Universal took its February 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299452: Rothe Computer Solutions, doing business as Rohmann Joint Venture, took its May 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the call. The venture challenged the award; the ruling tests the claims. Joint ventures get joint answers in bid court.
gao-gaoreports-b-309752: A mega-ruling from GAO in 2007: seven case numbers, two firms — Contingency Management Group and IAP Worldwide Services — all fighting over rapid-response federal deals. The combined call sorts each firm's gripes under one roof. Its sheer size mirrors the prize: the big, fast-moving contracts that feed off overseas operations.
gao-gaoreports-b-310552: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Singleton Enterprises-GMT Mechanical, A Joint Venture. The January 10, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-b-311452: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Hydro Fitting Manufacturing Corporation. Decided July 8, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-252: EPA's mercury math got a GAO look in 2005, and the report observes on the cost-benefit analysis of control options. The review checks the arithmetic. The clean air deserved the honest numbers. The analysis was observed. The clean air deserved the honest numbers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-452: Medicaid's new clinic payment system faced implementation issues in 2005, and GAO's report says state and federal problems needed resolving. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the rural clinics deserved fair pay. The issues had to be resolved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-552: Federal computer flaws kept biting in 2005, and GAO's report says the holes stayed open despite the new laws. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the agencies' data deserved protection. The agencies' data deserved protection. The holes had to close.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-652: First responders' all-hazards capabilities were evolving in 2005, and GAO's report says DHS efforts continued to develop. The findings take the measure. The report shows the heroes' readiness was being watched. The efforts had to continue. The heroes' readiness was being watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-852: U.S. efforts against Islamic extremism got a GAO review in 2005, and the report covers agencies' work on the issue. The findings take the measure. The report shows the counter-efforts were being watched. The efforts had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-952: Counting who serves got a GAO push in 2005, and the report says richer troop data would help Congress watch. The findings demand the details. The report warns that the troops' diversity deserved counting. The troops' diversity deserved counting. The details had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-352: Rocky Flats' nuclear cleanup offered lessons in 2006, and GAO's report says the Energy Department could use them to improve oversight elsewhere. The findings extract the wisdom. The report warns that the atomic messes needed smarter cleaning. The lessons had to be applied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-52: Transportation guidance needed better spreading in 2005, and GAO's report says better dissemination and oversight of DOT guidance could improve access. The findings demand the outreach. The report warns that the riders with limited English deserved access. The guidance had to be spread.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-852: The Pentagon's global posture needed measuring in 2006, and GAO's report says a comprehensive strategy and annual reporting were required. The findings demand the yardstick. The report warns that the worldwide footprint needed honest accounting. The strategy had to be real.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-152: Leaking gas station tanks were poisoning groundwater in 2007, and GAO's report says the EPA should ensure the cleanup money was well spent. The findings target the funding. The report warns that the buried tanks were ticking time bombs. The aquifers could not wait for action.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-352: Reagan National's runways were maxed out in 2007, and GAO's report updates the airport's capacity and the ripple effects on its neighbors. The findings map the squeeze. The report asks how many more planes the little airport on the river could take.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-52: Foreign doctors on visa waivers needed counting in 2007, and GAO's report says the data was required to address physician shortages. The findings demand the figures. The report warns that the doctor gap could not be managed blind. The numbers had to be gathered.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-652: Bird flu was circling in 2007 — GAO's report says the farm agency had taken real steps to ready for outbreaks, but sharper planning would speed the response. The findings credit the prep and prod the plans. The report treats the next poultry plague as a matter of when.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-752: Your Social Security number was public property in 2007 — GAO's report says federal moves could shrink its exposure in public records, though other leaks stayed open. The findings map the identity battlefield. The report argues for plugging the government's own holes first.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-252: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at homeland Defense: Steps Have Been Taken to Improve US Northern Command's Coordination with States and the National Guard Bureau, but Gaps Remain. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-452: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at medicare Part B Imaging Services: Rapid Spending Growth and Shift to Physician Offices Indicate Need for CMS to Consider Additional Management Practices. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-52: GAO told the Air Force in 2007 to write real rules for buying and running its business software. The service was spending big on finance and supply programs with no firm playbook for picking winners. The report targets a classic Pentagon trap: billion-dollar tech buys launched on hope, then nursed along long past the point of no return.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-852: GAO published its findings on homeland Security: DHS Risk-Based Grant Methodology Is Reasonable, But Current Version's Measure of Vulnerability is Limited in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
goodwin-graeco-egyptian-magic-1852:
Charles Wycliffe Goodwin published the first English rendering of a Greek magical papyrus in 1852. His edition presents papyrus PGM V from the British Museum's Anastasi collection. Greek text, English translation, and notes appear together in the volume.

The papyrus holds a working handbook of spells from Roman Egypt. Love charms, dream-sending rites, and prayers to Egyptian gods fill its columns. Goodwin, an Egyptologist and judge, recognized the text's importance early. His edition opened serious study of ancient magic to English readers. Historians of religion still treat the publication as a landmark. The spells mix Greek and Egyptian traditions freely.
guillaume-clerc-bestiaire-divin-hippeau-:
Guillaume le Clerc, a Norman poet, wrote the Bestiaire divin around 1210. It is a bestiary in French verse, each beast matched with its Christian meaning. Hippeau's edition of 1852 supplies this text of the great thirteenth-century poem.

Guillaume treats lion, unicorn, pelican, and dozens more in rhyming lines. He describes each creature's nature, then draws the lesson for the soul. His verse is graceful, and his morals are aimed at ordinary hearers. The poem stands among the finest of the verse bestiaries. Hippeau's careful edition kept it available to scholars. Together, poem and edition preserve a high point of medieval animal lore.
gulistan-eastwick-1852:
Edward B. Eastwick published his English Gulistan in 1852, the first translation of Saadi's Rose Garden into prose and verse together. Saadi of Shiraz wrote the Gulistan in Persian in 1258, after a lifetime of travel and study. Eastwick adds a life of the author drawn from the Atish Kadah.

Kings, dervishes, schoolboys, and wrestlers pass through eight chapters of tales and maxims. Each short story lands on a line of counsel about mercy, contentment, speech, or power. Saadi mixes prose with verse morals in the Persian manner, and Eastwick follows him. Persians have quoted the Gulistan for seven centuries as their handbook of wisdom. Eastwick's pioneering version opened it to the English world.
hahnemann-lesser-writings-1852:
Samuel Hahnemann wrote far more than the Organon, and The Lesser Writings of 1852 gathers that scattered work in one place. R. E. Dudgeon edited the volume, with notes by Richard Hughes. Essays, letters, and case notes sit side by side, spanning Hahnemann's long career as the founder of homeopathy and its first arguer.

Some pieces argue with critics, while others record single cures or early drug trials. Together they show his ideas forming well before the famous system took shape. Students who know only the Organon find a fuller Hahnemann here: sharper, more restless, and always testing his rules against practice.
hawthorne-blithedale-romance-1852:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Blithedale Romance in 1852, his novel of a utopian farm community. The book is a roman à clef of Brook Farm, where Hawthorne had lived in 1841. It is the first great American novel of utopian community and its discontents in fiction.

Poet Miles Coverdale, the narrator, spies on his fellow reformers from trees and hermitage hides in Blithedale. Hollingsworth, a stern prison reformer, bends the commune to his single driving cause of reforming criminals. Zenobia, proud and passionate, and meek Priscilla fall into a triangle that ends in river death. Coverdale's voyeur gaze makes him the least trusted teller Hawthorne ever built into a tale here. The book asks if reformers love mankind or only their own grand schemes.
hugo-napoleon-the-little-1852: Napoleon the Little, Victor Hugo's 1852 denunciation. The tyrant unmasked. This book preserves that polemic. Coming generations can find it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The text survives intact.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenstein-leop:
Leopold Löwenstein, a German rabbi born in Gailingen, Baden, on December 1, 1843, is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer. He studied at the gymnasium at Bischofsheim and learned Talmud from his father, a district rabbi. He then attended the University of Würzburg and the yeshivah of Rabbi Israel Hildesheimer at Eisenstadt.

In 1872 Löwenstein became district rabbi in his native place, and in 1887 he moved to Mosbach, Baden, serving three districts from there. He was decorated in 1891, and the article lists his histories of the Jews at Lake Constance and in Germany. Since 1900 he had also edited a journal supplement on Jewish history and literature. The entry captures a working rabbi who doubled as a local historian, and it names the books where his research can still be found.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maftir-10252:
Maftir, the last reader in the synagogue Torah service, is explained in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. On ordinary Sabbaths he repeats the closing verses of the weekly portion. On special Sabbaths and holy days he reads a separate portion tied to the occasion. That custom follows a ruling of Rashi, accepted by all congregations.

The article sets out the rules around the role. The maftir is not counted among the required seven readers on Sabbaths. Because his part is short, Talmudic practice compensated him with leading other prayers that day. As reader of the Haftarah, he must first read from the Torah himself. The prophetic text must run at least twenty-one verses. Five benedictions frame his reading, and the part often goes to a bar mitzvah or a bridegroom. The entry is a tidy manual of a small but honored synagogue office.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandelli-david-:
David Mandelli, a Hungarian linguist, gets a brief entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born about 1780 at Presburg, he died at Paris on December 22, 1836. The article calls him one of the greatest linguists of his time. His knowledge of languages was said to rival even Cardinal Mezzofanti's.

The entry lingers on the range of his studies. His favorites were Hebrew, Arabic, Persian, Chinese, Greek, and Latin. From a blend of these he formed a language of his own, the article reports. That detail, credited to Oettinger's biographical register, is nearly all the entry offers. No books or posts are named for him. The short notice preserves a reputation more than a record: a Jewish polyglot whose fame rested on the tongues he held in his head.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marx-karl-10452:
Isidore Singer and Max Cohen wrote the entry on Karl Marx, the German socialist leader and political economist, for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Treves on May 5, 1818, the son of an attorney who adopted Christianity in 1824. Marx studied at Bonn and Berlin and took a doctorate in philosophy. In 1842 he became editor of the Rheinische Zeitung, then the most radical newspaper in Germany. He died in London on March 14, 1883.

The entry follows his exile's itinerary. It covers Paris and the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, expulsion and Brussels, then the London congress of 1847. At that congress the Communist Manifesto he prepared with Engels was adopted. It covers his editorship in the revolution of 1848, his acquittal on a charge of incitement, and his banishment. It ends with his final refuge in England and the founding of the International Working Men's Association in 1864.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-edvard-10:
Edvard Meyer was a Danish journalist and author born in Copenhagen on August 6, 1813. His life began and ended in poverty, as Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer tell it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of very poor parents. He spent his boyhood in a Jewish charitable institution with almost no schooling.

At fourteen he was apprenticed to a wood-turner. In 1837 he founded a weekly paper. Later, back in Copenhagen, he started a humorous weekly and the sensational daily Flyveposten. For some years the daily earned him nearly 50,000 crowns a year. He also published poems, fairy tales, and Danish popular songs. After many ups and downs he died in 1880, in the same kind of charity home where he had grown up.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minhah-prayer-1:
Minḥah is the afternoon prayer service of Jewish liturgy. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein explain it in a Jewish Encyclopedia article published in 1906. Its name likely comes from Elijah praying at the hour of the evening offering. Tradition gives the service to Isaac. He went out to meditate in the field toward evening.

The article's core is timing. The day is split into twelve fixed hours. Major Minḥah opens at half past twelve, and minor Minḥah at half past three. No big deal or banquet may begin after the first time. No small meal may begin after the second, before praying. The service itself runs Psalm 145, the Amidah, supplications, and Alenu. It adds Torah reading on Sabbaths and fasts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-children-:
The Children of Moses, in Arabic Banu Musa, are the legendary descendants of Moses who live beyond the river Sambation. Joseph Jacobs and Max Schloessinger trace the legend in this Jewish Encyclopedia article. It grows out of Psalm one hundred thirty-seven, the exiles weeping by the waters of Babylon.

In the tale, Nebuchadnezzar orders the Levites to play their harps as they had in the Temple. They bite off their fingertips rather than sing for him, and God rewards them with a hidden land. There they live without government, envy, or illness, beyond a river that rages all week and rests on the Sabbath. Eldad ha-Dani became the chief source for the story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-levi-b-so:
Moses Levi ben Solomon of Beaucaire was a French writer who lived at Salon in the early fourteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His pupil Kalonymus ben Kalonymus of Arles praised him as the learned scholar and the ornament of sages.

Moses translated Averroes' greater commentary on Aristotle's Metaphysics into Hebrew, though the work is also ascribed to Moses of Salerno. With Abba Mari ben Eligdor he wrote a refutation of Joseph Caspi's Sefer ha-Sod. He also summarized Averroes' commentary on the Physics. The entry shows a scholar of Provence moving Greek and Arabic philosophy into Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mysh-mikhail-ig:
Mikhail Ignatyevich Mysh was a Russian jurist born at Koretz in Volhynia on January 2, 1846. Herman Rosenthal wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He graduated from the Jitomir gymnasium with a gold medal and took his law degree at Kiev in 1871. He settled in St. Petersburg and practised law there.

After the anti-Jewish riots of 1881, Mysh studied the legal condition of Russia's Jews at first hand. His guide to Russian legislation on the Jews reached a second edition in 1899. His general works on city ordinances ran through fourteen editions, a rare success for a law book. His son Vladimir became professor of surgery at Tomsk.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-feitel-1:
Nathan Feitel was a rabbi in Moravian towns. Gotthard Deutsch and S. J. Levinson wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served at Hotzenplotz and later at Austerlitz. His life fell in the seventeenth century. His books were printed at Cracow and Prague.

Feitel wrote a work called Hok Natan. It appeared at Cracow in 1609, with a preface by Horowitz. He also wrote a homily on the Sabbath lesson Wayiggash. That piece came out in 1613 and again at Prague in 1623. A book on the 1648 massacre is often tied to him. The entry corrects that error: his son Samuel wrote it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-netter-charles-:
Charles Netter was a French friend of Jews worldwide. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Strasburg in 1828. He studied there and at Belfort, then traded in Paris. He helped found the Alliance Israélite Universelle.

His house long served as the Alliance's only home. His great work was Jaffa's agricultural school for Jews. He gave years to farming among Palestine's Jews. At Berlin in 1878 he pressed eastern Jews' claims. The Treaty of Berlin formally owned those claims there. At Brody in 1881 he aided Russian refugees firsthand. He died at Jaffa, visiting his school, in 1882.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nisan-assyrian-:
Nisan is the first month of the sacred year. Emil G. Hirsch and Isaac Broydé wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In the civil count it stands seventh instead. Older Bible books call it Hodesh ha-Abib, harvest month. Tradition made it sacred for its burnt offering.

Public mourning and fasts are barred all twenty-nine days. The Tahanun prayer drops out of daily services. Three days in it recall deaths of the great. Nadab and Abihu, Miriam, and Joshua are so honored. Passover begins on the evening of the fourteenth. A barley sheaf is offered on the sixteenth. The counting of seven weeks starts that same day. Nisan falls, roughly, in the month of April.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-occupations-116:
Occupations traces the work Jews did through the ages. Joseph Jacobs and M. Grunwald wrote the long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The old Hebrews were farmers, fishers, and craft workers. They were seldom traders in their own land. King Solomon tried to spur trade among them. His push left no lasting mark, the piece says.

Abroad, Jews were oft barred from owning farm land. So they turned more and more to trade and craft. In Germany they led in trade for long years. Rich Jewish traders worked at Ratisbon, on the Danube. Goods from the East came up that river to them. In Sicily, Jews worked as smiths, weavers, and silk makers. They held the silk trade there for years on end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oran-arabic-and:
Oran, or Wahran, is the chief town of west Algeria. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands at the head of a bay on the sea. That sea is the great sea called the Mediterranean. No text tells when Jews first settled at Oran.

Oran was a trade hub as far back as the nine hundreds. So Jews may have come there at an early date. Under Arab rule their lot swung from fair to cruel. The Almohades drove at them with great force and hate. Many fled to the East to live in peace. Many took Islam to save their lives at home. In 1509 Spain took the town from Arab hands. In 1679 its Jews were cast out of the whole land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-painting-11852: Painting was the art least grown among the Hebrews. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote its short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. That fact owes much to a law of Moses, they say. The law barred the making of images for worship. So the art is scarce named in the Old Testament. Wall works were carvings in raised form, as in the Temple. Or they were lines cut with a sharp point, then filled with color.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pesah-peter-120: Pesah Peter was a baptized Jew in Germany around 1400. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He accused his former people over the prayer Alenu. That prayer ends the service with praise of God alone. Peter claimed one line secretly mocked Jesus. He pointed to the words for vanity and emptiness. He said their letters add up to a number tied to Jesus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pollitzer-adolp:
Adolph Pollitzer was a violinist born at Budapest in 1832. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied the violin at Vienna under Böhm. At fourteen he won first prize at the Vienna Conservatorium. He then toured Germany and studied in Paris under Alard.

In 1850 Pollitzer crossed to London and won quick fame. He led the orchestra at Her Majesty's Theatre. He led the new Philharmonic Orchestra as well. Critics praised his playing of classic chamber music most of all. As a teacher he ranked first in England in his day. He taught violin at the London Academy of Music from 1861. He led the Academy as principal from 1870 until his death in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-porging-hebrew-:
Porging means cutting away banned fat and veins from kosher meat. The Editorial Board and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In Judaeo-German the work is called treibern. The law of Moses bans the eating of fat and blood of cattle. That ban is called a lasting rule for all time.

The article works out which fat counts as banned. It is the fat that covers the inner parts. It is the fat on the kidneys and a lobe above the liver. Those parts were burned as gifts to God in the Temple. All other fat is ruled clean by contrast. The entry gives the rules a butcher must follow step by step.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-purple-12452:
Purple dye in the Bible is the subject of an article by Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Old Testament names two kinds of purple. The first is argaman, a bright red purple. It cost most when it had the hue of clotted blood. Seen straight, it looked black in tone.

Seen at a slant, that same dye shone red and bright. The second kind is tekelet, a blue purple dye. Philo and Josephus both describe its hue. It matched the sea, the air, or the clear sky. The article traces both dyes in cloth and rite. It asks which shells and crafts gave each color.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reich-ignaz-eiz:
Ignaz Reich was a Hungarian teacher and author born at Zsámbék in 1821. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Budapest on April 18, 1887. His father was a Jewish communal notary.

The article says he studied at Grosswardein and at Arad. Aaron Chorin influenced him while at Arad. He taught for forty years at a Jewish school. He also taught at a state school for the blind. He was the first Jew to teach pupils the Bible in Hungarian. He translated the prayer book and Haggadah as well. His Beth-El gives lives of leading Hungarian Jews. The entry honors a patriotic teacher in national dress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-riesser-lazarus:
Lazarus Jacob Riesser was a German rabbi born in 1763. Isidore Singer and E. Schreiber wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in the valley of Riess, hence his name. He died at Hamburg on March 7, 1828.

The article says his learning won him a notable marriage. He wed the daughter of Raphael ha-Kohen of Altona. There he served as secretary to the bet din. His Hebrew style is called classic by the writers. When his father in law resigned in 1799, Riesser lost office. He moved to Hamburg and entered business without much success. He wrote his father in law's biography in elegant Hebrew. Letters to his son Gabriel survive in print. That son became the famous Gabriel Riesser.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenfeld-sydne:
Sydney Rosenfeld was an American dramatist born in Richmond, Virginia, on October 26, 1855. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was first picked to edit the humor paper Puck, then turned to the stage.

Rosenfeld wrote plays such as A Possible Case, Imagination, and The Politician. He also created operettas, among them The Lady or the Tiger and The Passing Show. As an adapter he reworked many foreign pieces for American audiences. He worked hard, too, for a national theater, and by 1905 he headed the Century Theatre Company.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saadia-sa-id-b-:
Saadia b. David al-Adeni was a man of culture at Damascus and Safed between 1473 and 1485. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He commented on parts of Maimonides' great code, the Yad ha-Hazakah.

Saadia also edited an Arabic commentary on the Pentateuch, now fragmentary. He composed philosophical hymns in both Arabic and Hebrew at Safed and Damascus. At Aden in 1451 he had copied the dictionary of Tanhuma by hand. Strangely, he circulated a work of Ghazali under his own name. Its autograph, a defective copy, rests in the St. Petersburg Library.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salzburg-13052:
Salzburg is an Austrian duchy, once a German archbishopric, and its capital city. Isidore Singer and Aaron Tänzer wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Jews, among them a physician, appear in its records by the ninth century.

Two settlements bore the name Judendorf, Jews' village, by the eleventh century. Jews lived at Salzburg, Hallein, Pettau, and other towns by the thirteenth. In 1346 the archbishop granted them residence, protection, and free trade for payment. That Letter of Grace cost a large sum every year, though. Church councils meanwhile heaped harsh rules on the Jews there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-uri-:
Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. Its subject is Samuel ben Uri Shraga Phoebus, a Polish rabbi and Talmudist. He lived at Woydyslaw in the late seventeenth century. As a boy he studied under Rabbi Heshel in Cracow. He later married the daughter of Heshel's successor.

Samuel served as rabbi at Shydlow in Poland. In September 1691 he was called to the rabbinate of Fürth in Germany. He worked hard there and earned a good income. Still, he missed his old post. In 1694 he gladly returned to Shydlow. His chief work is a clear commentary on the Eben ha-Ezer part of the Shulḥan Aruk. It was printed at Dyhernfurth in 1689, the first Hebrew book printed in that town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saul-of-tarsus-:
Kaufmann Kohler wrote this long Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Saul of Tarsus. He is known as Paul, the Apostle of the Heathen. Kohler calls him the real founder of the Christian Church apart from Judaism. Paul was born before 10 of the common era. He died after the year 63. His parents were Jews of Tarsus in Cilicia.

Kohler argues that Paul was no Hebrew scholar. His letters quote Scripture from the Greek version, never the Hebrew. Acts says he studied under Gamaliel the First. Kohler finds no sign of such rabbinic training in his thought. Paul's ideas came from Hellenistic writings like the Book of Wisdom and Philo. The claim that he was of Benjamin's tribe also fails, Kohler says. No tribal pedigrees survived in his day. The article presses a fully critical case.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schatz-boris-13:
Herman Rosenthal and M. Franco wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Boris Schatz. He was a Russian sculptor. Schatz was born in 1866 in the government of Kovno. His father was a poor schoolmaster. He studied design at Wilna and art at Warsaw. In Paris he trained under Antokolski from 1890 to 1896. He has lived at Sofia since 1896.

Schatz made Jewish subjects his special study. His works show the oppressed Jew of the ghetto. They include a rabbi blessing a child and a Saturday evening scene. At the Paris Salon of 1892 he showed The Mother of Moses. His masterpiece, Mattathias Maccabee, came in 1896. He also carved Bulgarian types from the life around him. His reliefs portray Antokolski, Rubinstein, Pasteur, and Herzl. At St. Louis in 1904 he won a silver medal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scotland-13352:
Joseph Jacobs and Isidore Harris wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Scotland. The country forms the northern part of Great Britain. Jews settled there only in the early nineteenth century. In 1816 twenty Jewish families lived in Edinburgh. That city was the first in Scotland to draw Jewish settlers. Glasgow's community came later, in 1830.

Edinburgh and Glasgow hold nearly all of Scotland's Jews. They number something over 8,000 in all. Three smaller congregations stand at Dundee, Aberdeen, and Greenock. Dundee's 110 Jews keep a benevolent loan society by their synagogue. Aberdeen's tiny congregation once faced a lawsuit over Jewish slaughter. The Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals had attacked the method as inhumane. The entry rests on the Jewish Year Book of 1905.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shemaiah-b-sime: Shemaiah ben Simeon Zebi, also called Segal, was a scholar of the seventeenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Almost nothing is known of his life beyond his book. That book, Mazref la-Hokmah, was printed at Amsterdam in 1765, long after his time. It lists all 613 commandments of Jewish law. Each commandment is described in just eight words. Those words begin with initials that likely spell a form of his own name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-simedl-si:
Simon of Trent, called Simedl or Simoncino, was a child found dead in 1475. Joseph Jacobs and Aaron Tänzer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was the son of Andreas Unverdosben, a cobbler or tanner. He was born on November 26, 1472. He vanished on March 23, 1475, at twenty-eight months old.

A friar, Bernardinus of Feltre, had preached against the Jews that Lent. He had even predicted a ritual murder at Passover. The child's body was found in a river near a Jewish home. All the Jews of Trent were arrested on a prisoner's claim about blood rites. The long entry traces this grim blood libel case in detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-abr:
Solomon ben Abraham ben Samuel was a French Talmudist of the thirteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and A Peiginsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was rabbi at Montpellier in southern France. He led the movement against Maimonides in that region. When the Guide reached France in translation, orthodox scholars viewed it with suspicion.

Solomon was the first to attack the book openly. He lacked training in philosophy, the article argues. He faulted Maimonides for reading Talmudic tales in a non-literal way. He also faulted him for explaining miracles by natural causes. With two pupils he pronounced a ban in 1232. That ban split Judaism into two hostile camps for years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-speyer-13952:
Speyer was a German family that took its name from the city of Speyer. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Members settled at Frankfort-on-the-Main in the sixteenth century. From there descendants spread to Germany, England, and America. Many became bankers of note in those lands.

Joseph Michael Speyer left a fund of 4,000 florins at Frankfort. Isaac Michael Speyer was taken hostage by the French in 1792. He left a legacy worth 17,000 dollars by 1905. Philip Speyer founded a banking house in New York in 1837. His brother Gustav joined him there in 1845 for years. James Joseph Speyer led the New York firm from 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stilling-benedi:
Benedikt Stilling was a German anatomist and surgeon born in 1810. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Kirchhayn, Hesse, on February 22. He studied at the University of Marburg. He died at Cassel on January 28, 1879.

Stilling took his medical degree in 1832 and joined Marburg's anatomy institute. In 1837 he first brought ovariotomy into Germany. In 1840 he coined the term vasomotor nerves. His studies of the brain and nervous system became standard works. The French Institute awarded him several prizes for them. He also studied how blood clots form and heal. The entry honors a surgeon who opened new ground twice over.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sydney-14152:
Sydney is the capital of New South Wales in Australia. D. I. Freedman and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its Jewish congregation dates from 1817. About twenty Jews formed a burial society then. They won a corner of the general cemetery.

Prayer meetings met in a private house by 1828. London's chief rabbi sent a judge to help organize. A rented room became a synagogue in 1832. The first Jewish marriage in Australia came in 1830. A York Street synagogue opened for worship in 1844. Minister A. B. Davis served the congregation forty-one years. Under him its grand Elizabeth Street synagogue rose. The entry traces a community from burial plot to landmark.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tarrasch-siegbe:
Siegbert Tarrasch was a German physician and chess master born in 1862. Isidore Singer and A. Porter wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Breslau on March 5. He studied medicine at Berlin, Halle, and Nuremberg. He practiced as a physician in Nuremberg.

Tarrasch ranked among the most successful modern chess players. At Manchester, Dresden, and Leipsic he lost one game total. First prizes came at Nuremberg, Breslau, and Dresden. He won at Leipsic, Vienna, and Monte Carlo too. In 1893 he drew a match with Tchigorin, nine games each. In 1905 he beat Marshall while losing only once. His game annotations show great analytical power. He also edited a chess journal with Gottschall. The entry tabulates a champion's long winning record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-torre-lelio-hil:
Lelio della Torre was an Italian rabbi and educator born at Cuneo in 1805. Isidore Singer and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Orphaned at two, he was raised by a rabbi uncle. He tutored Hebrew at Turin from 1823. In 1827 he became assistant rabbi there.

Padua's new rabbinical college hired him in 1829. He taught Talmud, homiletics, and pastoral theology until death. He wrote Hebrew, Italian, and French with equal ease. His Hebrew poems fill the collection Tal Yaldut of 1868. He translated the Psalms and Israelite prayers into Italian. A work treated Jews under the medieval German empire. Cuneo carved his name on a bronze honor tablet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tribes-lost-ten:
The Lost Ten Tribes, carried off from Israel's northern kingdom, are tracked here. Joseph Jacobs wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Assyria deported most northerners to Halah, Habor, and Media. A mixed people replaced them in Israel's hills. Prophecies promise Israel's return to the land.

That promise creates a puzzle for literal readers. If the tribes vanished, prophecy cannot be fulfilled literally. If they survive, they must live under another name. Attempts to find them fill curious volumes. The Apocrypha assumes the tribes still exist. Fourth Ezra sends them beyond the Euphrates to Arzareth. Akiba linked Deuteronomy's other land to the ten tribes. Tradition splits them around the River Sambation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-types-anthropol:
Anthropological types among Jews, judged by hair and eye color, are reported here. Joseph Jacobs and Maurice Fishberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A type pairs hair color with matching eye color. Fair hair with blue eyes counts as blond type. Dark hair with dark eyes counts as brunette type. Mixed pairings form a third, mixed class.

Anthropologists had classed Jews as a brunette race. Virchow's study of German schoolchildren complicated that picture. Of 75,377 Jewish children examined, under half were pure brunettes. About eleven percent were pure blonds by his count. A full forty-two percent fell in the mixed class. Austrian and Bulgarian figures show similar mixing. Even North African Jews included many mixed types. The data undercut claims of a pure Jewish type.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vazsonyi-wilhel:
Wilhelm Vázsonyi was a Hungarian writer and member of parliament. He was born at Sümeg in 1868. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. At Budapest his fine speaking made him a student leader. Social questions drew his close study from the start.

Vázsonyi led a national campaign against dueling. Anti dueling clubs spread across Hungary as a result. He also pressed for state recognition of the Jewish religion. That goal became law in 1895. In 1894 he founded Budapest's first democratic club. He started a weekly paper in 1900 and won a seat in parliament in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wahltuch-adolph:
Adolphus Wahltuch was an English doctor and medical writer. Joseph Jacobs and Harry L. Rosenthal wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Odessa in 1837. He studied medicine at Kiev, Prague, and London. He qualified in 1863 and settled in Manchester.

Wahltuch wrote many professional books. They cover medicines, catalepsy, asthma, and massage. Later works treat healing by energy. He served as consulting doctor to the Victoria Jewish Hospital. He led Manchester's Clinical Society as its president. He also helped found the city's cremation society. A keen chess player, he edited a newspaper chess column. He founded several chess clubs in Manchester.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weissenberg-sam:
Samuel Abramowitch Weissenberg was a Russian doctor and anthropologist. Joseph Jacobs and Maurice Fishberg wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Yelizavetgrad on December 16, 1867. He studied at Carlsruhe and took his medical degree at Heidelberg. That degree came in 1890.

Weissenberg's chief work studies the Jews of South Russia. He published those findings in 1895. He also researched the Karaites of the Crimea. His papers appear in German and Russian science journals. He wrote often on Jewish folk lore for Globus. His studies of proverbs and folk songs stand out. He covered Purim plays and weddings as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ya-ish-david-b-: David ben Abraham ibn Yaish was a leader of the Seville Jews in the time of Asher ben Jehiel. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was most likely a brother of Solomon ben Abraham ibn Yaish. He was most likely the father of a second Solomon ibn Yaish. That son is named in a work by Judah ben Asher. The entry rests on a long list of books and notes, but it gives no more facts of his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zakkai-15152:
Zakkai was a scholar of Palestine in the second century of this era. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a peer of Judah ha-Nasi the First. He seems to have been a pupil of Simeon ben Yohai.

He passed on a rule in the name of Rabbi Jacob. He held law debates with two great men of his house. In tale lore men style him Zakkai Rabbah, the Great. One tale of his treats a verse on the sons of Jacob. He read it of the babes cast in the Nile by Pharaoh. Those babes were saved by the worth of Moses, he said. He lived to a vast age, the entry notes at last. When asked his key, he named two plain acts of care. He never called a man by a base nick name in life.
king-henry-iv-part-2-pg2252: "I know thee not, old man" falls like a hammer in this edition: the new King Henry V casts off Falstaff at his coronation. The tavern's laughter dies as the crown's weight settles. The saddest of the histories, farewell to all follies.
kircher-oedipus-aegyptiacus-vol1-1652:
Athanasius Kircher attempts to read the hieroglyphs in Oedipus Aegyptiacus, Volume One, in Latin from 1652. Obelisks in Rome supply his texts, and Coptic his hoped-for key. Kircher got the details wrong, yet in trying he founded the serious study of ancient Egypt for the European world of his age.

Hundreds of engravings make the work a feast for the eye. Gods, rites, and symbols of Egypt fill its vast, learned pages. Jesuit missions fed his cabinet with reports from three continents here. The book stands as baroque scholarship at its most splendid, magnificent in scope even where its readings miss the mark entirely.
las-casas-brevisima-1552:
In 1552 Las Casas printed his Brevísima relación, a short account of ruin in the Indies. The Dominican friar addressed his sharp tract to the Spanish court itself. He meant to shock Spain into changing how it ruled the New World.

Page by page, he lists massacres, forced labor, and whole peoples wiped out. The style is brief, blunt, and built for outrage and action. Read at court and printed across Europe, the tract spread fast. It changed how Europe judged the Spanish conquest for good. Many still call it the most telling protest pamphlet ever written.
maidstone-six-witches-1652:
Six women were condemned at the Maidstone assizes in 1652, and their story was sold as A Prodigious and Tragicall History. The Kent trial ranks among the major witch cases of the Interregnum, the years when England had no king. The pamphlet gives the charges and the court's sentences.

Its title sells wonder and sorrow at once, and the text inside keeps that tone. Readers learn who the six were, what harm was laid to them, and how the court dealt with each. The case shows the witch trial alive and well under the republic. Print and panic still walked hand in hand in 1652.
newman-idea-of-university-1852:
When Newman became rector of a new Catholic university in Dublin, he gave the lectures published in 1852 as The Idea of a University. They define what a university is for, beyond training for jobs or trades. The book became a foundational text of Christian higher education.

Newman argues that knowledge is its own end, and that a liberal education trains the mind to think clearly and whole. He also defends a seat for theology among the sciences, since each field of study needs the others to stay honest. College teachers still quote his lectures in fights over what schools owe their students.
openalex-w1985061352:
Sinead Fitzpatrick and co-authors studied the Chagas disease vector. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2008. Rhodnius prolixus is the main Chagas vector in Venezuela. Poor rural houses stayed infested despite decades of control. The Southern Cone had fared better against its vector.

Wild, forest-dwelling bugs were suspected of reinfesting houses. Genetic tools tested whether wild bugs colonize rural homes. The title reports that they do colonise houses. Molecular markers linked house bugs to wild populations. Control must therefore watch forests, not just houses. Spraying alone cannot hold gains while wild sources persist.
openalex-w2059134652:
Louisa Messenger, Martin Llewellyn, Tapan Bhattacharyya and colleagues studied the family history of the Chagas parasite. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2012. The parasite, Trypanosoma cruzi, has a complex genetic makeup. Its mitochondrial DNA evolves quite fast. That makes it a useful marker for tracing lineages.

The team built a fine typing scheme from mitochondrial genes. They typed a panel of parasite isolates with it. They compared family trees from different gene sets. The trees disagreed clearly between regions and groups. That mismatch signals past mixing between lineages. New sequencing also revealed mixed mitochondrial genomes in single cells. Such mixing had not been shown in this parasite before.
openalex-w2115545952:
Wouter Buytaert, Zed Zulkafli, Sam Grainger and colleagues reviewed citizen science in water research. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Earth Science in 2014. Citizen science enlists the public in research work. New sensors and phones have expanded its reach. Water data are scarce in many poor regions.

Volunteers can collect rainfall and river data cheaply. Their records can fill gaps between official gauges. The review covers chances for new knowledge. It also covers ecosystem management uses. Local data can support fairer development decisions. Quality control and volunteer training remain challenges. The authors see strong promise in mountain regions.
openalex-w2922176752:
Walter Jetz, Mélodie McGeoch, Robert Guralnick, and colleagues wrote this 2019 perspective in Nature Ecology and Evolution. It proposes a shared set of measures, called essential biodiversity variables, for mapping and monitoring species populations worldwide. Species ranges and numbers are changing fast, and policy needs reliable data to respond.

The authors define these variables as a cube that joins place, time, and species, covering the range or abundance of many species at once. Raw wildlife data are patchy and uneven, so the framework uses models plus satellite-based measures to fill the gaps. The result aims at predictions that are continuous in space and time and global in reach.
openalex-w2925057452:
Takeshi Fukao, Blanca Barrera-Figueroa, Piyada Juntawong, and Julián Peña-Castro wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Plant Science. It covers what happens to plants under submergence and waterlogging, when roots or whole plants sit in too much water. Flooding is a growing risk for farms and wild plant communities.

Excess water starves plant tissues of oxygen, raises the risk of attack by pathogens, and cuts the light reaching submerged leaves. After floodwater drains, plants then face oxidative stress as they recover. The authors review what is known about these harms and about breeding tougher crop varieties as a kind of genetic insurance. They also flag research gaps and understudied questions in the field.
openalex-w2956483952:
Vladimir Ryabinin, Julian Barbière, Peter Haugan, and colleagues wrote this policy review in Frontiers in Marine Science in 2019. It describes the United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development, planned for 2021 to 2030. The proposal came from the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO.

The Decade links ocean research to the United Nations 2030 Agenda for global development goals. Its aim is to rally the ocean science community around the most pressing protection issues. That means focusing research and new technology on the health of the oceans themselves. The authors, many from the proposing body, set out the reasoning and hopes behind the plan.
openalex-w3070973952:
Petek Taneri, Sergio Gómez-Ochoa, Erand Llanaj, and colleagues published this systematic review and meta-analysis in the European Journal of Epidemiology in 2020. It examines anemia and iron handling in COVID-19 patients. Both may play a role in the multi-organ failure seen in severe cases.

The team searched six databases to early August 2020 for studies reporting blood markers such as hemoglobin, ferritin, and transferrin. They pooled one hundred eighty-nine studies covering more than fifty-seven thousand patients. Average hemoglobin sat slightly below normal ranges, and inflammation-linked iron markers shifted in patterns the analysis quantifies. The authors also test whether these cheap, routine measures can forecast which patients will fare badly, a question of daily value on crowded wards.
openalex-w4200394152:
T. Jesper Jacobsson, Adam Hultqvist, Alberto García-Fernández, and colleagues built an open database for perovskite solar cell research. Their resource paper appeared in Nature Energy, with the database released in 2021. Perovskites are promising cheap materials for solar panels, but results are scattered across thousands of papers. Comparing them, or reusing their data, has been slow and error-prone.

The team gathered device data from the published literature into one free, searchable collection. It follows the FAIR rules: data should be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. Built-in tools let users plot and analyse the records without new software. A shared, open record of what has been tried should help the field spot what works faster.
openalex-w7125686452:
Shahreen Khalid, Ali Umer, Syeda Umm E Abeeha Zaidi, and colleagues examine how anaemia affects daily functioning in chronic heart failure. Their study appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2026. Heart failure leaves patients fatigued, breathless, and prone to fluid build-up. Anaemia often coexists with it.

Low blood counts develop through iron deficiency, inflammation, and hormone problems. The authors review evidence tying anaemia to steady declines in functional status. Anaemic patients face more hospital stays and higher death rates. The link matters because anaemia can often be treated. Spotting and correcting it may preserve patients' independence and quality of life. The study adds data on a burden that routine heart failure care can overlook.
openalex-w7128725752:
Ryuji Higashinaka, Kohsuke Sato, Ryosei Ideura, and colleagues report an emergent anomalous Hall effect in EuTi2Al20. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2026. In this crystal, europium ions form a diamond network. The compound is a cubic antiferromagnet with a symmetric structure.

Such centrosymmetric magnets can still host skyrmion-like spin swirls. Competing interactions, not the usual chiral force, stabilise them. A Hall effect beyond the ordinary signal can betray those swirls. The team measured the compound's Hall response and found the anomalous contribution. Emergent signals in simple, symmetric crystals widen the hunt for skyrmion materials. Those materials are candidates for dense, low-power memory devices.
openalex-w7212016852:
Victor Ferrarezi Nagel leads a dental team reporting one case of aesthetic repair with implants in the front of the upper jaw. Missing front teeth strike at looks, speech, chewing, and self-esteem all at once. That makes the front upper jaw one of the hardest zones to rebuild well. The report comes from a university in western Parana, Brazil.

The case uses implants that fuse with the bone, topped with fixed prostheses. The authors present this route as a sound choice for the zone. It can bring back both function and looks, with more stability and comfort than removable options. A single case cannot set rules for all mouths. But it lets clinicians walk through the plan, the steps, and the result in fine detail.
openalex-w7212054852:
Rebeca Setto Vieira and Jazam Santos ask how a firm that puts people first puts human rights into practice. Such firms aim past profit, at the well-being of staff and of the world outside. The study works from past books and papers, and from the UN guide on business and human rights. That guide asks firms to stop harm where they can, and to repair harm when it occurs.

Rights, the authors find, come to life in such firms through green and social acts. Care for the planet and care for people are the paths rights take. The study walks through what human rights mean, what such firms are, and how green duty works in trade. Its point is plain: a firm's stamp on the world is direct, for good or ill. The best firms choose the good on purpose.
openalex-w7212062952:
Lucia Helena Vieda Pimentel leads a veterinary team reporting a single case: an elderly female dog with two health problems at once. One was a tumor that grows on the wall of a blood vessel. The other was anaplasmosis, an infection spread by ticks that attacks the blood. The case was seen at a university clinic in Brazil. The report sets out how the two were found in the same patient.

Single case reports earn their place by joining facts that rarely meet. A vessel-wall tumor is not an everyday find in a dog. A tick-borne infection on top of it shapes each step of care. Vets must weigh the tumor, the infection, and the age of the dog at once. Reports like this one give clinics a reference point. The next team that meets the same mix starts from here.
openalex-w7212246752:
Silvana Fernandes Biangulo and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva write on what makes a school a place where all young lives count. More seats in class, they argue, is not the same as a warm place to learn. The pair read past work on gaps in wealth, youth voice, the range of homes kids come from, and plans for fair schools. Their aim was to trace how these threads bind.

A formal seat, they find, does not bring a sense of home or a voice in class. Adult-first habits block the young. So do stiff plans that treat all pupils as one shape. Tools for those with the most need work best when tied to close care and joint plans. A fair school, they close, is built each day. It asks staff to rework time, ties, and rules with the young at the core.
openalex-w7213527152:
José Roberto Coelho, as named in the sample, and co-authors analyse comparative law in a global setting. Their 2026 bibliographic, qualitative article traces the field from ancient origins to its standing as an autonomous science. It then turns to legal harmonization across countries.

Macro and micro comparison, comparative grids, and the functional method are presented as tools for rigour. Comparative law serves lawmaking, cultural understanding, and an emancipatory purpose, the authors argue. By joining technique, culture, and critique, it can strengthen plural legal reasoning. Solutions drawn from other systems, they conclude, work best when fitted carefully to local context.
openalex-w7215683352:
Samuel Henrique da Silva Xavier led a 2026 review on fractures of the mandibular condyle, the jaw's joint knob, one of the most debated topics in facial trauma. Doctors choose among closed treatment, standard open surgery with internal fixation, and endoscope-assisted surgery. Screening nearly two hundred records, the team kept nineteen studies, including randomized trials, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses, and weighed functional outcomes and complications.

Evidence leaned toward open fixation over closed treatment for mouth opening, jaw movements, bite, and pain, though one study they kept found almost no difference. Endoscope-assisted and standard open surgery matched on function. One trial found much less temporary facial nerve weakness with the endoscope, while a meta-analysis found no clear gap, and endoscopy took longer in the operating room. Whether the endoscopic route is better is not settled, the authors conclude, pending larger trials with uniform follow-up.
openalex-w7218847952:
António Wanga Muteka led a 2026 experience report from a Brazilian health equity program on welcoming health workers and students who are mothers. The mixed study covers two towns in Ceará and draws on project databases, in-person questionnaires, mapping of children's centers and health services, documents, and the authors' own records. The question is what support exists for those who mother while working or studying in health.

The three mapped children's institutions served children of public health workers, but none offered night or full-day care, and only one reported schedule flexibility or a support partnership. No breastfeeding support, set practices to soften parental work impacts, or complaint channel were found. Families spoke of insecurity, scarce resources, dependence on grandmothers, and incompatible schedules. Welcoming, the authors conclude, requires intersectoral coordination, flexible hours, breastfeeding and mental health support, and strategies for joining work, study, and family life.
openalex-w7220372052:
Kelly Cristina dos Santos led a large 2026 integrative review comparing educational strategies for teaching atherosclerosis and shaping cardiovascular risk perception. Cardiovascular diseases are the world's leading cause of death and are strongly tied to this artery-clogging process. Searching three databases for studies from 2014 to 2025, the team kept ten and compared formats head to head, including educational videos and cardiovascular risk calculators.

Videos proved more effective for understanding how the disease process works inside the arteries. Risk calculators had the greater impact on how people perceived their own individual risk. Combined strategies showed the best overall results, joining comprehension with personal relevance. For health educators, the lesson is to match the tool to the target. Show the mechanism to teach it, personalize the number to make risk felt, and combine both when both changes are wanted.
ovid-heroides-amores-art-riley-1852:
Henry T. Riley turned Ovid's early love poems into English prose for Bohn's library in 1852. The volume gathers four works of the young Ovid: the Heroides, the Amores, the Art of Love, and the Remedy of Love. Together they made Ovid the teacher of love for the Roman world and for ages after.

The Heroides are letters from mythic heroines, Penelope, Dido, and Medea among them, to the men who left them. The Amores chase a mistress through Rome in witty elegies. The Art of Love then gives mock-serious rules for winning and keeping a lover, and the Remedy cures the wound. Riley's prose keeps the sense plain for students.
plos-pbio-0020152:
Paolo Norio and Carl L. Schildkraut studied how a virus copies its DNA in PLOS Biology in 2004. Epstein-Barr virus lives in human cells as small DNA rings called episomes. Each ring must be copied once per cell cycle, from start points that can shift.

The team found that where copying starts on the ring is flexible, a trait called plasticity of initiation. The virus does not depend on one fixed start site. That freedom may help it persist in many cell states without failing to copy. Epstein-Barr virus is tied to several cancers, so its copying rules matter. Knowing them can point to weak spots in how the virus maintains itself.
plos-pbio-0020352:
Jeb Gaudet, Srikanth Muttumu, Michael Horner, and their team charted gene activity in the early gut in PLOS Biology in 2004. The foregut gives rise to organs like the liver, lungs, and pancreas. Using the worm C. elegans, the team read gene activity across the whole genome as the foregut formed over time.

The time series shows waves of genes switching on in order, each wave preparing the next stage. Many of those genes match ones used in our own gut organs. A simple worm thus gives a timed script for a process that is hard to watch in mammals. The data set serves labs that study organ birth defects and stem cell work aimed at growing gut tissue.
plos-pone-0000052:
Raúl de la Fuente-Fernández weighed a hopeful idea about Alzheimer's disease in a 2006 paper: if doctors could protect nerve cells, neuroprotection, would fewer people develop the disease? Alzheimer's incidence, the rate of new cases, rises steeply with age, and no treatment then could prevent it. Prevention was the prize.

His analysis considers the impact neuroprotection could have on incidence, reasoning from what is known about how the disease develops over years before symptoms. Even delaying onset changes the arithmetic of an aging population, since many would die of other causes first. The paper makes that population-level case, a style of argument that now anchors Alzheimer's prevention planning.
plos-pone-0000152:
Raffaele Vardavas and Sally Blower published this modeling paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It looks at Botswana, where HIV treatment programs had expanded, and asks when transmitted drug resistance would pass the World Health Organization's detection threshold. Transmitted resistance means new infections already carry virus that resists first-line drugs.

As treatment scales up, some resistance is expected to spread; the question is how fast. The authors model the rise of resistant virus in the population. Their timing estimate helps treatment programs plan surveillance, so resistance gets spotted by testing rather than by watching patients fail therapy.
plos-pone-0000252:
Guangcheng Zhang, Amir H. Assadi, Robert S. McNeil, and colleagues published this neurobiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Reelin is a signal that guides young neurons to their places in the developing brain, acting through a receptor called VLDLR. The authors show that the Pafah1b complex, tied to the brain disorder lissencephaly, interacts with that receptor.

When brain layering goes wrong, as in lissencephaly, children face severe disability. Connecting Pafah1b to the Reelin pathway joins two lines of evidence about how layers form. The paper helps explain how migrating neurons read their directions during development.
plos-pone-0000352:
Roy R. Chaudhuri, Chuan-Peng Ren, Leah Desmond, and colleagues published this bacterial genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genome sequencing of European isolates of Francisella tularensis subspecies tularensis, the tularemia bacterium, shows a surprise. They are almost identical to the US laboratory strain Schu S4, a strain kept in labs for decades.

Wild strains from Europe matching an old lab strain so closely is odd for a bacterium. It hints that this subspecies changes very slowly and spread only in recent times. Tularemia is a watched disease, so its family history matters when tracing outbreaks.
plos-pone-0000452:
Anthony I. Jack and colleagues charted how the brain's visual territory is organized, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Vision begins in early visual cortex, at the back of the head, and spreads forward into extra-occipital regions that handle faces, places, and objects. The team studied changing human visual field organization along that route.

A visual field map records which part of what you see each patch of cortex handles. As maps change from early to later areas, they reveal how the brain trades precise geography for meaning. Understanding that organization underlies work on vision loss and on how the brain rebuilds the world from the eye's signals.
plos-pone-0000552:
Patrick S. Sullivan and colleagues studied why some HIV patients skip their medicine, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Antiretroviral therapy works only if taken consistently; missed doses let the virus rebound and develop resistance. The team identified patient and regimen characteristics associated with self-reported nonadherence to therapy.

Knowing who struggles, and with which kinds of regimens, lets clinics target support instead of blame. Simplifying regimens and matching them to patients' lives are practical responses. Adherence research of this kind quietly determines whether powerful drugs deliver their trial results in the real world.
plos-pone-0000652:
Létitia Jean, Benjamin Thomas, Abdessamad Tahiri-Alaoui and colleagues revisited a suspect enzyme in Alzheimer's disease for PLOS ONE in 2007. Diseases of abnormal protein folding need an initial trigger, which may be infectious, inherited, inflammatory, or unknown. Cutting proteins into vulnerable pieces, such as the amyloid-beta peptide, can start the aggregation.

Their angle is heterologous amyloid seeding, one protein's aggregates seeding another's. They ask what role acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme long tied to Alzheimer's, plays in that seeding. The question revisits an old player with a new mechanism in mind. If one aggregate can seed others, the spread of damage in the brain reads differently.
plos-pone-0000752:
Andy Gardner, Stuart A. West and Ashleigh S. Griffin asked whether a survival trick in bacteria counts as social behavior. Antibiotic resistance by mutation is well reported. Less known are persister cells, which resist antibiotics not by inheritance but by switching to a slow-growing state that drugs cannot kill. Within one population, only some cells make that switch.

If persisters protect their relatives by outlasting treatment, persistence could be a social trait maintained for the group's sake. Their 2007 PLOS ONE paper tests that framing. The answer shapes how doctors think about relapsing infections, and how evolution explains cells that seem to sacrifice growth for the colony.
plos-pone-0000852:
Jianing Wei, Lizhong Wang, Junwei Zhu and colleagues showed that plants call in wasp bodyguards with a specific scent chemical, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Plant volatiles play an important role in defending plants against insect attacks by attracting their natural enemies. Green leaf volatiles and terpenoids emitted from herbivore-damaged plants were known to help parasitic wasps locate hosts, the caterpillars the wasps lay eggs in.

Their title narrows the signal: plants attract parasitic wasps by releasing hexenol, one green leaf volatile. A single named molecule makes the defense testable and usable. Farmers could one day spray hexenol-like signals to summon wasps instead of spraying insecticide.
plos-pone-0000952:
Wolfgang Forstmeier asked whether female birds differ in their own readiness to mate outside the pair, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Extra-pair paternity is common in wild birds, and many studies count how often it happens. Much less is known about whether individual females have a stable personal tendency toward it.

Forstmeier separates the female's own propensity from the push of circumstance. If readiness is a lasting trait, it could evolve like any other. If it is mostly situation, then opportunity rules. The question reframes a familiar field result: behind every extra-pair brood sits a female decision, and those decisions may not be equal.
plos-pone-0001052:
Ansar Pathan, Clare Sander, Helen Fletcher and colleagues tested boosting the TB vaccine with a modified virus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. BCG is the standing tuberculosis vaccine, and its protection fades. The booster candidate, MVA85A, is a modified vaccinia virus carrying a TB antigen called 85A.

The team investigated the safety and immune effects of giving the boost shortly after BCG. They compared results with BCG alone and with an earlier trial using a longer interval. Timing can make or break a booster, since the first vaccine's response is still rising. Their comparison helps set the schedule for larger efficacy trials.
plos-pone-0001152:
Some macaques infected with SIV, the monkey relative of HIV, keep the virus under tight control. John Loffredo and colleagues studied these elite controllers in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Killer T cells are widely accepted to play a key role in holding immunodeficiency viruses down.

The team showed that CD8 T cells from the controller monkeys recognize viral pieces presented by a molecule called Mamu-B*08. They also tracked how the virus varied under that immune pressure. Work like this parallels human studies of HIV control and informs what a vaccine would need to achieve.
plos-pone-0001252:
When yeast cells meet DNA-damaging agents, they switch on a massive program of gene activity. Ivan Rusyn and colleagues sorted out which part of that program answers DNA damage specifically, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The complication is that damaging agents also harm other cell components, proteins and membranes included.

The authors studied transcriptional networks in Saccharomyces cerevisiae linked to an accumulation of intermediates from base excision repair, the pathway that fixes small DNA lesions. By tying gene responses to those repair intermediates, they isolate the DNA-specific signal. The work clarifies how cells sense and answer genome damage.
plos-pone-0001352:
Paramecium bursaria is a single-celled organism that carries several hundred green algae living inside itself. Toshiyuki Takahashi and colleagues studied its internal streaming, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The cell shows rotational, microtubule-based cytoplasmic streaming. Granules and the symbiotic algae flow in a constant direction. Why the flow matters was unclear.

The authors report that arrest of cytoplasmic streaming makes the algae multiply in the green paramecia. Stop the flow, and the resident algae grow fast. That coupling suggests the host uses streaming to manage its tenants. It is a neat finding about how the two partners live together.
plos-pone-0001452:
Jo Fleming and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on blood vessel loss in scleroderma. In this immune ill, harm to small vessels drives much of the disease burden. The team used stains and gene readouts to chart vessel state in patient tissue. They asked whether stem cell care can grow vessels back.

Their data explore whether treated patients show signs of new vessel growth. They also weigh whether the disease traits can in part reverse. Small vessel repair would be a real shift for a disease with few good options. The study gives a base for larger trials of stem cell care in scleroderma.
plos-pone-0001552:
Geoffroy Berthelot and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the arc of world records in sport. Records show the top edge of human speed and strength. The team charted how records have risen over time and what shaped that rise. Past gains had come in a near steady climb.

Their charts show the climb now bends toward a flat top. They read this as the close of a brief era of peak gains. Wars, drugs, gear, and wealth all left marks on the curve. A flat top would shift sport's focus from raw records to other forms of contest.
plos-pone-0001652:
Rulong Shen, Yin Ye, Li Chen, and their co-authors asked where the blood vessels inside tumors come from, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tumors need new vessels to grow, invade, and spread. Most accounts credit angiogenesis, in which nearby vessels sprout into the tumor. But tissue studies had hinted that tumor cells themselves might seed the vessel lining.

The team worked with precancerous stem cells, cells that are not yet full cancer but are on the way. Their results support the idea that such cells can act as progenitors for tumor vessels. The full text gives the cell markers, the vessel structures they formed, and the tumor tests. If tumors build part of their own blood supply, drugs that only block vessel sprouting may miss a route of growth.
plos-pone-0001752:
Usha Chinappen-Horsley, Glen M. Blake, Ignac Fogelman, and their co-authors hunted genes for bone length in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Human height is highly heritable but complex, and finding its genes had proven harder than expected. One reason may be that height lumps many bone lengths into one noisy measure.

Using DEXA imaging, which measures bones precisely, in the Twins UK cohort, the team ran a genome-wide linkage scan for bone lengths. They report quantitative trait loci on chromosome 5. The full text gives the twin data and the linkage peaks. Measuring single bones instead of total height is a cleaner way to find the genes that build the skeleton.
plos-pone-0001852:
Federica Chiara and co-authors studied a sugar burning enzyme's role in cancer cell death in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article.
