Their model, AOW-YOLO, tweaks a known light design in three ways. It scores its own errors in a smarter way. It keeps more fine detail when it shrinks an image. And it swaps in a leaner core. On test data it beat rival light models. It also ran about a third faster than the base design it grew from.
plos-pone-0347652:
Johan Ljunggren and seven colleagues ask how declining kidney function reshapes the body's chemistry. Their 2026 study draws on three Swedish population cohorts, over thirty-four hundred people in total. Kidneys normally clear many small molecules from the blood. When they weaken, those molecules pile up. Some may help explain why kidney problems raise heart disease risk.

Mass spectrometry measured nearly eight hundred metabolites per person. Ninety-six metabolites tracked kidney function consistently across discovery and validation samples. The team then used genetic methods to probe which links might be causal. Their adjustments accounted for body fat, diabetes, medicines, and heart risk factors. The catalogue gives researchers concrete candidate molecules for explaining the kidney-heart connection, rather than vague suspicion about waste build-up.
plos-pone-0347852:
Lai-Ying Zhang and colleagues take a single-cell census of lung wash fluid in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Bronchoalveolar lavage, a rinse of the airways, is a routine test in interstitial lung disease, a family of scarring lung conditions, but its cells had never been profiled one by one.

Profiling samples from twenty-four men with conditions including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis, and silicosis revealed sixteen distinct cell populations, with macrophage subgroups following diverging paths between diseases. The team also checked whether short telomeres, the chromosome caps tied to fibrosis risk, changed the picture, and cross-referenced the data with genetic studies. Such maps could sharpen diagnosis, since lavage is already collected in clinic.
plos-pone-0348352:
Kai Zhao and co-workers search for faulty gene changes behind a disorder of the tiny hairs that sweep mucus through airways. About half of patients with this disorder also have organs mirrored left to right. Their 2026 study reads the full gene set of three unrelated patients and checks one suspect gene closely, modeling how each change would disturb its protein.

Seven suspect changes turned up in that gene, all at spots evolution kept unchanged. Each patient carried a matched pair, one from each parent, fitting the disease pattern. The changes were predicted to weaken the protein and bend its shape. The cases widen the known list of changes in this gene and can sharpen genetic counseling for affected families.
plos-pone-0348952:
Aihua Li and colleagues asked whether a simple combined index of belly fat and blood fats predicts death risk in younger adults with type 2 diabetes. Diabetes is rising fast in young adults, and this cardiometabolic index blends waist and height with triglycerides and protective cholesterol. The team followed more than two thousand Americans aged twenty to sixty-five from national survey data.

Those with higher index values died more often, from all causes and from cardiovascular causes in particular, and the relationship rose in a straight line rather than a curve. Splitting the data into subgroups did not change the picture. A cheap index built from routine measures could help doctors spot the young patients who need the closest watching.
plos-pone-0349252:
Lv and colleagues, in a 2026 study, measure how hot industrial slag particles trade heat with air inside a spinning heat exchanger. Steelworks pour off molten slag in huge amounts, and granulating it while recovering its heat could save energy. The exchanger blows cold air against the falling hot particles. Two slags were compared: blast furnace slag alone, and steelmaking slag mixed with metal bits.

In tests backed by computer simulation, the exchanger reached its best efficiency under a sweet spot of settings, recovering most of the heat for the pure slag. The mixed slag did slightly worse, and the more metal bits it held, the worse it got. Where particles spread inside the chamber mattered a great deal to the result. The authors give designers a clearer basis for sizing and running such exchangers, a step toward steel plants that harvest their own waste heat.
plos-pone-0349352:
Shane Guenin and four colleagues test a basic assumption of airport wildlife management in this 2026 meta-analysis. Managers spend heavily to reduce bird numbers near runways. The logic seems obvious: more birds nearby should mean more collisions with aircraft. Yet nobody had checked the evidence across studies. The team searched the literature and pooled the results.

Thirteen studies provided twenty usable effect sizes. Across them, bird abundance and strike frequency did move together, with a moderate positive correlation. That supports the standard management approach. But the evidence base looks shaky. Studies disagreed a lot with each other, and signs of publication bias appeared. Statistical power was low, and methods varied widely. The tenet survives the test, though the authors urge better-designed studies before airports stake even more money on it.
plos-pone-0349852:
Manigandan Chockalingam and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE laying out a planned review of what patients themselves say about relative motion orthoses. These finger splints protect healing tendons and joints while still letting the hand move and be used, and earlier reviews focused on clinical results rather than daily-life experience. The planned review will gather studies reporting how acceptable the splints feel, how easy they are to use, and how they affect everyday activities.

The protocol follows established scoping review methods, with searches across major medical databases plus dissertations and other grey literature. Two reviewers will screen and extract the patient-perspective data independently, with a third settling disagreements, and no formal quality scoring is planned. The project is registered openly in advance. The finished map is meant to show clinicians and designers where patient experience evidence is rich, and where it is missing.
plos-pone-0349952:
Omar Hafidi and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of wheat roots. It asks how wheat variety shapes the bacteria living around and inside roots. It also asks how that links to resisting Fusarium root rot. Four varieties with known grades of tolerance were grown and compared. The team studied root shape and root chemistry. They also mapped the microbes in the soil near roots and in root tissue.

The most tolerant variety, Concret, grew roots whose traits lined up with more helpful bacteria. Those bacteria included Bacillus and Lysobacter. Chemical tests found a small set of root compounds that set the varieties apart. Those compounds also tracked with certain bacterial groups. The authors argue that breeding for root traits could steer root microbes toward protection. That would offer a living complement to chemical disease control.
plos-pone-0350452:
Laura Bravo-Merodio and co-authors used UK Biobank data in 2026 to ask why schooling seems to protect thinking skills in later life. One idea is that education strengthens brain networks through a chemical messenger system linked to alertness.

Machine learning and mediation tests combined genes for that messenger system, brain scans of a front-to-side network, and test scores. Education and biology together explained thinking scores better than either alone. Links within the right side of that network carried much of education's effect. The results hint that lifelong learning may protect the mind partly by keeping key brain connections strong.
plos-pone-0350552:
Jennifer S Albrecht and co-authors published the plan for RETRO-TBI in 2026, a study of mild brain injury in older adults. This age group suffers the most hospitalisations and deaths from head injury, yet recovery in later life is the least studied. No results are reported yet.

Two hundred fifty people aged sixty-five and over will be followed at home for a year after injury, across body, mind, mood, and sleep. Blood samples at each visit support biomarker work. The aims trace recovery paths and their predictors within and across domains. The design treats recovery as several linked journeys, not one score.
plos-pone-0350652:
Yingyang Li and colleagues studied delirium, a sudden state of confusion, in intensive care patients in 2026. They focused on a blood measure that compares stress-driven high sugar with a person's usual sugar level, asking whether that ratio predicts who becomes delirious.

Records for more than two thousand intensive care patients were reviewed. The link was not a straight line: below a low turning point the ratio mattered little, but above it the odds of delirium rose sharply. Certain patient groups showed a stronger link than others. If confirmed, a simple ratio from routine blood tests could flag patients who need closer watching and early care.
plos-pone-0350952:
Danail Georgiev Ivanov and Petar Peev studied nineteen players from FC NSA Sofia Women, the Bulgarian women's football champions. Their cross-sectional screening study appeared in 2026. They measured knee strength with a handheld device. They also compared hamstring strength against quadriceps strength. Two kinds of vertical jump were recorded, with both legs and with one leg, broken down by playing position.

Almost every player tested had at least one leg where hamstrings fell below the usual balance mark. More than half also jumped unevenly between legs in the single-leg squat jump. The authors argue that regular balance and jump checks belong in elite women's training. They also say conditioning should build hamstrings and quadriceps together, rather than chasing hamstring strength alone.
plos-pone-0351152:
B Vishnu Vardhana Naidu and co-authors tested cleaner fuel mixes for diesel-type engines in 2026. They blended two plant-based biodiesel fuels, from juliflora and kapok, and added hydrogen, a fuel with high energy for its weight, to see how the engine behaved.

One blend with hydrogen raised heat efficiency and power measures while cutting fuel use and most exhaust gases, including carbon monoxide and smoke. One harmful gas, nitrogen oxides, rose, which is the trade-off to solve. Computer methods helped find the best mix and predict performance. The work supports pairing hydrogen with waste-plant fuels for transport that pollutes less.
plos-pone-0351252:
Edwin Estomii Ngowi and Angela M Jesse judged a farm support project for villages along the Mara River in Tarime District, Tanzania. The project pushed climate smart farming, new income options, and fairer roles for women. Evidence came from more than two hundred and fifty small farmers, group talks, key interviews, and project papers.

Three quarters of farmers had taken up methods that cope better with a changing climate. Most villages had drawn up plans that respond to womens needs, and about two thirds of homes added side incomes like poultry or bees. Yet poor access to markets held sales back, and custom still limited how fully women could join in. Lasting gains will need roads to buyers and shifts in social rules, not farm training alone.
plos-pone-0351352:
Margo Gustina and Robert Berrens published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Its title states the theme: voters reveal public library value. The evidence comes from United States referendums, public votes where communities decide directly whether to fund their libraries.

Referendum results are honest measures of value because voters back them with their own taxes. Economists struggle to price public goods people do not buy in shops, and library votes offer rare real numbers. Library advocates and local officials preparing funding measures are the readers for evidence drawn from actual ballots.
plos-pone-0351552:
George Reiss and six colleagues report results for a glaucoma procedure in this 2026 study. Open-angle glaucoma slowly strangles vision when eye pressure stays high. The procedure opens a drainage cleft inside the eye with a microsurgical cannula. It then reinforces that cleft with a sliver of donated scleral tissue, a first-of-its-kind implant. Forty-one eyes from thirty-eight patients were followed prospectively across several centres. Two-thirds had resisted earlier treatment.

A year out, the numbers looked strong. Mean eye pressure had fallen by thirty-one percent, landing inside the normal range. Medication counts, complications, and any need for more glaucoma surgery were tracked as well. Most eyes were hard cases, including failed previous operations. Real-world evidence matters because surgical innovations often shine in trials and fade in ordinary clinics. A standalone, implant-supported drainage route could widen options for patients running out of them.
plos-pone-0351652:
Shots that guard against human papillomavirus prevent cancers, yet safety worries slow uptake. Siqi Zhang and colleagues mined the United States vaccine side-effect reporting system for reports filed after these shots between 2006 and 2024, in this 2026 PLOS One analysis.

Nearly seventy-eight thousand reports were included, most about girls and women, and almost half about people under eighteen. Headache and tiredness appeared most; fainting was the most common strong signal, and a heart-rhythm condition showed the strongest statistical link. Most reports came within a month of the shot. The authors note such reports show patterns to study, not proof the vaccine caused each event.
plos-pone-0351752:
Boris Camiletti and colleagues studied California avocados to learn when fruit should be picked so it ripens well without rotting. They tracked ten varieties, including Hass and several newer types, across seasons. The team measured dry matter, the usual sign of maturity, and watched for stem rot, body rot, and streaking inside the fruit during storage.

Lab work named the fungi behind the decay, mostly species of Neofusicoccum, plus Colletotrichum and Diaporthe. One Neofusicoccum species proved the most damaging in tests on fruit. Dry matter rose in clear seasonal patterns, and for some varieties it helped predict disease. The results support setting both lowest and highest maturity limits for picking, not just a minimum.
plos-pone-0351952:
Nyagawa and colleagues asked relatives of hospital patients in Dar es Salaam about donating a kidney in a 2026 study. Transplant beats dialysis for kidney failure, but Tanzania relies on living relatives as donors. More than four hundred relatives at the national hospital answered questions on knowledge, attitudes, and willingness.

Willingness was low overall, and most relatives lacked solid knowledge about donation. A positive attitude raised willingness sharply, while older age, being female, and informal work each lowered it. Teaching programs that build accurate knowledge and address fears could widen the donor pool. Without more willing relatives, many patients will stay on dialysis far longer than needed.
plos-pone-0352152:
Di Feng and four colleagues published this 2026 study of China's Grand Canal in Huai'an, where an old working waterway is being remade as a cultural attraction. The team surveyed how visitors perceive the canal's heritage value and what experiences they want, then used correlation analysis to map how the two sets of views connect.

The link proved uneven rather than simple: storytelling value and the spirit of the place drove demand for educational experiences especially hard. Feng proposes a dynamic model for turning industrial heritage into living cultural space without freezing it in the past.
plos-pone-0352252:
Ellen Kuipers and colleagues sorted people preparing for weight-loss surgery into groups by their behavior and state of mind, rather than treating them as one uniform crowd. Questionnaires before surgery covered health, quality of life, social support, eating habits, and mood for two hundred seventy-two patients. A statistical method then let natural clusters emerge from the answers.

Four profiles appeared. The largest, nearly half, reported no real deficits in any area. Another group paired decent emotional health with weaker physical functioning and problem eating, and the remaining profiles mixed struggles in different proportions. Knowing which profile a patient fits could help clinics aim support where it is needed, extra eating-behavior help for one person, mood care for another, instead of giving everyone the same preparation.
plos-pone-0352352:
Ritbano Ahmed Abdo and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One scoping review from Ethiopia. It covers research on contraception offered to mothers right after birth. The focus is long-acting methods like implants and coils. These methods prevent closely spaced pregnancies. But the Ethiopian proof base is scattered. The reviewers charted forty-two studies from databases and grey sources.

Reported uptake ranged widely. It ran from about a fifth to just over half of mothers. Personal, service, and family factors shaped the choice. Most studies were one-time surveys centered on women. Few looked at partners, at whole towns, or at lived experience. The authors call for stronger, more inclusive study designs. Such work would support true shared decisions after birth.
plos-pone-0352452:
Qin and Lee traced how talk about Fukushima wastewater changed on Chinese social media in a 2026 study. Japan's plan to release treated water from the damaged plant drew both safety worries and anger tied to national pride. The team sorted themes in more than fifty thousand posts on Weibo, a large Chinese platform.

Early posts mixed technical and safety talk with patriotic claims, but patriotic talk soon took over. Ordinary users drove most of that shift, voicing anger at Japan rooted in past wars and wider distrust of Western powers. Well-known posters stayed more technical, though some boosted anti-Western claims, which shows how a safety issue became a test of loyalty.
plos-pone-0352752:
Andrea Salas-Ortiz and seven colleagues ask whether a manager's own character shapes how well HIV clinics are run. This matters in Eswatini, where clinics serving key groups work under real money strain. The 2026 study covers forty-five community sites and their managers. Each manager filled a standard Big Five inventory. Management strength was scored from site records and direct checks. Records also captured each site's size, age, and funding.

Sites sorted into two clusters by how they were run. Sites in the stronger cluster differed clearly in how strongly they were led. Their money and people handling stood out as the main gap. Traits like openness and warmth tagged along with the stronger cluster. Who runs a clinic, it turns out, may shape the care it gives. Training that stops at buildings and budgets misses the person in charge.
plos-pone-0353352:
Han Gao and four colleagues hunt for genes that link the cell's recycling system, autophagy, to atherosclerosis, the artery-clogging disease behind most heart attacks and strokes, in this 2026 study. They mined four public gene expression datasets from patients and controls. They crossed the results with a catalogue of autophagy-related genes, then used machine learning and protein network analysis to narrow the field.

Five genes survived validation in two further datasets as characteristic markers of the disease, and their activity tracked with immune cell patterns in the tissue. Follow-up experiments in animal and cell models singled out one of them, CASP1, which ran high in diseased samples. The authors present CASP1, best known for driving inflammation, as a promising candidate for future drug work, alongside the regulatory networks they mapped around all five genes.
plos-pone-0353552:
Elena Kukhar and four colleagues published this 2026 veterinary study of three captive steppe eagles in Kazakhstan. All three birds suffered chronic bumblefoot, a stubborn footpad disease that had not healed with antibacterial drugs. The team sampled the deep lesions and identified the culprit with lab, chemical, and gene tests.

Every isolate proved to be Candida metapsilosis, a yeast that can feed on keratin and tolerate heat. The sores healed once targeted antifungal treatment began, supporting a real role for the yeast. Kukhar advises checking for fungi whenever raptor foot wounds refuse to close.
plos-pone-0353652:
Hadi Rezaei and seven colleagues chart bee, wasp, and hornet stings in northwestern Iran, in this 2026 PLOS ONE review of hospital records from 2021 to 2024. Two hundred and twenty-five patients treated across East Azerbaijan Province were analysed for who gets stung, where on the body, and when. Most patients were male, and cases peaked both in young children and in working-age adults.

Summer brought over half the stings, and the head and neck were the commonest sites — a pattern the authors link to clothing customs and work habits. Slightly more incidents happened in towns than in the countryside. The authors recommend household awareness campaigns and protective clothing for outdoor workers, tuned to local dress and jobs.
plos-pone-0353852:
Dongming Gao and three colleagues test a familiar blood-pressure drug as a possible treatment after brain injury, in a 2026 study on rats. No effective therapy exists for the memory and thinking problems that follow traumatic brain injury. Earlier work hinted that propranolol might help, and the team suspected the brain's waste-clearing network, the glymphatic system, was involved.

Rats with a controlled injury to the brain's surface scored better on thinking tests after propranolol treatment, and their waste-clearing function recovered. Harmful protein deposits fell, damaged wiring was better preserved, and a key water channel in brain support cells increased. Blocking two molecules in the same signaling chain produced similar benefits, supporting the idea that the drug works by calming that chain. The results point to a cheap, well-known drug worth testing further.
plos-pone-0353952:
Mehrbanoo Kazemi Alamouti and seven colleagues catalogue the brain chemicals that control feeding in a major wheat pest, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The sunn pest, Eurygaster integriceps, devastates grain across the Middle East and Central Asia. The team examined thirteen feeding-related neuropeptides — small signalling molecules — charting their structures and where and when each is switched on in the insect's body.

Most were far more active in the head than the gut, fitting a command role in the brain, and many ran higher in males than females. Activity peaked early in life. The atlas gives pest scientists precise targets: blocking one such signal might stop the pest feeding without broad-spectrum poisons.
plos-pone-0354152:
Bibi Hajira and three colleagues publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for mapping research on mental health around childbirth among women who moved to Canada from South Asia. Pregnancy and the year after birth are risky times for mental health, and migration can add isolation, stigma, and language barriers. South Asian women form one of Canada's largest and fastest-growing immigrant groups, yet their evidence base has never been gathered in one place.

The planned review will search five databases plus government and community sources for work published since 2000. It will chart outcomes, risk and protective factors, and the paths women take to find help. The map is meant to expose gaps for researchers and policymakers.
plos-pone-0354252:
Huang and Li, in a 2026 safety review, gather what is known about side effects of camrelizumab, a cancer immunotherapy drug used mainly in China. Real-world safety reports are scarce, so the team mined the World Health Organization's global side effect database and published case reports from the drug's first years on the market.

Six hundred reports sat in the global database, nearly all from Asian patients and most from men. Blood problems led the list, including bone marrow suppression and low platelet counts, followed by skin reactions such as rash and itching. A growth of tiny blood vessels on the skin is a signature side effect of this drug. Rare but serious events included heart muscle inflammation and severe blistering skin reactions. Case reports added timing: effects appeared a median of eight weeks in. The authors give clinicians a watch list, stressing blood counts, skin, and heart checks.
plos-pone-0354352:
Emile Charles, Suzanne Soares-Wynter, and Shu Ng survey in 2026 what primary school children in Jamaica drink, and how school surroundings shape those choices. About nine hundred children aged seven to eleven reported their drink habits, tastes, and knowledge, while audits covered the food setting inside and outside their thirty schools. Sweet drinks are common in Jamaica and schools occupy much of a child's day.

A fifth of children reported not drinking water at all. Child level factors shaped every drink type, while outside school factors weighed heaviest for sweet drinks and classroom rules mattered more for unsweetened drinks. The authors back school rules that promote plain drinks and discourage sweet ones.
plos-pone-0354452:
Ubukata and colleagues, in a 2026 study, teach artificial intelligence to spot retinitis pigmentosa in eye photographs. This inherited disease slowly kills the light-sensing cells of the retina and can end in blindness. Early signs are easy to miss, yet photos of the back of the eye are taken at routine checkups all the time and rarely screened for it.

The team fine-tuned three image models that had first learned general vision tasks, using about three hundred photos from a Tokyo-area university hospital. The best model matched the average accuracy of eye doctors, sorting patients from healthy subjects correctly in nearly every case. Heat maps of its attention showed it looked at the outer retina and the rear pole of the eye, areas where this disease leaves its marks. The authors propose the tool as a screening assistant that flags suspect photos for a doctor's closer look.
plos-pone-0354752:
Ling Zhang led a team of eight authors on this 2026 smart grid study of sorting households by their daily electricity use patterns, which utilities need for demand programs. Labeled examples are scarce, so their system, GridCL, learns from unlabeled data by comparing slightly altered versions of each day's usage curve.

Across anonymized data from three cities, the method grouped users well and, with only a tenth of users labeled, classified new ones accurately and steadily. Zhang presents self-teaching on raw meter data as a practical answer to the label shortage.
plos-pone-0354952:
Sukrit Narula and co-authors examine in 2026 whether inherited risk can spot high blood pressure missed in clinic visits. They studied younger adults in Liechtenstein who took part in a population health project. Two kinds of inherited clues were compared: a combined genetic score and simple family history.

Daytime pressure measured away from the clinic was tied to both clues, yet the two clues barely overlapped with each other. Adding the genetic score slightly improved a proven prediction tool, while family history added almost nothing. The authors stress the gain was modest, so wider work is needed before such scores help in everyday care.
plos-pone-0355552:
Sebastian Arrizabalaga and co-authors test in 2026 a new way to prepare human neural stem cells for an eye disease that wastes the central retina. They compared the older cell mix with a fresh single cell suspension in rats bred for retinal decline. Cells were placed under the retina in one eye, with salt solution in the other.

Both cell forms survived in place and kept nearby light sensing layers thicker. The new form spread more widely and gave better vision test results. Because the study bridges toward human trials, the finding matters for plans to treat a common cause of sight loss in older adults.
plos-pone-0355652:
Xiaoyuan Weng and colleagues examined in 2026 how fairly a risk score for triple-negative breast cancer holds up when it is tested across different patient groups. The score is built around mitochondrial proteostasis, the upkeep of protein quality inside the cell's energy factories. The authors focus on three traps in judging such a score: overlap of patients between cohorts, the way scores are scaled relative to each group, and the biological context of the tumors.

Cross-cohort evaluation is where promising scores often fail, because hidden overlaps and scaling choices can flatter the numbers. By naming and testing those traps directly, the study offers a caution and a checklist. It matters for any reader weighing whether a molecular score is ready to guide real treatment choices.
plos-pone-0355752:
Omaira Valencia and Oscar Bernal design a care model for people living with several chronic illnesses at once, set in Colombia's split insurance-based health system. Care there is built around single diseases, and hand-offs between insurers and providers break continuity for complex patients. Their study first gathered published evidence, then built a model from it, then asked local experts and stakeholders whether the model could work.

Evidence pointed to five structural building blocks and four recurring gaps in putting such models into practice. The resulting provider-led design ties those blocks together so one team can adapt care across conditions. Experts judged the design feasible. Valencia and Bernal offer it as a grounded option for fragmented systems in middle-income countries, where most such patients live.
plos-pone-0355852:
Yiheng Li and co-authors compared side-effect reports for two antihistamine sprays used against allergies. Azelastine and levocabastine both treat hay fever and eye allergy, but their harm profiles had not been set side by side. Their 2026 study mined the World Health Organization's public reporting database for both drugs.

More than eleven thousand adverse events were logged across the pair. General and application-site problems ranked high for both. Azelastine drew more reports involving the nervous system, while levocabastine's profile tilted differently across body systems. Li and colleagues offer the comparison as a starting map for doctors matching drug choice to patient risk, while noting reporting data cannot prove causation.
plos-pone-0355952:
Lisa Shah and seven colleagues document what life is like for people whose autonomic nervous system, the body's autopilot, fails them, in this 2026 mixed-methods study. Nearly five hundred people with conditions marked by autonomic dysfunction completed surveys, with deliberate recruitment from marginalized groups, and forty-five gave in-depth interviews. Their symptoms are often invisible and poorly captured by standard tests.

Participants most often reported anxiety, depression, sleep problems, brain fog, and fatigue, and many had cut back or stopped working. Encounters with dismissive clinicians left deep marks, while being believed transformed experiences for the better. People described researching wellness treatments on their own more than following provider suggestions. The authors describe a harmful loop in which invalidation breeds distress and mistrust, which may itself worsen the underlying dysregulation, and they call for systems that support patients and providers alike.
plos-pone-0356052:
Muhammad Hanif Abd Latif and co-authors surveyed psychiatrists in Malaysia about losing a patient to suicide. Such deaths are among the most distressing events in psychiatric practice, yet they are little studied in lower-income settings. Their 2026 survey reached psychiatrists in government, university, and private care.

About four in five respondents had experienced at least one patient suicide, often early in their careers. Most rated the emotional impact high, and over half said their clinical confidence suffered. Women reported a stronger sense of personal responsibility than men. Almost none took time off, and few sought outside support. The authors call for clear procedures, supportive leadership, and peer support after such deaths.
plos-pone-0357452:
Prabin Bajgain, Jacob M Jungers, and James A Anderson report breeding progress in intermediate wheatgrass, a perennial grain crop under development in Minnesota since the early twenty tens. Perennial grains could protect soil year-round, but yields lag annual wheat. The team grew family lines in rows at two sites over three years and tested whether gene-based prediction models, including ones that borrow information across traits, could speed selection.

Models that combined traits beat single-trait models by a wide margin, and sites differed in how well they predicted each other. Each breeding cycle gained a modest step in grain yield while plants grew slightly shorter. Bajgain and colleagues say family plots plus combined models give the young crop a workable path forward.
plos-pone-0357752:
Haizhu Wu and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study in PLOS ONE proposing a new kind of blood marker for Alzheimer's disease. Current diagnosis leans on spinal fluid tests or expensive brain scans, so a simple blood signal would help catch the disease early. The team focused on abortive transcripts, tiny eight-letter RNA fragments cut short during gene reading, and asked whether they ride inside exosomes, the small parcels cells release into blood.

In mice bred to model Alzheimer's, fragments from several disease-linked genes rose sharply in brain tissue, and the same rises appeared in blood exosomes. In dish-grown immune cells exposed to amyloid, one fragment in particular was packed into exosomes at very high levels, showing the loading is active, not accidental. Because exosomes protect their cargo and reflect brain chemistry, these fragments, the authors say, could become an early blood test, pending proof in human patients.
plos-pone-0357952:
Raghini Rajaram and colleagues published a 2026 methods study in PLOS ONE on measuring nitrate and nitrite in human muscle. These chemicals tie to nitric oxide, a signaling molecule affecting blood flow and muscle. Blood left in a biopsy sample can distort the readings, so labs wash the tissue or add a preserving solution, but nobody had checked which steps help. They took muscle from healthy adults and processed pieces with or without a salt-water wash and the preservative.

Washing clearly mattered for nitrate: washed samples read much lower and agreed better with each other, while unwashed samples were noisy and biased. Nitrite readings barely differed between washed and unwashed tissue, and the preserving solution changed neither chemical's result. The authors recommend the wash as a simple reliability step, noting they did not directly measure the blood pigments involved. That should make future muscle nitric oxide studies easier to compare.
plos-pone-0358252:
Christopher Wells and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies a human variant of TLR1, a sensor protein of the innate immune system, restricted to endosomes, compartments inside cells. The work highlights a role for the adaptor protein MyD88 in detecting Pam3CSK4, a molecule that mimics bacterial parts.

Where a sensor sits in the cell changes what it can detect and how it signals. Pinning down this pathway refines the basic map of how humans first sense bacterial invaders. Immunologists are the readers, and the detail matters for understanding why TLR1 variants affect infection responses between people.
plos-pone-0358352:
Desalegn Dawit Assele led a team of five authors reviewing HIV treatment evidence in Ethiopia, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Antiretroviral drugs suppress HIV only when patients take them faithfully every day. The team pooled evidence from many studies on how adherence affects the rate of viral suppression for Ethiopians living with HIV.

Assele's pooled evidence quantifies the payoff of adherence in hard numbers for program planners. Clinics can use those numbers to justify adherence support, from counseling to reminder systems. Ethiopia-specific synthesis matters because drug supply, distance, and stigma shape adherence locally. The review turns scattered clinic studies into one clear message about what consistent treatment achieves.
plos-pone-0358452:
Tippayarat Yoonuan led a team of six authors studying a hard clinical problem in PLOS ONE in 2026. Some patients are sure that parasites infest their skin, even when tests find none, a condition called delusional parasitosis. They often bring samples of what they believe are the pests for lab checking.

Yoonuan's group examined what those samples actually contain when checked in the lab. Setting what patients perceive beside what is really there helps doctors respond with facts and with care. Clear lab answers can guide the mix of skin care and mental health support these patients need, and can spare them harsh anti-parasite drugs that cannot help.
plos-pone-0358552: Morikawa and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how repeated skin stimulation changes pain and perception. Strong, rapid stimulation can make nearby skin extra sore, an effect called secondary hyperalgesia. The team found it also shifts how people judge which of two touches came first. Brain scans pointed to one hub, the precuneus, growing more central in its network.
plos-pone-0358652:
Fitri Ariyanti Abidin leads a team of seven surveying the mental health of university academics across Indonesia, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Nearly fourteen hundred lecturers and professors from thirty-two provinces answered questions on workload, stress, anxiety, depression, and the pressures around them. Higher education's race for publications, heavy teaching loads, and insecure posts form the backdrop the authors wanted to measure rather than assume.

More than forty percent worked beyond the legal forty hour week, spilling into evenings and weekends. Most reported low anxiety and moderate stress, with depression mostly minimal or mild. The strain concentrated in women, younger academics, those without children, and junior ranks on lower pay. Two workplace poisons stood out everywhere: publication stress and unwanted behavior from colleagues. Both tracked reliably with worse wellbeing and higher distress. The survey gives Indonesian universities a map of where their own systems wound their staff.
plos-pone-0358752:
Libo Wan leads a team of eight engineering a fever warning earplug for pigs, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The device carries a coating that changes color with heat, so staff could spot a feverish animal without handling it, an early alarm for swine fever outbreaks. The puzzle is that the coating sits away from the heat source, inside the earplug body. So the team tuned filler content, coating thickness, and dye. The goal was a sharp color change even at a distance.

Simulations set the target: with a forty degree source, the coating should flip at about thirty-four degrees. Adding a heat conducting filler sped the change and stretched the sensing distance from just over two to nearly four centimeters, though too much filler dulled the color contrast. A mid range coating thickness gave the strongest difference. The work turns heat sensitive coatings toward a practical barn side tool.
plos-pone-0359352: Ruiz and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study that checks two mental health questionnaires. One gauges how much people avoid hard thoughts and feelings; the other, PsyFlex, gauges mental flexibility. Instead of simple scores, the team used network methods, which show how each question links to the rest. A close check like this helps therapists trust what the tools measure and spot weak or repeated items.
plos-pone-0359552: Blandon and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on laser care for dark patches on the skin. The condition, acquired dermal macular hyperpigmentation, leaves lasting marks that trouble many patients. The review covers gentler lasers that remodel skin without burning the surface away. As a scoping review, it maps what treatments have been tried and what results were reported.
plos-pone-0359652:
Alyssa Smith and Daniel Smilek wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article in psychology. It revisits whether taking oral contraceptives relates to how engaged people feel in daily life, how absorbed they are in what they are doing. The authors give formulation a central role: which pill recipe a person takes.

Treating all oral contraceptives as one thing may have blurred earlier findings, since formulations differ in hormones and doses. A fresh look separated by formulation can reconcile conflicting past results. Psychologists studying hormones and cognition, and clinicians counseling patients about side effects, are the readers for this refinement.
plos-pone-0359952:
Christian Sommer and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It introduces roadDB, an R software package for exploring early prehistory and past environments. The package opens up the ROCEEH database on the human move out of Africa, a large collection of archaeological and environmental records.

R is the free statistics language many researchers already use, so a package plugs the database straight into their workflow. Scholars studying how early humans spread out of Africa can pull sites, dates, and climate data together for analysis. Tool papers like this one earn their keep by saving every later research team the same data-cleaning labor.
plos-pone-0360052:
Kumanan Govaichelvan and colleagues benchmarked in 2026 computer models that pick out the rice genes most involved in surviving drought. Their comparison covers ensemble methods, which combine many simpler models, and deep learning models. The models are fed multi-omics data, several layers of molecular measurement from the same plants, and asked to rank genes by their likely role in drought response.

A fair benchmark matters because breeders and biologists need to know which ranking tool to trust before spending seasons testing its picks. Drought is the largest single threat to rice yields in many regions, and yields must hold as climates dry. The study helps turn a flood of molecular data into a short list of genes worth experimental attention.
plos-pone-0360152:
Ruisheng Qin, Jiaxing Qin, and Shiquan Wang studied in 2026 whether giving supervisory boards artificial intelligence tools makes them more effective. Supervisory boards watch over company management on behalf of shareholders, and their work is mostly processing information: reading reports, spotting risks, asking questions. The authors frame their evidence through an information processing lens, asking how AI changes what a board can take in and act on.

Their analysis tests whether AI empowered boards oversee more effectively, and under what conditions. The question is timely, since companies are adopting AI in the boardroom faster than governance research can follow. Evidence of this kind helps regulators and shareholders judge whether the tools strengthen oversight or merely speed it up.
pmc-1140952:
Saha, Chant, Welham, and co-authors review studies on how common schizophrenia is around the world. Knowing the share of people affected shapes both health service planning and research into causes. Schizophrenia is a severe mental illness, and counts of it vary widely between places and studies.

The team searched in a systematic way for all sound studies, gathered them in one place, and summed up what they found. A careful overall picture helps planners decide how many services and staff are needed. It also gives researchers a firm base for asking why rates differ between groups.
pmc-13196252:
Nabila Y Al-Tamimi and colleagues present a 2026 case report on low vision care. Their patient was a 70-year-old woman with age-related macular degeneration in both eyes. That disease harms the center of the retina, the light-sensing layer, and blurs central sight.

Tests showed weak distance and near sight, central blind spots, and warped vision. Glasses alone gave only slight gains. Care then added a small telescope for distance and a lighted hand magnifier for reading. Staff also advised home changes and glare filters, plus food guidance and checks with a grid card. At three months her vision held steady. The case shows how tailored aids can help a person stay independent.
pmc-13197652:
Ricardo Fernández-Ferreira and colleagues present a 2026 case report on stomach cancer spread to the skin. Skin spread from stomach cancer is rare and marks late disease. Their patient also carried the HER2 marker, a growth signal that targeted drugs can block.

The patient was a sixty-year-old woman with stage four HER2-positive stomach cancer. Red, hairless patches marked her scalp, and a large firm red lump sat on her upper back. A three-drug regimen included the HER2-targeted drug trastuzumab. By the sixth cycle the scalp patch had cleared fully, and the back lump had shrunk by more than half. Gains held at one year. Fewer than twenty such scalp and neck cases appear in English reports.
pmc-13198452:
Katie M Douglas and colleagues followed women with polycystic ovary syndrome through treatment in a 2026 study. The syndrome affects hormones and can shape mood and social reading. The team asked whether anti-androgen treatment, which lowers male-type hormone action, shifts how women read facial feelings.

Thirty-three women took varied standard treatments for twelve weeks, mostly spironolactone or birth control pills. Forty healthy women served as controls. The treated group improved on ten of nineteen face-reading measures. Depression and anxiety scores also eased. The group grew faster at spotting disgusted and neutral faces and misread neutral faces as angry less often. Better fear reading tracked better mood.
pmc-13199852:
Hiroshi Adachi and colleagues present a 2026 case report on spinal cord inflammation after a flu vaccine. MOG antibody disease attacks the coating of nerves. Eosinophils, a type of white blood cell, rarely appear in spinal fluid in this disease, which made this case stand out.

Their patient was a 24-year-old man with numbness in limbs and trunk plus urine retention after influenza vaccination. Cord scans showed bright lesions inside the cord, while brain scans were clean. Spinal fluid held many white cells, with eosinophils at about six percent. Tests found MOG antibodies in blood and spinal fluid, confirming the diagnosis. The authors speculate that allergy-type signals drew eosinophils into the lesions.
pmc-13202152:
Hospitals want to track their environmental and social footprint, but the guides on offer are fragmented, and a 2026 plan authored by Guillaume C F Pain plans to consolidate them. The plan presents a scoping review of guides for monitoring the multidimensional sustainability of healthcare organizations.

The reviewers will search eight databases for studies issued from 2009 onward that apply or develop such guides at the organizational level. Two reviewers will screen titles, abstracts, and full texts against set criteria before extracting data with a custom tool. Thematic analysis will then merge the findings into one consolidated guide tied directly to how healthcare organizations actually operate.
pmc-13207752:
Growing antigen-presenting cells in a dish depends on the broth, and a 2026 study headed by Gabriel Cordeiro compares eight recipes head to head. The research article differentiates immune cells from mouse bone marrow using either GM-CSF or supernatant from L-929 cells, at several concentrations, and reads the results by flow cytometry.

GM-CSF cultures produced up to six times more of the desired presenting cells than the L-929 approach in the reported comparisons. Marker brightness on those cells also ran several times higher with the growth factor treatment. L-929 supernatant barely beat untreated controls, so the authors recommend GM-CSF while weighing yield against faithful cell character.
pmc-13234552:
Nurwidodo Nurwidodo led this 2026 education study in Indonesia, testing a hands-on learning model called EMKONTAN with future biology teachers. The model moves students through mapping local nature problems, field observation, action, and review, rather than teaching about the environment only from books.

The study compared three class setups: EMKONTAN, problem-based learning, and regular teaching. Of 120 eligible students, 108 had full test data. The EMKONTAN group scored highest on all three measures: knowledge of environment issues, creative thinking, and teamwork. The authors suggest the action-based cycle can help prepare teachers who can run active, local projects in their own schools.
pmc-13240852:
Mago and an international team offer a brain-first model for the beings people meet during psychedelic experiences. Such entities, reported as spirits, elves, or ancestors, feel strikingly autonomous. The model centers on DMT and the active inference view of the brain. It merges earlier ideas about entropic brain activity and felt beings.

Under psychedelics, sensory signals grow less predictable for the brain to explain away. The model holds the brain then credits sights and feelings to agents other than the self. A weaker self-other split, through reduced sensory attenuation, helps the illusion along. The framework aims to explain both the shared shape and cultural variety of these encounters.
pmc-13241352:
Kim of Kangwon National University writes to challenge a study claiming the food additive 4-hexylresorcinol worsens intestinal inflammation. Fan's team fed fruit flies the compound and modeled colitis in mice. Kim questions whether the doses resemble anything people eat. The letter also probes the proposed molecular mechanism.

Even the lowest fly dose ran ten to twenty times above realistic food residues. Higher doses exceeded them by orders of magnitude, suggesting toxicology rather than diet. Short injury models, Kim adds, cannot support claims about chronic exposure. Direct blocking of the ERK kinase remains unproven without dedicated enzyme assays.
pmc-13242352:
Kelly, a nurse scholar at Texas Woman's University, borrows social theory's Matthew Effect to probe her own field. Merton's 1968 concept describes how fame snowballs: early notice attracts more notice. Nursing, she argues, never studies this pattern from within. Her essay asks what that shared silence costs.

Values that prize practice and teamwork discourage inward scrutiny, and the theory base is thinning. Research-intensive posts enjoy funding and guarded research time that teaching settings lack. A 2025 federal scare over degree labels exposed nursing's thin insulation. Kelly prescribes open selection, active backing, and rotated chances.
pmc-13242452:
Joao Miguel Lopes de Melo Lima and co-authors screened plant-derived compounds in the computer as candidate treatments for two devastating shrimp diseases. Their paper appeared in Archives of Microbiology in 2026. White spot syndrome virus and a bacterial necrosis disease kill farmed shrimp in large numbers, and few effective treatments exist. The team modeled derivatives of carvacrol and thymol, aromatic compounds from herbs, against key proteins of both pathogens.

The derivatives bound most convincingly to PirB, a toxin protein of the bacterium, and their complexes stayed stable through the simulations. Binding to the viral enzyme looked weaker, though the molecules overlapped the spot where a known ligand sits. Two compounds, shortened to CVC and TMC, performed best overall. The authors present the pair as leads for laboratory testing, not as proven drugs. Shrimp farms urgently need options that do not rely on antibiotics.
pmc-13243752:
Asish Das and co-authors describe a new way to wash out the jaw joint in this 2026 case report. The patient was a 26-year-old man with pain in front of his left ear and a mouth that opened only two centimetres, after five years of jaw clicking.

Standard joint washing uses two needles, which can be fiddly and may need repeated tries. The team instead used two thin spinal needles through a single entry point, one for fluid in and one for fluid out. They report that the method washed the joint well, cut down tissue damage, and could make the procedure quicker and easier for other clinicians.
pmc-13244552:
Hiroyoshi Nozaki and colleagues hunted for what predicts bad reactions to injections of a reformulated psoriasis drug. Their short report appeared in Acta Dermato-Venereologica in 2026. Ixekizumab, an antibody against interleukin-17A, works well against psoriasis but often stings. In late 2022 its maker removed a citrate ingredient blamed for discomfort, yet many patients still reacted. The team reviewed twenty-three patients on the new formulation.

Age, sex, body measures, disease subtype, and general treatment history had already failed to explain who reacts. The authors zeroed in on a narrower suspect: which specific biologic drug a patient had used before switching. Their analysis raises prior exposure to particular biologics as a potential risk factor for administration reactions on the modified product. With so small a series, the finding is a lead, not a rule. It tells clinics which switchers deserve a warning and a watchful first dose.
pmc-13245152:
Malassis and colleagues asked how people learn patterns without being able to explain them, in this 2026 Neuroscience of Consciousness paper. Standard tests of implicit and explicit learning rely on spoken instructions, which excludes young children, animals, and people who cannot use language. The team rebuilt one classic test so that no words were needed.

Thirty-two adults learned spatial sequences, then had to either copy them or avoid them, discovering the rules by trial and error. Only participants who later described both the rules and the sequences could actually control their copying. The result supports awareness as the marker of explicit learning, and gives researchers a word-free test for other populations.
pmc-13245752:
Larson and co-authors looked for hidden heart injury in men with HIV who use stimulants, in this 2026 PLOS One study. People with HIV already face higher cardiovascular risk, and stimulant drugs may add strain. The team analyzed seventy-two men in a South Florida cohort, grouping them by HIV status and recent stimulant use.

Blood tests measured high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T, a protein released when heart muscle is stressed. Men who had both HIV and stimulant exposure were far more likely to show detectable troponin, and higher drug metabolite levels tracked with higher troponin. The authors suggest doctors assessing heart risk should ask about stimulant use, while noting bigger studies are needed.
pmc-13246952:
Sukienik, Nakamae, and Miyagi reviewed large-animal models of a leaky heart valve in this 2026 Journal of Cardiovascular Translational Research article. Tricuspid regurgitation, leakage of the valve between the right heart chambers, is increasingly treated, yet doctors lack solid evidence on when to intervene, so realistic animal models matter. The authors sort existing sheep, pig, and dog models into direct approaches that damage the valve parts and indirect ones that strain the right heart.

Direct models reliably cause leakage and suit primary valve disease. But most human disease is secondary: the valve itself is normal while the ring around it stretches and the heart remodels, which current models reproduce poorly. The authors guide researchers toward leaflet-preserving models that mimic that common form.
pmc-13250252:
Lin and a large team compare two diets for belly fat and blood lipids in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes. Their 2026 Food Science and Nutrition trial enrolled eighty-nine patients after two weeks of intensive insulin therapy. One group ate a low glycemic load diet, and the other a standard calorie-restricted diet, matched for total energy.

Over one year, with checks every three months, both groups lost weight around the waist and improved several metabolic measures. The low glycemic load group differed mainly in diet makeup and in changes to a blood sugar control marker. No clear advantage appeared for waist size, body mass, or fat-related indexes between the diets. The authors conclude that the two approaches work about equally well after insulin therapy.
pmc-13250652:
Wang and co-authors search for gene markers shared by metabolic syndrome and coronary artery disease. Their 2026 Endocrine Connections study mines five public gene expression data sets covering both conditions. The two disorders often travel together in older adults, but sensitive shared markers for spotting them have been lacking.

Comparing changed genes across the data sets left a small overlap, and network plus machine learning methods narrowed the field further. Two genes, ADRB2 and KDM6A, ran lower in both diseases and separated patients from healthy samples well in tests. Single-cell data and laboratory checks of patient samples backed the pattern. The authors offer the pair as candidate diagnostic markers and as clues to the shared biology of the two conditions.
pmc-13252752:
Napat Jantaraprasit and a large team build a sharper palm oil forecast for Thailand in this 2026 study. Yield forecasts guide farm choices and climate planning, but coarse weather data and bias in crop models have limited their accuracy.

Their pipeline first shrinks weather and climate data to fine local scale, then feeds a process-based crop simulator whose errors a machine learning model corrects. In Surat Thani province, the crop model alone badly overshot yields, while the hybrid cut the error by nearly two-thirds. Seasonal forecasts reached eight months ahead with useful skill. Long-range climate runs suggest southern Thai palm output is fairly resilient, dipping mid-century before steadying.
pmc-13253152:
Jarrod Ludwig and colleagues read salmon diets in the fats of their eggs in this 2026 study from California. In 2020, several salmon populations were found short of thiamine, vitamin B1, and the team wanted to know whether what mothers ate at sea explained the shortfall.

From 2020 to 2022 they collected unfertilised eggs from Chinook salmon, coho salmon, and steelhead, plus the ocean prey those fish eat, and profiled fats in both. Eggs whose fat pattern matched a herring-rich diet carried more thiamine. Eggs matching anchovy or krill diets ran lower. Fat quality, not quantity, drove egg thiamine, a warning as ocean prey mixes shift.
pmc-13253552:
Emily Krauss wrote this 2026 commentary on an updated classification of nerve injuries. Surgeons sorting damaged nerves must judge which injuries will heal alone and which need an operation, and they lean heavily on electrical tests of nerve and muscle.

The paper under discussion expands the classic Sunderland scale at both ends. A new grade zero covers a blood-flow block that silences a nerve while electrical tests stay normal, a pattern long recognised informally. Grade six, added earlier by the senior author, covers mixed injuries. Krauss praises the update's teaching cases and test-reading guidance, calling it essential reading for trainees and a step toward a surgical decision roadmap.
pmc-13253652:
L van der Broeck and colleagues price broken bones that refuse to heal in the Netherlands in this 2026 study. When a long bone fracture never knits, called a non-union, patients face repeated care and long absences from work, and the full societal bill was unmeasured.

Using questionnaires at a specialist clinic, the team counted health care, family, and lost-work costs over the three months before the visit. Health care averaged about 8,900 euros per patient, family costs about 1,400, and lost productivity about 4,300. Quality-of-life scores sat far below population norms. Worse non-union severity and lower quality of life, not the original injury type, drove higher costs.
pmc-13253752:
Juan Sánchez-Mateos and José David Flores-Félix review ways to block bacterial talk in a 2026 paper. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a germ that causes hard, lasting infections, mainly in people with weak immune defenses. It uses quorum sensing, chemical signals between cells, to switch on attack factors and build biofilms, slimy cell layers.

The review covers five ways to jam those signals, from blocking signal making to breaking signals down with enzymes. It also covers blocking the cell parts that receive signals. Gains are real, the authors note, but drug stability and uneven strains still limit use in patients.
pmc-13254252:
Enkui Lian and co-authors describe a simpler lithography set-up in a 2026 methods paper. Lloyd's mirror interference lithography uses overlapping laser beams to print fine patterns into a light-sensitive coating. Their system needs only a fibre-coupled single-frequency laser, a flat mirror, and an optional wave plate.

Using a factory-set fibre laser removes the tricky manual alignment of older set-ups. The system is cheap, robust, and easy to run, the authors say. With a 405-nanometer laser, it made one- and two-dimensional arrays with spacing below 220 nanometers. Full steps for sample prep, exposure, and processing are given.
pmc-13257652:
Shouchang Jiao and colleagues created plastic films that glow with a twist, literally, after the light goes off. Their 2026 work combines long-lasting room-temperature phosphorescence with circularly polarized light. Such chiral glow is hard to achieve, yet prized for secure displays and labels.

They stirred chiral naphthyl phosphoric acid derivatives into an epoxy resin, then hardened it with heat. The rigid network calmed wasted energy loss and steadied the excited states behind the glow. One blend kept phosphorescing for nearly a second and flipped its emission from fluorescence to phosphorescence on curing. The films were demonstrated in multi-layer anti-counterfeiting designs.
pmc-13259552:
Omar Brijawi, Frank Epitropoulos, and Patrick Chen present a 2026 case report of a delayed complication after an intramural duodenal hematoma. That term means a collection of blood inside the wall of the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine. Their patient was a 59-year-old man with coronary artery disease who developed the hematoma after abdominal surgery for a blocked small bowel. He improved with stomach drainage and acid-blocking drugs and went home.
