A scope exam found diffuse severe erosive duodenitis, meaning raw inflamed duodenum, with shallow ulcers and a red spot blamed for the bleeding. Biopsies confirmed acute inflammatory injury. Transfusion and high-dose acid-blocking treatment stopped further bleeding.
pmc-13260452:
Rodolfo Christiansen leads a 2026 geoscience study of natural hydrogen generation during serpentinization. Serpentinization is a reaction in which water alters mantle rocks and releases hydrogen gas. The team studied two rock types: fertile lherzolites in the Western Pyrenees and depleted harzburgites in Northern California. They combined three-dimensional geophysical imaging, which maps rock properties underground, with numerical models of fluid-rock reactions to estimate production rates.

Estimated rates were low, at about 0.1 to 0.5 tonnes of hydrogen per year per cubic kilometre of reactive rock. Across the full reactive volumes, that totals roughly 300 to 600 tonnes per year. Rates were limited mainly by hydrogen saturation in the fluid and by reaction speed. The authors conclude that large, economically useful accumulations would need thousands to tens of thousands of years to form.
pmc-13261052:
Claire M Broderick leads a 2026 human challenge study of how flu infection affects control of mycobacterial infection, the family that includes tuberculosis. People in a flu challenge study gave blood before and after flu infection. A glowing growth test showed how well their blood controlled mycobacteria in the lab. Gene activity, cytokines, and cell tests tracked how flu changed immune reaction to the bacteria.

Flu reduced the immune control of mycobacterial growth in the assay. Innate immune pathways, including type 1 interferon pathways, were switched on by flu, but their later response to mycobacteria was reduced. Many genes' responses to a test microbe were muted after flu. The authors suggest flu may be a risk factor for progression to TB disease, and that flu shots might help protect high-risk groups.
pmc-13261152:
Seamus O'Reilly and co-authors write a 2026 editorial on spreading planetary health research at cancer conferences. Planetary health links human health to the state of the planet. It discusses a study by Delaye and colleagues that scanned a major cancer meeting for work with green benefits.

At the 2025 European Society of Medical Oncology Congress in Berlin, 2,937 abstracts were presented to over 37,000 attendees. Delaye's team found 10 abstracts readable through a planetary health lens. They suggested meaningful cuts in drug use, clinic visits, treatment length, or care load. The topics ranged from preventive care and gentler treatment to marker-guided choices and non-drug measures. None had directly measured green impact. It argues meetings are influential spaces that can spread this message, since health depends on the planet's health.
pmc-13262852:
Qiuling Li and co-authors study support cells in the brain after stroke in rats in a 2026 journal article. After a blocked artery is reopened, a chemical messenger called glutamate builds up and harms brain cells. Astrocytes, star-shaped support cells, clear most of it through a transporter called GLT-1. The team tested how a growth signal pathway affects that transporter.

In their rat model, injury switched the pathway on, stirred up astrocytes, and lowered GLT-1 levels. Blocking the mTOR part of the pathway restored GLT-1, calmed astrocytes, and reduced inflammation, cell death, and movement problems. Blocking the Akt part gave no such protection and lowered GLT-1 further. The authors suggest mTOR blocking as a possible protective route.
pmc-13262952:
Zhijuan Wang and colleagues test a plant compound against liver cancer tied to hepatitis B in a 2026 journal article. The compound is quercetin, a natural substance found in many food and medicinal plants. Using network analysis, docking tests, cell studies, and mouse tumors, the team looked for its main target and how it slows the cancer.

Analysis of the target network pointed to EGFR, a growth signal receptor, as the principal target. In cell tests, quercetin curbed cancer cell growth and movement, with stronger doses weakening EGFR and a chain of signals below it. It also reversed a process that helps cancer cells spread. Mouse studies, checked against a known EGFR blocker, supported the same mechanism, the authors report.
pmc-13263252:
Henna Uosukainen and colleagues follow the long-term health of children who had PFAPA syndrome in a 2026 journal article. PFAPA causes repeating fevers with mouth sores, sore throat, and swollen neck glands, mostly under age five. The Finnish team surveyed former patients treated at three university hospitals from 2008 to 2018, five to sixteen years later, against matched population controls.

Replies came from 98 patients and 490 controls. Allergy-type conditions, called atopy, were the only chronic condition clearly more common in former patients. They also reported more ear infections, ear tube surgery, bronchitis, fungal infections, and hospital stays for infections. Other chronic conditions and childhood exposures matched controls. The authors suggest health care seeking may explain part of the infection gap.
pmc-13263952:
Abdelrahman I Hleeba and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on how well false teeth stick to a 3D printed denture base. They tested sandblasting, which roughens a surface with fine grit, on both standard teeth and milled teeth. Bond strength was the main measure.

The team made 48 samples in three groups: no blasting, blasting with fine grit, and blasting with coarse grit. Both blasting and tooth type changed bond strength, and blasting had the larger effect. Bonds rose as grit size rose, and milled teeth held best in every group. The strongest result came from milled teeth blasted with the coarse grit. Failure patterns also shifted with treatment.
pmc-13264552:
Helena F Alacha, Daniel A Waschbusch, and Dara E Babinski wrote a 2026 study of strain in caregivers of girls with behavior and attention problems. Most past work focused on boys. The team tracked girls aged 10 to 15 for one year to see how symptoms and strain move together.

The study held 197 girls and their caregivers. Symptoms of ADHD, defiant behavior, and borderline personality traits all rose over the year, while total strain slightly fell. Each symptom type linked to every form of strain, both at one time and later. Defiant behavior grew more tied to strain over time, while the ADHD link to practical strain weakened. The authors say strain is specific to symptom type and shifts as girls grow.
pmc-13264652:
Chenchen Yang and colleagues published a 2026 computer study on Perilla frutescens, a medicinal herb, against atherosclerosis, the fatty buildup that clogs arteries. Herbs act on many targets at once, which makes their action hard to pin down. The team combined network analysis, single-cell data from human plaques, and machine learning to find the herb's key targets.

Their search gave a core set of 10 genes tied to how plaque macrophages, immune cells in the plaque, turn into foam cells stuffed with fat. The gene set sorted patients well in an outside data set. One cell signal route stood out as a hub for inflammatory talk between cells. Computer docking showed the herb's main active compound, luteolin, binds one target strongly, and motion simulations backed that bond. The authors offer the targets for lab testing.
pmc-13265252:
Momoko Soda and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a chest wall abscess caused by Gordonia sputi, a rare soil bacterium, in a healthy man. These germs grow slowly and are hard to identify, so diagnosis often drags. Their patient was a 45-year-old man with no immune problems.

After blunt trauma, a painful mass grew on his left chest wall, though he had no fever. Scans showed a contained abscess, and surgeons drained it. First cultures grew nothing, but tissue study hinted at an actinomycete germ. After the wound split open, a second cleaning gave samples that a rapid protein test and gene sequencing named as the rare bacterium. Based on drug tests, he took amoxicillin by mouth for six months. The wound healed fully with no return in a year of follow-up.
pmc-13266052:
Xiaoyang Li and co-authors wrote a 2026 study on a gentler brain-computer interface that reads brain waves from flicker-free text patterns. Classic systems flash bright blocks, which tire the eyes and confine signals to the back of the head. Their method presents sequences of text characters as the steady stimulus instead.

Sweep tests showed the text method evoked responses at both the back and side-back of the head, unlike plain flicker. It also cared less about stimulus size and brightness. The team built a forty-target speller and tested it live: it transferred about 235 bits per minute, a high speed, and users rated it significantly more comfortable on questionnaires. The authors present text stimulation as a practical direction for fast, comfortable visual interfaces.
pmc-13269952:
Michael A Mastroianni and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on Major League Baseball pitchers returning after a second elbow ligament reconstruction, called revision surgery. Results after first-time surgery are well known, but not after revision. Records covered 61 pitchers who had revision surgery from 2014 to 2024.

Only 1.6 percent were back playing at one year, rising to 44.1 percent at two years and 63.2 percent at three years. Average return took 605 days. After first-time surgery, returns were far higher, at 71.9 percent by two years and 82 percent by three. Just 14.3 percent regained their pre-injury value rating within three seasons. The authors call revision outcomes clearly worse.
pmc-13270252:
Cheng-Yi Fan and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 testing a score called SADFUL for spotting blood infection in patients who return to the emergency department unplanned. Records came from two Taiwanese hospitals of different levels, covering March 2019 to December 2022. The score was compared with three simpler tools.

Blood infection was present in 2.2 percent of 5,455 returning patients. The SADFUL score scored 0.64 on an accuracy curve at the academic center, significantly beating the rival tools there. At the rural hospital it scored 0.72 but was not significantly better. Its best cut point also differed, at 2 versus 4. The authors rate all the tools as limited for this job.
pmc-13270552:
Chanelle Galea and Rita Pace Parascandalo report a 2026 cross-sectional study, a one-time survey, on acupressure in care around pregnancy and birth in Malta. Acupressure means firm pressure on set points on the body, and it has been linked to less nausea, pain, and anxiety.

The authors surveyed members of the Malta Midwives Association, inviting all 240 members, and received 94 replies between July and September 2024. Midwives showed strong interest, but only 12 said they used acupressure in practice. Lack of training, lack of schooling on the topic, and lack of clear, evidence-based guides were the main reasons for holding back.
pmc-13271052:
Jiaqi Tong is lead author of a 2026 study protocol, a published plan for a trial not yet reported, comparing two pain drugs after stomach cancer surgery. Patients will have keyhole removal of part of the stomach, plus a nerve block for the upper abdomen, and the question is whether oxycodone controls inner, deep pain better than sufentanil.

The single-centre, double-blind trial will enrol 96 patients and assign them evenly to patient-controlled pain pumps with one drug or the other. The main outcome is a recovery quality score 24 hours after surgery. Other measures include pain scores at rest and in motion, total opioid use, and gut recovery. No results are reported in a protocol.
pmc-13271152:
Keyao Huang is lead author of a 2026 secondary analysis, a new look at earlier interview data, on lung transplant recipients returning to work. Going back to work is a key sign of recovered quality of life after transplant, yet re-employment rates are typically poor, and patients' needs differ widely.

The authors re-analysed deep interviews with 38 recipients from a major hospital in Jiangsu Province, China, and built four user profiles. Rapid Return patients recovered well and rejoined society fast. Meandering Return patients worked but kept balancing health and job demands. Life-Centred patients chose not to work, putting health first. Conflicted and Hesitant patients wanted to work but faced physical, mental, and social barriers.
pmc-13272252:
Ayman El-Menyar is lead author of a 2026 retrospective study comparing mechanical and manual cardiopulmonary resuscitation in traumatic cardiac arrest. Resuscitation means chest compressions to keep blood moving. Heart stoppage after trauma kills most patients despite better trauma systems. Ambulance services increasingly use compression machines during transport.

The review covered 610 patients with blunt trauma arrest treated from 2016 to 2024, average age 34 and mostly male. In total, 220 received mechanical compressions during transport and 390 manual compressions at the scene only. The mechanical group reached hospital alive far more often, at nearly ninety-nine percent against about thirty-nine percent. Yet restored circulation on arrival stayed low in both groups. Overall thirty-day survival for everyone was under one percent.
pmc-13273852:
Pařízek and colleagues test atropine in pigs whose hearts slow during oxygen starvation. Their 2026 journal article is a randomized cross-over trial. The setting mimics emergencies where a patient cannot be intubated or oxygenated.

Eight anesthetized pigs each underwent two apnea episodes. Apnea means breathing was stopped. At the onset of slow heart rate, pigs got atropine or placebo. The order was random. Time to cardiac arrest was the main outcome. Atropine gave 142 seconds, placebo 138 seconds. The difference was not significant, with p equal to 0.803. Four animals arrested faster on atropine, four slower. No gains appeared in oxygen delivery or resuscitation. The authors advise treating the hypoxia itself first.
pmc-13274052:
David Emad Sobhy and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial comparing two surgical routes for broken bones around the eye and cheek. Such fractures can be reached through the eyelid lining, but extra reach may need a cut near the eyebrow. The trial tested a stair-step extension of the eyelid route against the standard route plus that eyebrow cut.

Twenty patients aged eighteen to sixty were split evenly between the two methods. Both gave the same access and exposure time, but the stair-step route took less total operating time. Its patients had less swelling, faster return of feeling below the eye, and only that group had scars described as not noticeable.
pmc-13274552:
Benoît Ferment and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on predicting who responds to a cell therapy for multiple myeloma, a blood cancer of plasma cells. The therapy, idecabtagene vicleucel, re-engineers a patient's own T cells to hunt a marker called BCMA. It is the only such product available in France, and immune factors behind its success were little studied.

The team reviewed every patient treated at Saint-Louis Hospital between October 2021 and December 2024, profiling blood and T cells at collection and tracking the engineered cells' growth over the first month. As the title reports, how strongly the CAR T cells expanded after infusion predicted patient outcomes. Response was judged at six months by international criteria.
pmc-13274852:
Xiang Gao and colleagues present a 2026 journal article sorting Chinese elementary students into profiles of social-emotional competence, skills like managing feelings and getting along with others. The survey covered 11,323 children in grades three to six across forty-two schools in eastern, central, and western China. A statistical grouping method called latent profile analysis did the sorting.

Four profiles emerged: high competence in 25.8 percent of children, medium-to-high in 36.2 percent, low-to-medium in 31.3 percent, and low in just 6.7 percent. Girls, urban students, children with siblings, and those not left behind by migrant parents were more likely to sit in the high group than the small low group. The authors suggest support tailored to each profile.
pmc-13275152:
Ferris Zeitouni and colleagues present a 2026 practical review of AI tools that draft clinical notes from patient conversations. Note-writing burden drives doctor burnout, and AI scribe services have spread fast in response. The article is a primer for doctors weighing these platforms for their own practice.

Across products, core features include live transcripts, note drafting, many languages, custom templates, and health privacy safeguards. Deeply linked systems can summarize old notes and draft referral letters but demand long setup. Simpler tools start fast with weaker record linking. The authors flag real risks alongside the time savings: invented content, privacy exposure, and open legal risk when an AI note is wrong.
pmc-13276152:

Under heat stress, their cells moved internal cargo more slowly and took up fewer signaling molecules. Young nerve junctions looked normal in shape, but markers of synapse maturity, the signals at connection points, were disrupted. The authors offer the fly as a model for tracing how these mutations disturb the developing brain.
pmc-13276252:

Sixty healthy children aged ten to twelve were assigned by chance to the three rinses for three weeks. Saliva samples were taken before and after. Bacteria counts ended far lower in both the alkaline water and mouthwash groups than in the tap water group. The mouthwash still beat alkaline water head to head. The authors call alkaline water a promising extra hygiene aid, while stressing that longer trials must test whether it truly prevents cavities.
pmc-13276552:
James Bruzzese and Lisa Doan present a 2026 case report on burning back nerves in a patient with a leadless pacemaker. Radiofrequency neurotomy uses heated needles to quiet the small nerves feeding painful spinal facet joints. Its electric current raises fears of disturbing implanted heart devices, and leadless pacemakers, tiny capsules inside the heart, lack specific guidance.

Their patient was an eighty-one-year-old man whose diagnostic blocks had confirmed facet pain. Heart specialists first verified he did not depend on the pacemaker to live. The device was checked but not reprogrammed before the procedure. The team used a bipolar technique, keeping current between two needle tips, under continuous heart monitoring. Everything finished without incident, the device checked out normal afterward, and the patient reported significant pain relief. The authors share their precautions for a growing patient group.
pmc-13276752:

The seventy-three-year-old man, who had schizophrenia, arrived with severe oxygen shortage and a collapsed left lung. Scans showed an oval object completely plugging his left main airway. Through a flexible scope, doctors saw a whole grape wedged tight. Forceps slipped off its smooth, fragile skin repeatedly. They cut a narrow channel through the grape and threaded in a balloon catheter. Inflating the balloon behind the grape and pulling gently freed it intact. The authors propose this balloon method as a rescue for large, soft airway blockages.
pmc-13278852:

At three months, past-month abstinence was fifty-five percent in the sham-training control group and fifty-two percent in the training group, a non-significant difference. All secondary outcomes were also non-significant. Longer admissions and session counts may shape any effect, exploratory analyses hinted.
pmc-13279052:

Both groups mostly agreed their degree had developed each attitude, with agreement strongest for appreciating how pharmacology matters to society. The weakest area in both groups was spotting job opportunities and pursuing career goals. Graduates answered with more spread and stronger views at both ends than students still studying.
pmc-13279952:
Lucy R. Boxall and colleagues report a 2026 interview study of what helps or blocks cuts in free sugar intake. Free sugars are sugars added to foods or in juices and honey. By group checks, advice groups held more know how, with practical fixes, than the control group. Early hopes and intent ran high, then met habit and life strain over weeks. Success at twelve weeks split by those forces. Timed interviews catch change as it forms, not just in hindsight.
pmc-13280552:

pmc-13281952:

Shared needs, they argue, are where pandemic readiness should invest.
pmc-13282052:

pmc-13282252:

For complex lesions, though, they judge the robot approach safe and helpful, especially where delicate inside work is needed.
pmc-13282452:

Tests identified Staphylococcus aureus, a common aggressive bacterium. Targeted intravenous antibiotics treated her successfully, and draining the abscess by surgery proved unnecessary. They stress early diagnosis and prompt treatment to prevent lasting damage, and remind clinicians that back pain in teenagers can hide structural causes.
pmc-13282552:

pmc-13282752:

pmc-13282852:

The authors say the tool can audit triage quality directly.
pmc-13282952:

They reported pain relief, social support, and new insight for daily coping. They liked small groups, song sharing, and guided music imagery. They also used session recordings and shared playlists between meetings. Findings guide a larger future program.
pmc-13283952:

Electrode types include laser-written graphene and graphene blends with other minerals. Reported devices show tiny detection limits and strong bending tolerance. Heat tolerance reached high levels in some cited designs.
pmc-13284752:

That same dose did not harm human gum fibroblasts and boosted their growth and collagen output, while lowering an inflammation marker. The authors see a clear dose window worth further study.
pmc-13285552:
Root fungi of a rare orchid vary sharply by home ground, Yu Wu and co-authors show in a 2026 field study of Paphiopedilum barbigerum. Knowing which fungi ride with this endangered slipper orchid could aid captive growth and return to the wild. Roots came from twenty-one plants at seven sites: guarded wild ground, unguarded wild ground, and one return site.

Sequencing sorted the fungi into thousands of species, led by two big phyla. Guarded wild roots held the richest fungal mix, laced with dry-hardy kinds. The return site fungal crowd looked much like the unguarded wild crowd, a hopeful sign for replanting. Three shared fungi formed a core set across sites. The authors offer the map for breeders.
pmc-13285752:
D Pesántez and colleagues describe a 2026 test of a smart assistant for early cancer drug trials. Trial teams must answer hard questions from long, tangled protocol files, and hunting through them eats hours. The team built a tool that pairs document search with a large language model to answer queries in plain chat form.

In a two-arm test, staff answered trial questions with or without the assistant, ten people in each arm. Those with the tool replied in about 15 minutes on average, against roughly 27 minutes for the control group. Blinded experts scored answers in both arms as mostly correct, with no real gap in quality. Users also reported high satisfaction, which points to faster trial work at no cost to accuracy.
pmc-13286052:
Anil Pant and co-authors present a new antiviral lead against poxviruses in a 2026 drug discovery study. Mpox keeps spreading, smallpox remains a feared what-if, and the shelf of proven drugs holds only a few entries with shaky human proof. A screen of the team's own compound library hunted for a fresh chemical that could stop these viruses in human cells.

One compound, a hydroxypyridone analog coded ZW-2038, curbed vaccinia, monkeypox, and cowpox viruses at low doses in skin cells. It also cut virus growth in gut tissue models from people and monkeys and in mouse lung tissue kept alive in the lab. Inside infected cells it blocked copying of viral DNA and the gene activity that follows. Mouse tests showed poor uptake by mouth, so the authors frame it as a strong but unfinished lead.
pmc-13287252:
Yuhei Yamaguchi and co-authors rechecked tumour samples in 2026 from 84 patients with spreading breast cancer. Each HER2 level had first been read with an older test. It was later read with a newer one used to judge eligibility for a targeted drug. Retesting took place between May 2023 and November 2024.

Results disagreed for 60.7% of patients, most often stepping down one grade. Samples taken from spread sites and tumours lacking progesterone receptors were more likely to change. About a quarter of patients whose results changed lost the low-HER2 label that opened access to the drug. The authors urge care when old and new readings are compared in clinic.
pmc-13287452:
Claudia Neubauer and co-authors tested a new photon-counting scanner in 2026 for staging breast cancer through the chest and abdomen, with magnetic resonance imaging as the reference. Seventy-five women with 79 newly found cancers had both scans, with the new scan taken lying face down.

Readers rated cancer visibility and image quality as excellent. Tumour size matched the reference scan closely. Accuracy was good for tumour stage, spread pattern, and armpit nodes, and very high for chest-wall nodes. It was weaker for a non-invasive cancer form. Iodine uptake inside tumours differed by subtype, lowest on average in triple negative cancers. Larger confirmatory work is still needed.
pmc-13288052:
Yu-Hsu Chen and co-authors mined the Taiwan Biobank in 2026 for signs that flag low bone density. A learning model covered 19,868 adults aged forty and over. All had bone scans between 2020 and 2022. Explanatory plots then ranked which body measures drove each prediction, separately for women and men.

Low density affected 44% of participants. Model accuracy was fair in women and weaker in men. Age, menopause state, and body mass led for women; age, body mass, and waist size led for men. Blood counts, fat share, blood pressure, and kidney and liver markers also carried weight. The authors argue screening should use sex-specific sign sets.
pmc-13288852:
Paul C Toboltoc and co-authors review blood cancer care in the COVID-19 years in 2026. Their piece is a narrative review. Blood cancer needs fast diagnosis. It needs frequent visits and transfusions. Intensive therapy and transplants also feature. The pandemic scrambled all of that.

The authors drew on disruption studies. Registries, remote-care cohorts, and transplant surveys joined in. Harmful delays were split from useful inventions. Protected routes and risk triage helped. Clean infection circuits helped too. Remote review suited stable patients. The advice is to keep the discipline. Crisis limits that only rationed care should go.
pmc-13288952:
Xuanhe Liu and colleagues offer a 2026 trial plan in Anhui, China. The trial tests value-led care for heart risk. Village clinics will take part as whole units. The plan covers 32 clinics in all. Half will get the new care model. Half will keep usual care.

The model ranks care steps by cost value. It guides doctors to pick high-value steps first. Training and feedback will back the model. The trial will enroll 1,920 adults. All will have high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart disease. Cost per good health year is the main result. Checks run at 12 and 24 months.
pmc-13289052: A 2026 correction notice fixes a figure error in a 2015 cancer study. The study dealt with the gene MTA1 and mesothelioma spread. One wound-healing image in Figure 2 was used twice by mistake. An image from one cell line stood in for another. The notice prints the correct figure and its full caption. The caption sums up tests of invasion, migration, and cell growth. No new data or changed claims appear in the notice. It is short and deals with the image swap alone.
pmc-13289252:
Fan Cao and coauthors present a 2026 global analysis of autoimmune disease burden in men over three decades. Autoimmune diseases occur when the immune system attacks the body itself. Using Global Burden of Disease estimates for 204 countries from 1990 to 2021, they tracked new cases, total cases, deaths, and years lost to illness or early death.

Overall burden in men fell worldwide across the study years. In wealthy countries, however, new-case rates rose after 2005, and total cases plus years lived with disability rose after 2015 in those settings. Care quality scores in 2021 still varied widely, from 74.97 in low-middle income settings to 90.55 in high income settings as reported. Gaps for young, working-age, and older men point to uneven access that still needs fixing.
pmc-13289652:
Marwah I Bin Abdulqader and coauthors offer a 2026 critical review on artificial intelligence in drug discovery. Classic discovery loses most candidates, costs a great deal, and takes many years, while resistance and complex cancers raise the stakes. Machine learning promises faster search of chemical space and smarter molecule design, but real impact needs sober review beyond hype.

The narrative review covers work from 2000 to 2026 across small-molecule drugs, antibodies, anticancer agents, and antibiotics. Methods ranged from classic machine learning to deep learning models of many designs. Selected studies had to report direct drug discovery use, excluding vague or incomplete reports. Strengths in early lab settings are weighed against limits in data, validation, and clinic translation.
pmc-13289852:
Shinya Ohno and colleagues report a 2026 case of conversion surgery after strong response to zolbetuximab-based chemotherapy in stomach cancer. Zolbetuximab targets a protein called Claudin 18.2 on tumor cells. A 59-year-old man with stage IV, Claudin-positive cancer and suspected belly spread got the antibody plus capecitabine and oxaliplatin as initial therapy.

After six courses, imaging showed marked tumor shrinkage for the patient. A camera check of the belly found no spread, so surgeons removed part of the stomach with clear margins in a keyhole operation. Tissue grading showed a strong response, final stage fell to IB, and he stayed free of return at twelve months. Heavy bleeding during surgery, likely from treatment scarring, urges caution.
pmc-13289952:
Sohail Agha headed a 2026 quasi-experimental study on social media campaigns to lift HPV vaccination in Bangladesh. Cervical cancer kills many Bangladeshi women, and a single-dose school campaign launched nationally in 2024 across six divisions. Four intervention mixes were tested against a control group, with caregiver surveys before and after involving thousands of respondents online.

Baseline held 3,823 caregivers and follow-up held 7,004 caregivers of girls aged 9 to 17 for comparison. Coverage rose from 10.1 percent to 32.9 percent even in controls, reflecting the national drive everywhere. Targeted social media, alone or with school awareness, added the largest extra gains in adjusted models. School awareness alone added only a small edge.
pmc-13290452:
Genes behind leaf spot resistance and seed dormancy in peanut are hunted by Jie Zhang and colleagues in a 2026 genome-wide association study. Peanut is a major oil and protein crop, and both traits matter to breeders trying to protect yields and seed quality.

The team resequenced 87 accessions from the US peanut mini-core collection, generating 217 Gb of data and 87,726 markers across 20 chromosomes. The accessions fell into three gene pools, and marker density proved sufficient for association mapping. Three candidate genes stood out: one tied to early leaf spot resistance, one to late leaf spot resistance, and one, an ICE1 homolog, influencing both germination and dormancy. Zhang and colleagues propose the markers for selection programs aimed at hardier, better-seeded varieties.
pmc-13290952:
The cell body alone carries a fingerprint of interneuron identity, Maheshwar Panday and colleagues show in an atlas study from 2026. Parvalbumin-positive inhibitory neurons steer cortical plasticity, and while their wiring and genes show rich variety, whether plain soma shape under the microscope holds the same information was unknown.

The team measured 97 shape features in over 14,000 labeled cells from mouse visual and somatosensory cortex. Clustering sorted the cells into 13 shape groups arranged along partly independent size and shape gradients, summarized as four size and five shape categories. Mapped back onto cortical layers, particular shapes concentrated in particular layers, matching the cortex's circuit architecture. Panday and colleagues say standard labeling plus this quantitative lens can extract far more anatomy than size and density counts ever did.
pmc-13291152:
Drug pairs that may raise pancreatitis risk are hunted in a 2026 safety study led by Issei Kazume. Some diabetes drugs based on incretin hormones have been linked to pancreas inflammation. Less clear is how other drugs taken at the same time change that risk.

The team mined a large United States database of reported side effects. Data ran from late 1997 to early 2024. Single drugs were scored for links to acute pancreatitis. Pairs used with the diabetes drugs were then checked for extra risk. Several drugs showed raised reporting rates. Time trends were tracked across six spans. Such signals can guide safer prescribing, though they do not prove cause.
pmc-13291252: Fernando Dias Correia and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 to a study on home recovery after knee replacement. The record here consists solely of that correction notice. One flow diagram gave a wrong count of excluded patients. A results table also held wrong spread values for knee bending. Two scores were printed as averages instead of middle values. The fixed diagram and table are reprinted in the note. Judging the study itself requires the full article, not this note.
pmc-13291852:
Guangjun Wang and a large team survey a 2026 review topic: using artificial intelligence to predict biological age rather than counting birthdays. Biological age aims to capture how fast a body is actually aging. The review walks through biomarker choice, feature building, model design, bias correction, and performance checks.

Methods range from classic machine learning to deep networks that fuse several data types at once. The authors highlight asynchronous aging, where organs age at different speeds, as a pattern AI is well placed to detect. Uses include disease risk scoring and population health monitoring. They close with open problems: uneven data, weak general use across groups, hard-to-explain models, and slow movement into clinics.
pmc-13292152:
Tingrun Cui and co-authors test a 2026 diagnostic idea for infected artificial joints: reading neutrophil extracellular traps in joint fluid. These web-like structures spill from neutrophils during infection and are hard to judge with standard tests alone. The retrospective study covered arthroplasty patients from 2018 to 2023, measuring three trap components alongside cell counts and cultures.

Of 153 patients, 64 had confirmed infections. Two trap markers, cell-free DNA and citrullinated histone H3, ran much higher in infected fluid and tracked with white cell counts. A combined index the authors call NETRI reached an area under the curve of 0.922 in their analysis. One-marker positivity suited screening, while two-marker positivity, at 95.5 percent specificity in the data, suited ruling infection in. The authors propose trap testing as a fresh discriminator.
pmc-13292752:
Marwa Bawazir and Sibel A Antonson stage a 2026 reliability contest in adhesive dentistry. Five veteran dentists and five first-year students each bonded six hundred dentin surfaces, split between a universal adhesive and a classic etch-and-rinse system. Surfaces came wet, moist, or dry, and everyone worked both before and after a demonstration of the makers' technique.

The universal adhesive barely noticed who held it: median bond strength was 25.53 megapascals for dentists and 24.96 for students, with tight spreads. The etch-and-rinse lagged and wobbled, at medians of 17.79 for dentists and 13.52 for students. Overall the universal product beat its rival by about 7.38 megapascals across conditions. Dry and moist dentin outbonded wet dentin. The authors conclude operator experience matters for the older system, not the universal one.
pmc-13292852:
Francesco Angelucci and colleagues review, in 2026, what is known about spermidine and Alzheimer disease. Spermidine is a natural compound in cells and food that supports cleanup of worn cell parts, a process that falters as the brain ages.

Animal work links spermidine to better memory, healthier synapses, and less inflammation and cell stress. Human data are thinner: diet studies hint that higher intake goes with better thinking, but they cannot prove cause. The few trials so far were small and mixed, with no steady gain on main memory tests. The authors say firm proof is still lacking and larger trials are needed.
pmc-13293652:
Tiphaine Douanne and co-authors probe, in a 2026 study, how straight-line ubiquitin chains help drive pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death set off by the NLRP3 sensor. This death guards against infection but must stay tightly controlled to avoid harm.

Chains built by an enzyme team called LUBAC formed in both the priming and killing phases, even without the sensor present. Removing LUBAC parts or blocking them weakened the death, while removing OTULIN, an enzyme that strips these chains, strengthened it. A light-based model that skips priming still needed the chains for the killing phase. Chain control thus gates this death.
pmc-13293852:
Lei Ma and coauthors survey 1,040 university students in China in a 2026 study on artificial intelligence literacy and new ideas. Students reported how well they understand and use AI, plus their anxiety about AI, mental flexibility, and innovative behavior. The authors test whether anxiety and flexibility carry part of the link between literacy and innovation.

Higher literacy went with more flexibility and more innovative behavior, and with less anxiety. Three indirect paths were significant, through anxiety alone, flexibility alone, and both in sequence. Students fell into low, moderate, and high literacy groups, and the pathways differed across groups, which suggests tailored teaching by skill level.
pmc-13294152:
Sam Er Bader and colleagues test brain effects of aortic balloon occlusion during severe bleeding in a 2026 pig study. The REBOA technique blocks the aorta to restore pressure near the heart and brain, but brain metabolism under raised skull pressure was unclear. Bleeding dropped mean arterial pressure to about 40 mmHg, then zone 1 occlusion lasted 90 minutes while brain dialysis tracked lactate and pyruvate.

Shock raised the lactate-pyruvate ratio in both normal and raised pressure groups, signaling starved brain tissue. After occlusion the ratio eased back toward baseline in both groups. Raised pressure slowed only the first 10 minutes of recovery. Acute brain chemistry thus recovered despite high skull pressure.
pmc-13294452:
Samriddhi S Gupte and coauthors propose a stewardship-linked path for reserve antibiotics in India in a 2026 article. India faces too little access for some patients and reckless use for others, both feeding resistance that caused 1.14 million direct deaths globally in 2021 in the cited count. New last-line drugs often never reach poorer countries at all.

Their plan ties facility access tiers to proven stewardship quality, with early planning, targeted oversight, and live use monitoring. Hospitals earn broader access by showing careful prescribing, protecting new drugs while still reaching patients who need them. The model could travel to other countries facing the same access-versus-excess squeeze.
pmc-13294652:
Sadie E Larsen and colleagues describe updating an online decision aid for posttraumatic stress disorder treatment in a 2026 article. Effective treatments exist, yet no method yet shows which option suits which patient best. The National Center for PTSD first released its aid in 2017.

A small team revised the aid with expert and consumer input to match newer guidelines and technology needs. People who screened positive tested core tasks, and Veterans Administration patients and clinicians tried the aid during appointments. Early field testing suggested the aid felt acceptable and balanced, eased decisional conflict, and strengthened confidence in choosing treatment.
pmc-13295752:
Margaret B Allison and colleagues test a collagen-seeking scan for lung scarring in scleroderma in a 2026 report. Lung disease strikes about half of systemic sclerosis patients at diagnosis and drives most deaths from the illness. A PET probe that binds type 1 collagen had worked in another scarring lung disease but not yet here.

Patients received the probe and underwent combined PET and MRI scanning under a registered trial protocol. Uptake readings were averaged across divided lung regions for whole-lung comparison with healthy volunteers. The work marks the first use of this probe in scleroderma lung disease, opening a path toward earlier spotting of scarring and better timing of treatment.
pmc-13295852:
Sadiq Rehmani and colleagues examine, in 2026, whether side effects from cancer immunotherapy predict longer survival among United States veterans. Earlier reports linked such immune-related events to better outcomes, but type and severity may matter more than presence alone.

Records for 1,707 patients treated between 2010 and 2023 were reviewed, and about a quarter had at least one such event. Overall, having an event did not clearly improve survival once timing bias was handled. Milder events needing no steroids, especially thyroid and skin ones, did link to better survival, while steroid-treated events trended worse. Organ type, the authors argue, shapes the signal.
pmc-13296052:
Nimet Turgut and co-authors measure, in 2026, the small openings in the middle skull base of dogs using cone-beam scans. These holes carry key nerves and vessels, and their size may shift with skull shape, which matters for surgery and diagnosis.

Scans from forty healthy dogs were grouped by skull size using a brain-case length measure. The main openings sat in matching places and shapes on both sides, growing larger as skulls and body weight grew. One small opening was missing in small-skulled dogs. The authors offer the values as a reference for varied dog types.
pmc-13296952:
Hakan Işıker and colleagues apply, in 2026, a butterfly-inspired optimiser to the problem of running power grids cheaply and cleanly at once. They adapt the method with shrinking populations and self-tuned settings, then test it on standard thirty- and fifty-seven-node networks.

Four goals, cost, loss, emissions and voltage steadiness, were paired into combined problems, including cases with renewable uncertainty. The method found compromise settings balancing cost against emissions and emissions against loss, beating most published rivals on the same tests. The authors claim a first use of this optimiser for such multi-goal power problems.
pmc-13297352:
Leopold Eckhart, Supawadee Sukseree and Heinz Fischer review, in 2026, holocrine secretion, the self-destructive final step where oil gland cells burst wholesale into sebum. These glands oil hair and skin, and their finishing cells dissolve their own nucleus and parts before the membrane ruptures.

Animal evidence points to a lysosomal enzyme digesting nuclear and mitochondrial DNA, giving the cell's recycling sacs a starring role. The review weighs how tight junctions place the bursting zone, how self-eating tunes the process and what might pop the membrane. Clinical relevance stays an open question.
pmc-13297752:
Your blood type may come with a distinct signature of circulating molecules, indicates a 2026 pilot study by Alessia Di Salvo and co-authors. They measured 73 blood molecules in 56 healthy donors: 24 with group O, 19 with group A, and 13 with group B.

Group A donors carried higher levels of many signals tied to inflammation, vessel growth, and tissue remodeling, including IL-13, IL-23, VEGF family members, and MMP-1. Group B donors stood out for IL-22, P-selectin, and amyloid β1–42, among others. The authors read these profiles as biological differences that might help explain why disease risk varies by blood group, while cautioning that the small exploratory study needs confirmation.
pmc-13298452:
Tests for prostate disease still blur the line between plain swelling and true cancer. Imola Donath-Miklos and her team ask in a 2026 review if fresh blood marks can sharpen that line. They focus on three leads: YKL-40, mannose-binding lectin, and broad marks of DNA methylation in the blood.

Each mark taps a unlike layer of the disease. One tracks immune tone in tissue, one tracks inborn immune range, and one tracks long-set marks left by past immune stress. None is fit to stand alone as a test today. The team place them as add-ons next to PSA, gene tests, and MRI scans. They call for set lab norms and forward-looking trials in prostate care before any clinic use.
pmc-13300052:
Viruses hiding in the brain may not match those in blood or spinal fluid, a question Xin Dang and colleagues tackled in a 2026 study. Using matched postmortem samples from the National NeuroAIDS Tissue Consortium, they compared brain, cerebrospinal fluid, and peripheral tissues from people with and without HIV and substance use disorder.

A targeted enrichment method called ViroFind detected material from 27 viruses across the sample sets. Spinal fluid held the narrowest mix, while peripheral samples carried the heaviest load. Hepatitis B and C viruses turned up inside the central nervous system, though neither is classed as nerve-seeking. HIV raised peripheral burden and diversity; substance use disorder did not.
pmc-13303252:
Reflection belongs inside competency training, not bolted on afterward, Sara Horton-Deutsch argues in a 2026 commentary on nursing education. Writing solo, she responds to Armstrong and Sherwood's paper on embedding reflective practice across competency development to make feedback learner-centred. Their model follows reflection through three moments: before action, in action, and on action after the fact.

Horton-Deutsch hears a deep harmony with Watson's Theory of Human Caring, where knowing oneself grounds clinical competence. She walks through their practical tools, from Ask-Tell-Ask conversations to mindful pauses, and draws out consequences for faculty development and curriculum design. Reflection, on this reading, builds the habits of mind that sustain a career.
pmc-13303652:
Lei Luo and co-authors present a 2026 computer modeling study of how pores weaken 3D-printed concrete. Layer-by-layer printing traps air and leaves gaps between layers, which cut the strength of finished parts.

Using a phase-field cohesive zone model, the team varied pore size, shape, tilt, and layout one factor at a time. A single pore hurt most when its flat side faced across the pulling force. In groups, the angle linking pores mattered more than spacing, and rows of pores lined up sideways could trigger sudden brittle breaks. Clusters of small pores proved worse than one large pore alone.
pmc-13304552:
Amanda Cristina Machado Carloto leads a 2026 lab study of curcumin, the turmeric compound, against the parasite that causes leishmaniasis. The spice chemical kills germs in tests but absorbs poorly in the body, limiting real use.

Free curcumin slowed free-swimming parasites and stirred stress inside them, raising reactive chemicals, swelling power units, and packing fat droplets until cell death programs engaged. Packed into beeswax-based nanoparticles, the compound turned gentler on host cells while still clearing infected immune cells. Pairing the particles with a standard drug also cut infection, opening a route toward safer parasite treatment.
pmc-13304652:
Omar Abdelaziz and co-authors review eye surface and cornea problems tied to contact lens wear in a 2026 clinical survey. Lenses correct vision for millions, yet they can disturb the eye surface from mild irritation to blinding infection.

Common troubles such as discomfort, dry eye, and lid bumps are usually mild and settle with simple care. Mid-range inflammation can mimic early infection and confuse first assessment. Germ infection of the cornea is the gravest risk and can advance fast when missed. Risk-based sorting, quick referral, lens hygiene, and patient teaching anchor safe frontline care.
pmc-13304852:
Chen Chen and co-authors warn that ion-beam microscopes can fake the very features they reveal in energy materials in a 2026 perspective. Cutting samples with focused ion beams exposes buried battery layers, but milling, vacuum, and imaging can also reshape them.

Each tool in the chain, from beam cutting to atom probing, may shift shape, chemistry, or phase, especially in light elements and fragile coatings. The authors propose judging every claim against the smallest control that can separate real structure from tool damage. Porous electrodes and reactive interfaces get detailed checklists for trustworthy evidence.
pmc-13304952:
Wei Luo and colleagues tune germanium-silicon quantum dots with high heat in a 2026 study of on-chip light sources. The dots glow at telecom wavelengths and fit silicon chip making, suiting combined electronic and optical circuits.

Fast heating at rising temperatures first deepened then shifted the glow color, while brightness climbed steeply. At the top heat the glow narrowed to a single peak near the key telecom band with about twenty times the starting strength. Microscopy and vibration spectra tie the change to element mixing and a strain flip inside the dots. Heat treatment thus offers a simple tuning knob.
pmc-13306552:
Lissethkaren Alvarez Vargas described kidney disease uncovered through swollen glands in a 2026 case report with literature review. Mikulicz disease, an IgG4-related swelling of tear and saliva glands, can mask wider immune disease that also scars the kidneys.

A 49-year-old man reported two years of excess urination and foamy urine, with blood creatinine at 4.2 mg/dL and daily protein loss of 2874 mg in reported tests. Both parotid glands were enlarged on examination. The authors stress separating true Mikulicz disease from look-alike gland swelling, since late kidney diagnosis can leave lasting damage.
pmc-13307152:
João Carlos Ramos compared bending strength of temporary dental materials with and without reinforcement in a 2026 study. Standard bars sized 2 × 2 × 25 mm were made from acrylic resin, a printed resin and a bis-acryl resin for provisional crowns.

Each material split into plain, two glass fibre and one metal reinforced groups in the reported design, then faced three-point bending. Material and reinforcement both shaped strength and stiffness clearly. One fibre product, EverStick C&B, gave the highest values across all bases, strongest in the acrylic resin group. Stronger short term crowns may cut breakage while the final tooth work is still being made.
pmc-13308952:
Liansheng Mai and co-authors report in 2026 three cases of stomach holes blamed on fish bones, where surgery found no bone in two of the three. Each patient came in with sharp upper belly pain after a recent fish meal, and scans showed a thick gut wall plus a line like bright streak.

All three had keyhole surgery at once, and two were switched to open surgery for a fuller search inside. Holes were sewn, washed, and drained in each case, and no snags arose after care for any patient. A fish tale plus scan signs still merit the fish bone call, even when the bone itself hides from the surgeon.
pmc-13309352:
Jaein Cho and co-authors test in 2026 whether a five item frailty score can flag risk in older adults who face lumbar spine surgery. Spine wear drives more such work each year. They drew charts for 967 adults aged 70 years and up at one large Korean hospital from 2020 to 2021, with a year of follow up.

Severe frailty, a score of 3 or more, marked 132 people, or 13.6 percent of the group in the raw count. After weight based tuning for mix ups, severe frailty still tied to in hospital problems, with odds near 1.8 times those of the less frail. High anaesthesia risk grades, need for daily help, and in hospital problems each foresaw harms in the year after.
pmc-13310052:
Xiaoyu Wu and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, the two-sided role that natural killer cells play in the liver during sepsis. Sepsis is organ failure driven by a runaway response to infection, and the liver sits at its center as a filter and immune organ. Killer cells in the liver differ from those in blood and can both guard and injure the organ.

On the guard side, these cells fight microbes, release calming signals, and protect vessel walls by lowering a growth factor. Their killing power also checks viruses inside liver cells. Yet the same killing can damage healthy tissue when control slips. The authors weigh factors that tip the balance and sketch treatment ideas built on that balance.
pmc-13310252:
Yuzhe Pan and co-authors argue for a regional frame to judge healthy eating patterns in China in a 2026 comment. National dietary guidance sets shared principles, summed in the Chinese Food Guide Pagoda. Local food systems, budgets, and habits decide whether those principles can actually reach the table.

Eating advice lands through markets, canteens, cooking habits, and food culture, all of which vary by region. A regional assessment frame could sort when a pattern fits local guidance, when it needs adaptation, and when it can feed back into national advice. The authors lay out the gap between national standards and daily practice. Their aim is guidance that households can afford and accept.
pmc-13310652:
Gui-Long Tanzhu and co-authors review the living neighborhood around brain tumors in a 2026 article. Brain tumors, both those born in the brain and those spread from elsewhere, carry grim outlooks. Their surroundings mix tumor cells, immune cells, neurons, vessels, matrix, and chemical signals in constant cross-talk.

Single-cell and spatial gene methods have newly exposed how varied and arranged those surroundings are. Parts and jobs of each element are summarized, along with the signals they swap and how those swaps steer growth and treatment response. Clinical hopes and hurdles get direct treatment, from immune access to drug delivery. The authors aim the review at researchers designing microenvironment-aware trials.
pmc-13310952:
Go Yoshimichi reports a 2026 case of severe high blood sugar syndrome with lasting higher brain trouble. A woman aged 64 years with type 2 diabetes arrived unconscious and got standard care for hyperglycemic hyperosmolar syndrome. Sugar and body chemistry improved, yet speech loss and failure to recognize objects remained.

A scan method that maps blood flow without dye showed raised flow in the left temporal and parietal brain lobes. Such flow changes may explain why brain signs linger after body chemistry clears. Flow mapping could aid study of brain harm in this acute diabetes crisis.
pmc-13311152:
Yeela Talmor-Barkan leads a 2026 study called RetiMap on retinal vessel measures as windows to body health. Sharp eye photos can show tiny vessels directly, and smart tools can now measure vessel width and density at scale. Past work linked such traits to heart risk, yet often looked at few traits or few risk factors.

Large biobank data have tied vessel traits to blood pressure, smoking, sleep apnea, and blood sugar. Deep tools have also foretold death risk and weight linked ills from photos alone. The new work aims at a wider joint map of vessel traits and body risk to sharpen early warning.
pmc-13311752:
Tsidiso Tolla and co-authors set out a 2026 scoping review protocol on poor mental health in male students and its ties to their sexual violence against women students at African universities.

The review will search six databases plus Google Scholar, open-access listings, and grey sources. A population-concept-context frame will judge which studies fit. Search methods mix phrase and Boolean logic, citation chasing, and filters. Work from rich countries links masculine norms and male distress to such violence, but African evidence is unmapped. The map should show what is known and where research must go next.
pmc-13311952:
Yannan Ding and co-authors give a 2025 bibliometric map of research on information technology in hospital antimicrobial stewardship over twenty years. Software now helps teams curb antibiotic overuse and resistance.

A Web of Science search for 2000 to 2025 yielded 258 English papers. Output rose unevenly to a peak of 49 papers in 2024. The United States led with 131 papers, and hub institutions included Harvard and Imperial College London. Hot terms joined stewardship with machine learning, decision support, records systems, and AI. The field's center of gravity is shifting toward predicting resistance and tailoring treatment.
pmc-13312052:
Giovanni Taverna and colleagues offer a 2026 state-of-the-art review of how several imaging methods together can assess arrhythmic mitral valve prolapse. The valve condition is common and usually harmless, but a minority of patients face dangerous heart rhythms and sudden cardiac death, and telling them apart is the hard part.

The review covers ultrasound of the heart, cardiac magnetic resonance, computed tomography, and PET scanning, weighing what each adds on structure, function, and tissue makeup. The authors tie valve shape and ring mechanics to heart muscle injury and scarring, both diffuse and patchy, as the path toward rhythm risk. Newer magnetic resonance measures that map tissue change may flag early damage, and the review closes by noting where proof is still thin.
pmc-13312452:
Edoardo Simonetti and co-authors report a 2026 spectroscopy study of the electronic structure of the photoactive yellow protein chromophore dissolved in water. This light sensor's core molecule was known to oxidize in sunlight, but no one had measured the energy needed to pull an electron off it in solution.

The team used X-ray, extreme ultraviolet, and multiphoton ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy on a liquid microjet, with high-level quantum chemistry. They pinned the vertical electron detachment energy at 6.8 electron volts, give or take a tenth, and the adiabatic value near 5.9 electron volts. Multiphoton runs also showed a strong two-photon resonance near the detachment threshold that likely drives the known photooxidation, plus a three-photon feature above it. The authors showcase the paired method for weakly soluble light-active compounds.
pmc-13314752:
Maki Yamaguchi and colleagues study how exercise shifts polyamine chemistry in unlike muscles, in a 2026 paper. Polyamines are small molecules that help cells grow, and their handling may set whether a muscle swells with training.

Rats ran freely on wheels, and the team read enzyme patterns in a slow, swelling soleus muscle and a fast plantar muscle that did not swell. Making enzymes rose in the swollen muscle, while breaking enzymes rose in the flat one, in step with more energy proteins, as the authors report. They reason the breaking surge caps growth in fast muscle as its aerobic gear rises. A precursor called putrescine was also fed, yet it barely moved muscle chemistry. The fiber-split result refines how training gains are explained.
pmc-13315452:
Jiaying Hu and a very large team searched blood proteins in 2026 for a marker of calciphylaxis. That is a rare and often fatal disease of kidney patients, where small vessels harden, clot, and kill skin. They compared patients with the disease and patients with uremia, before and after stem cell therapy from human amnion tissue.

Protein screens pointed to thrombospondin-1 as the top raised hub protein, and levels fell after stem cell treatment. Lab tests linked it and a TGF-beta binding protein to clotting and wound repair, and blocking related signals weakened serum-driven cell sticking and clotting. Confirmatory tests in a larger combined group supported the marker.
pmc-13315852:
Junting Liu and colleagues review in 2026 brain-computer interface neurofeedback training as rehabilitation for major depressive disorder. Standard drug and talking treatments still face limits in stability, side effects, and relapse, while neurofeedback lets patients steer their own abnormal brain states with real-time signals.

The review covers theory, brain mechanisms, and clinical formats, for both non-invasive and invasive feedback tools. Combined plans are discussed, including a paired approach joining wearable brain devices with aerobic exercise at the meeting point of sports neuroscience and psychiatry. Early evidence suggests the training may help, though stronger trials are still needed.
pmc-13316652:
Tanapan Sukee leads an Australian team that read, in a 2026 study, the full mitochondrial genomes of foreign freshwater snails now living in Australia. These snails can carry fluke parasites that harm people, livestock, and wildlife, so telling them apart quickly matters for biosecurity.

Fifteen complete genomes were built with long-read sequencing for four settled foreign types plus one high-risk invader not yet established. Genome sizes ran from 13.7 to 14.3 thousand bases, with shared layout and a strong tilt toward A and T letters. Settled types showed little inner variation, a sign of small founding groups, while one European genus hid deep splits. The references now support DNA tests and water-based tracking of risky snails.
pmc-13316852:
Alexander A Puretzky and colleagues probe, in a 2026 physics study, Janus monolayers: atom-thin sheets whose two faces differ, giving them a built-in electric tilt. Starting from tungsten disulfide, they swapped top sulfur atoms for selenium step by step using pulsed laser blasts.

Light scattering tuned across colors revealed how tightly the sheet's vibrations grip its light-born excitations, the A, B, and C bands. As selenium share rose toward halfway, those bands slid to lower energies and coupling grew in a mode-selective way. Computer simulations matched the measured profiles closely. The recipe of controlled making, light probing, and predictive theory points toward tuning these sheets for future light-based devices.
pmc-13317252:
Christopher Hampf and a large German team propose, in a 2026 blueprint paper, a trusted third party service that manages patient consent across hospitals in federated medical research. Germany's new data networks link 34 university hospitals, yet tracking each patient's yes, no, and withdrawal across sites remains a patchwork.

Their design, called fTTP Consent, extends the existing privacy office that already pseudonymizes records and links them safely. Two use cases anchor it: automatic checks that consent data are legally and technically correct, and automatic alerts when consent appears, changes, or is withdrawn. The goal is uniform respect for patient choices without burying sites in phone calls and paperwork.
pmc-13318252:
Ako Pierre Elischama Brou and colleagues present a 2026 laboratory study on making biogas by digesting poultry manure together with cocoa pod husks, two farm residues common in West Africa. Their work speaks to waste build-up and weak energy access in the region.

Batch tests ran at warm and hotter settings, 37°C and 55°C, across carbon-to-nitrogen ratios from 20 to 35, using an ANKOM system. Digesting the two feedstocks together beat either one alone, peaking at a ratio of 25 under the warmer, lower setting with 348.65 mL/g VS of biogas produced. Keeping the ratio near 25 to 30 under those milder conditions is presented as a practical route for small local energy systems.
pmc-13318552:
Sushma Ashwin and colleagues provide a 2026 cost analysis of two sedation drugs. They compare remifentanil with the more familiar fentanyl. Both drugs sedate ventilated intensive care patients. Figures come from a pilot randomised trial at Nepean Hospital in Australia.

Altogether 210 patients were analysed, 104 given remifentanil and 106 fentanyl. Costs used national pricing for 2020–2021 from a health payer view. Drug purchase costs were similar between groups. Total hospital bed-day costs came out lower with remifentanil. The gap was clearest in patients aged 65 or older. It also showed in those ventilated for up to 72 hours in the trial. Survival and quality of life at six months did not differ. The authors call the findings exploratory.
pmc-13318652:
Nothemba Thobela and Lieketseng Ned report a 2026 qualitative study from South Africa. They explore how wheelchair basketball affects community reintegration after spinal cord injury. The setting is the Western Cape province. Reintegration is a major challenge where trauma injuries are common and rehab services are limited.

Only four players took part, two men and two women aged 19 to 26. They came from the one local club still running after COVID-19. The team used two integration questionnaires plus semi-structured interviews. Three themes emerged: better functional independence, more inclusion and social contact, and stronger self-esteem. Players felt more integrated than objective measures showed. The authors call for wider stakeholder support to sustain the benefits.
pmc-13318952:
Dominique E. Teskey and co-authors report a 2026 mouse study of metformin, a diabetes drug proposed as an anti-ageing therapy, during flu infection. Young and aged mice ate treated or plain food for six weeks. They then caught a mild H3N2 flu strain. A different flu strain challenged them thirty days later.

The team tracked immune memory in the lungs across the second infection. Metformin changed only some parts of the response, mostly in young mice. In aged mice it did not improve memory T cell populations after the first infection. Older treated mice lost slightly less weight during the second challenge. Yet their lung virus levels briefly ran higher than controls. The authors conclude metformin could not overcome ageing's full effect on immune memory here.
pmc-13319652:
Tuğba Nur Öztürk and Esra Yıldız soak dental crown materials in common drinks in a 2026 lab study of stain and wear. Machine made crowns with a resin and ceramic mix are prized for their natural look, but daily drinks may dull that look over time. Three crown types were steeped in water, coffee, cola, or red wine to compare the harm.

A total of 168 samples were checked for color shift and surface roughness at the start and after 3, 6, and 12 days at body heat. Red wine stained all types most, with coffee next, while cola and water did least harm. One type faded and roughened most by day 12, and one held its look best. Diet advice and fresh polishing may help crowns last.
pmc-13319952:
Isabella Burda and co-authors study how cell stress shapes petal guard leaves in a model plant in a 2026 article on even growth. Wild plants make four guard leaves of near equal size even though each cell grows at its own pace, because ups and downs cancel out across space and time. A mutant with faulty cell power houses breaks that evenness and makes uneven leaves.

Harmful oxygen forms built up in the mutant, and lowering them restored even size and shape. High levels of those forms made inner cell rails more crossed and stiff, and cells with crossed rails grew slower in linked waves. Linked growth stops ups and downs from canceling, so organ shape turns uneven. Calm cell chemistry thus guards steady form.
pmc-13320252:
Noemi Ravaglia and co-authors build a smart scaffold for lost muscle in a 2026 study that pairs egg white protein with a ceramic that makes electric signals under pressure. Big muscle wounds heal poorly on their own, and still scaffolds alone rarely restore full function. A scaffold that turns sound waves into tiny electric cues may coach new muscle to grow.

The mix was tuned to match soft muscle in pores, flex, and breakdown pace, then charged so its signal lasts. Muscle starter cells on the charged scaffold clung, spread, and matured better, and sound pulses lifted early growth genes further. A small live test over 28 days showed no harm and good hold. The platform may suit wounds where muscle bulk is lost.
pmc-13320352:
Inge Jonkman and co-authors study an over wound immune system in dialysis patients in a 2026 article on innate immune memory. People on blood filtering face lasting swelling, more infections, and higher death rates, with guard cells that overreact to alarms. Whether that overdrive reflects trained memory in those cells, and what drives it, was the open question.

Patient guard cells ran high in number and spat out more alarm signals after test triggers than healthy cells. A key alarm protein in blood rose in step with that overdrive, and gene reads showed its pathways lit up most in the strongest responders. Lab tests proved the memory effect needs that protein, made by helper immune cells. Blocking it may calm harmful overdrive.
pmc-13320452:
Giuseppe Ippolito and Alimuddin Zumla wrote a commentary in 2026 on getting Europe ready for home grown dengue spread. Dengue was long read in Europe as a travelers illness brought back from the tropics. Repeat home grown outbreaks in Italy, Spain, and France in recent years tell a new story, since the fever now returns season by season where its mosquito carriers have settled.

Awareness still lags outside expert circles, among clinic staff, students, travelers, policy makers, and the public at large. World counts of dengue have hit record highs of late, and climate shift, carrier spread, city growth, and world movement all push Europe risk up. Lasting watch systems, clinician training, and public teaching are set as the top ready steps.
pmc-13322052:
Xin Yang and colleagues issue a 2026 correction to their study of a nanozyme platform for brain injury after restored blood flow. The original article, in Journal of Nanobiotechnology, tested a tannic acid modified manganese dioxide nanozyme carrying honokiol to ease cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by activating sirtuin 3 pathways. The correction adds a missing funding note.

The funding section should have stated that Yunnan Beisite Biotechnology took part as a collaborating partner of a blood transfusion department at a Yunnan hospital. The corrected statement also records animal ethics approval, numbered BST-PZ-MICE-20251014-01 in the notice. The original article has been updated, and no results are changed by the correction.
pmc-13322752:
Benjamin J. Pullicino and co-authors make a new high pressure form of strontium tellurite in a 2026 chemistry study. Pressing a strontium oxide and tellurium dioxide mix at 8.8 gigapascals and 900 degrees in a multianvil press gave the new crystal form. X-ray work showed a non-centrosymmetric layout, backed by light doubling tests as strong as quartz.

The structure closely resembles a barium cousin but adds weak extra contacts between tellurite groups, and that detail breaks its symmetry. Heating brought phase changes near 225 degrees and again at 545 degrees toward the normal high temperature form. Light tests gave direct and indirect band gap values of 4.2 and 4.0 electron volts in the report.
pmc-13323152:
Jin Zhao, Xianguo Liu and Jinhai Liu survey why school sport teachers keep using smart wearables, in a 2026 study of 755 physical education teachers across kindergarten to grade 12 settings. Devices promise data-driven monitoring and feedback in lessons, yet lasting use depends on teacher choice.

Two adoption models were joined, with self-efficacy and data privacy added. Fit between task and technology proved the strongest driver of intent to continue, ahead of expected benefit, social influence and confidence. Task features predicted that fit, while technology features did not, and privacy worries pulled against continued use. Set-based analysis found several distinct paths to high or low intent, rather than one single recipe.
pmc-13323252:
Sha Su and co-authors review engineered extracellular vesicles for ischaemic heart disease, in a 2026 systematic review. Single treatments struggle against the tangled damage of reduced heart blood flow, so vesicles that carry healing signals to set targets draw growing interest.

Searching eight databases, the team kept 50 animal studies. Engineering routes included loading cargo inside, altering the surface, fusing membranes, pairing with biomaterials and pre-treating source cells. Targeting used guide peptides, antibodies, membrane fusion or direct delivery into heart tissue. Reported benefits ran through less scarring, calmer inflammation and better function across several pathways. Human proof remains ahead, the authors note.
pmc-13324452:
Osamah Badwan and colleagues ask whether frailty predicts outcomes after left atrial appendage occlusion in a 2026 cohort study. The procedure prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation patients who cannot take long-term blood thinners, but many are old and medically complex.

Using the TriNetX network, the team sorted patients treated between 2015 and 2024 by the five-item modified frailty index. Groups ranged from robust to frail, and matched comparisons followed long-term results. Greater frailty came with stepwise higher death, ischemic stroke, heart events, and geriatric problems. The authors support checking frailty before the procedure so that risk talks and care plans reflect real patient vulnerability.
pmc-13325452:
Orie Saigo and colleagues test whether pharmacists can ease decisions about cancer genome testing in a 2026 randomized study in Japan. Genome profiling is routine there, yet patients face hard choices with unfamiliar information.

A total of 180 patients were split between standard medication counseling and added structured teaching about genome profiling. The share whose decision conflict fell did not differ, at 49.4 percent against 41.9 percent for the control group. Still, conflict about treatment choice rose far less in the teaching arm, gaining 1.98 points against 3.61 on the conflict scale. Early pharmacist input thus blunted growing doubt even when final choices matched.
pmc-13327352:
Linda S Klavinskis wrote a 2026 personal account of a career spanning viral immunology, vaccines, and brain inflammation. She grew up in a small mill town near the Yorkshire Dales, the daughter of immigrants who reached England after the Second World War. Their stress on learning and hard work shaped her path.

She first aimed at dentistry, then switched to biomedical sciences with microbiology after school dissection work showed her strengths lay elsewhere. Summer jobs in public health laboratories in Leeds gave her cell culture skills and early lab grounding. Her account traces how family history, teachers, and new tools such as recombinant DNA guided a research life, and why she now works to widen access for others.
pmc-13327852:
Liang Chen, Ting Yu, and Yanqing Pan build machine learning forecasts for a lung surgery complication in a 2026 study, working with Guodong Ma. Prolonged air leak, lasting over five days, follows keyhole lung segment removal in many patients and stretches hospital stays. Records covered 610 patients treated between January 2019 and September 2025.

Five learning methods were trained on 70 percent of cases and tested on the rest, using health, lung function, surgery, and tumor details. Air leak occurred in 76 patients, 12.46 percent of the group, and the XGBoost model forecast it best, reaching an AUC of 0.874 on the test set, ahead of standard regression. Explanation tools ranked which factors drove each forecast.
pmc-13327952:
Takahiko Nagamine writes a 2026 letter proposing a brain-heart lens for burning mouth syndrome. The condition brings chronic mouth pain with no clear tissue damage, and standard views treat it as a local nerve problem. Nagamine argues it fits nociplastic pain, where the central nervous system turns pain processing up too high.

Sleep trouble, fatigue, anxiety, and depression often travel with the syndrome. The letter frames them as part of the mechanism, not mere side effects. Low mood can lower pain thresholds while pain deepens low mood. Faulty autonomic control links mouth, brain, and heart in one loop. The framework invites treatments aimed at central calming rather than the mouth alone.
pmc-13330652:
Giulia Manzi and a large team build a self-care measure for children with complex long-term conditions in a 2026 study. Care at home grows as survival improves, and parents share the work as children mature. Work ran from 2022 to 2023 in four phases, from theory-based drafting to expert review and family interviews.

Eleven tailored versions cover five age groups and three care dimensions: upkeep, watching, and handling change. Eighty-six experts, including clinicians, parents, and patients, judged content in the middle phases. Family interviews with 5 patients and 13 parents checked clarity at the end. Each version holds about 37 items on average in the reported build. Validity scores are detailed for later testing.
pmc-13330852:
Luciana Da Fonseca Da Silva reviews primary tricuspid valve leakage in adults with congenital heart disease in a 2026 article. Causes include Ebstein anomaly and valve dysplasia from birth, plus later damage from infection or other disease. Severe leakage swells the right heart chambers, sparks rhythm trouble, and cuts exercise capacity over time.

Some patients stay nearly symptom-free for decades despite worsening disease. Poor signs include a very large heart, weak ventricles, low oxygen, and rhythm problems. Surgery is advised for symptoms, falling exercise capacity, or growing right chamber size. The Cone repair can restore native valve function with low risk in expert centres. Earlier, tailored repair is backed.
pmc-13332452:
Roshan Giri and co-authors report a 2026 quality improvement project that raised a Nepalese tertiary hospital pharmacy to full good practice standards in five months. Global pharmacy standards are hard to meet in low- and middle-income settings where money and infrastructure run short.

Working in plan-do-study-act cycles, the team decentralized some services, wrote 21 standard operating procedures under the ALCOA+ framework, and trained staff, then audited progress four times against a 125-point national checklist. Median compliance climbed from 57.1 percent to 100.0 percent by the final audit, and the share of high-scoring domains rose from 17.6 to 88.2 percent. Root cause work showed most documentation gaps came from awkward logbook placement rather than staff skill, fixed by moving books to the dispensing counters. The authors offer the project as a repeatable roadmap for similar hospitals.
pmc-13333752:
Ying Weng, Wanqi Yang, and Yong Lai authored a 2026 review on how gut microbes and their chemical products may shape cognitive problems after stroke through epigenetic routes. The microbiota-gut-brain axis links the intestine to inflammation and repair in the injured brain.

After stroke, gut imbalance changes levels of short-chain fatty acids, B vitamins, tryptophan products, bile acids, and other active compounds. Many of these molecules steer DNA methylation, histone changes, and non-coding RNA activity, switching genes tied to cognition and recovery.
