The review connects those mechanisms to brain inflammation, oxidative stress, blood-brain barrier damage, and neuron death. It closes by weighing therapies that adjust microbes, supply metabolites, or target epigenetic marks directly.
pmc-13335452:
Shakti P Pattanayak and co-authors found that blocking KDEL receptors can make tumors regress without T cells at first, in a 2026 cancer immunology study. These receptors normally haul escaped proteins back from the Golgi to the endoplasmic reticulum.

Inhibiting one receptor, mainly KDELR2, in even a small fraction of tumor cells triggered heavy infiltration by macrophages and neutrophils. Both immunogenic and non-immunogenic tumors shrank, driven initially by this innate response. During regression, anti-tumor T cells were primed, and animals later resisted a second tumor challenge. Delivering KDELR2-silencing RNA in lipid nanoparticles into tumors reproduced the effect. The authors propose KDEL targeting as a way to ignite immunity in cold tumors that resist T cell therapies.
pmc-13336552:
Qiang Yin and co-authors examine in a 2026 chemistry study why phenol breaks apart under light far faster at the surface of water than deep inside it. They look at two controls acting together. One is access to dark energy states in the molecule. The other is how well nearby water can hold the charge that moves during the break.

Large slab models of the surface, unlike small clusters, showed surface states shifted lower by about 0.7 eV compared with bulk water values and spread more widely. Loose, weakly held water settings matched the lowest energies. The findings give modelers fresh inputs for predicting light-driven change where air meets water.
pmc-13336852:
Hao Meng and co-authors use machine learning to lift printable perovskite solar cells in a 2026 study. These cells skip costly hole conductors and precious metals, yet their efficiency had stalled. The team built a clean database of cell recipes and trained a stacked learning model to predict performance.

Across 8 validation experiments, prediction error stayed within 2.16% of measured values in the reported runs. Digging into the model revealed which factors matter most and yielded screening rules for good additives based on molecular fingerprints. Guided by the model, the team built cells reaching an efficiency of 19.36% in hands-on tests, with projections up to 24.32% after fuller tuning. Interpretable models plus targeted tests may speed solar design.
pmc-13337052:
Wenyun Mu and co-authors engineer nanoparticles that attack tumors yet calm nearby tissue in a 2026 study. Heat and radical therapies can harm healthy areas and stir inflammation around tumors. Their gold-ceria hybrids, ACEF, change behavior with their surroundings: folate guides them to tumors, where cell enzymes and calcium trigger clumping.

Clumped particles in tumors convert near-infrared light to heat better and generate harmful radicals for therapy. Scattered particles in normal tissue instead scavenge radicals through cerium chemistry, easing oxidative stress. In animals the particles suppressed main tumors and lung spread, with no obvious body-wide toxicity under the tested conditions. Self-adjusting particles could make aggressive therapy gentler at its edges.
pmc-13337652:
Dragana Milutinović and colleagues surveyed female health workers in Serbia in 2026 about bladder symptoms. Their cross-sectional study covered urinary incontinence and overactive bladder, two parts of lower urinary tract symptoms. It measured how common the problems were, what staff knew, and how they felt about them.

A total of 493 women from primary and tertiary sites in Novi Sad took part using standard symptom and knowledge questionnaires. Incontinence affected 35.5 percent of respondents and overactive bladder affected 53.1 percent, with stress leakage the most common type. Knowledge scores were moderate and attitudes were mostly positive. Findings highlight a care gap even among staff who treat these conditions.
pmc-13338052:
Xiaoji Zhou and colleagues rebuild bladder nerve anatomy in three dimensions in a 2026 cadaver study. Rebuilding bladder function after spinal cord injury requires restoring emptying power while lowering resistance. Sympathetic nerves that tighten the outlet are a key limit.

Bladder tissue from four cadavers, two male and two female, was sliced every 4 mm and stained for a nerve marker. Nerve counts and distance from the inner surface were measured level by level. Density peaked at the bladder neck in women and the prostatic urethra in men. Back regions held far more nerves than front regions in both sexes as reported.
pmc-13338852:
Tan Tian, Yongjie Niu, and Shanjun Bao test boxing-specific sprint training in elite male boxers in a 2026 trial. Repeated sprint work boosts leg power, yet its effect on arm strength and punching was unknown. Sixteen boxers were split into training and control groups of eight.

The training group added three weekly sessions of short all-out heavy-bag punches for four weeks. Upper-body power on a lab Wingate test rose by 16.7 percent for peak power and 20.6 percent for mean power in the reported gains. Bench press power also rose sharply. Post-test gaps versus controls were large, supporting bag sprint work for punch power.
pmc-13342052:
Two routine scans are fused to read marrow immunity in myeloma, in a 2026 study by Minjie Gao and colleagues. Their ImmunoCast-MM system combines stained bone marrow smears with whole-body PET/CT from diagnosis in 243 newly diagnosed patients.

One branch classified cells through learned embeddings; the other built an inflammation fingerprint across tumor, spleen, nodes, and marrow. Contrastive fusion aligned both against flow cytometry, producing an Immune Dysfunction Index. Decoded indices correlated with true cell fractions at ρ values of 0.68 to 0.81, and clustering separated immune-competent from immune-exhausted patients with differing outlooks and drug responses.
pmc-13342852:
Kensington S. Hartman and co-authors report a 2026 plant study on how physical force guides the final cell division that forms stomata, the tiny leaf pores used for gas exchange. Working in the leaf surface layer, the team asked how the last symmetric division lines up so pores end up evenly patterned across plant organs.

The authors found a force-responsive pathway that reads mechanical signals in the tissue and turns the division plane to match broad tissue axes. Without that guidance, the paired guard cells that make a pore fail to form properly. Force, in other words, acts as a patterning cue in leaf growth, alongside the chemical signals long known to shape plant tissues.
pmc-13343352:
Turki Alsaeed, Tracy Washington, and Bo Xia systematically review elderly care in Saudi Arabia in 2026. The kingdom's older population will jump from 5 percent in 2015 to over 20 percent by 2050. That growth strains health and social systems built for a younger nation. The authors gathered the scattered evidence on care today.

Following PRISMA rules across English and Arabic sources from 1995 to 2025, the review finds real progress: more long-term care, hospital geriatric programs, and Vision 2030 reforms pushing integrated digital care. Gaps persist in trained geriatric staff, reliance on migrant caregivers, rural access, and cultural reluctance toward institutional care. Technology-led, workforce-focused reform, plus far more aging research, tops their agenda.
pmc-13346852:
Navodika Yaparathna and colleagues analyse outcomes for removable partial dentures in a university clinic study from 2026. Records for 317 patients aged 34 to 90 years were drawn from the clinic system. Ten outcomes were tested against 23 patient, mouth, denture, and process factors with regression models.

Success was tied most clearly to which arch held the denture, what sat opposite it, and how many visits followed fitting, with single-arch cases doing better overall. Lower dentures facing a full upper denture, and cases with dentures in both arches, fared worse, while upper denture success fell as more upper teeth were missing. The findings support judging upper and lower cases apart.
pmc-13347352:
Renata De Carvalho Feitosa and a large team build a wound film. Their study was published in 2026. The film uses chitosan loaded with a plant compound. The compound sits inside sunflower oil droplets. Its name is beta-caryophyllene. Droplets measured near 114 nm wide. The best mix packed in 96 percent of the compound. Films were then cast at skin-friendly acidity.

Each gram of dressing held 13.3 mg of the compound. Films stayed stable under heat checks. Handling checks gave the same result. Cell work showed good tolerance. The film also fought oxidation. It sped fibroblast movement as well. A scratch gap closed fully within 24 hours. That is a hopeful sign for chronic wound care.
pmc-13348252:
Zhi-Ming Yu and Yugui Yao highlight a new infrared instrument. Their commentary appeared in 2026. It also covers a giant chiral light effect. The effect sits in a magnetic crystal. Yuan and collaborators built the instrument. It resolves polarisation under strong magnetic fields. Mode swaps need no warming of the magnet. The team used it on a Weyl semimetal. That material is of type-II. Its slanted cones were long thought to cancel light preference.

The result broke that expectation. Giant wide-range circular dichroism appeared. It was seen for the first time in this crystal family. A direct window on chiral states opens up. Strong fields can now be applied during reads. Most natural matter gives weak chiral signals. Those signals also stay narrow. A broad strong effect could feed new sensors. Light switches may benefit too.
pmc-13348352:
Alice Wickersham and colleagues link school test paths to later offending in a nationwide cohort, in a study from 2026. Linked school and police records for 4.3 million pupils in England, born across seven school years, traced standard test standing at ages 7, 11. 16, then first cautions or convictions into young adulthood.

Among pupils whose standing slid over school years, one in three was cautioned or convicted before leaving school in the reported counts. Pupils who started low yet improved carried only 4 percent higher odds of young adult offending, against 53 percent higher odds for those who stayed low. So watching falls in standing could trigger timely support.
pmc-13348852:
Maryam Maghbool and colleagues report a rare tonsil growth mixing lymph channels, fat, and muscle, in a case report published in 2026. A 28-year-old Iranian man with a sore throat carried a smooth stalked mass on his right tonsil measuring 2 by 1 by 0.3 cm. The tonsil was removed whole without prior scans given the small, benign look of the lump.

Tissue study showed widened lymph channels in a fatty frame with patches of smooth muscle, fully cut out with clean edges in the pathology report. No return appeared over one year of follow-up, supporting full removal as curative while warning that only tissue study can name such rare lumps with certainty.
pmc-13349752:
Ahmed J. Alaraibi and colleagues pool studies on troponin watching during cancer immunotherapy, in a systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2026. Checkpoint drugs can trigger rare yet deadly heart muscle inflammation that hides behind vague signs. So databases to October 2025 were searched for troponin tests that flag the condition or forecast later heart events and death.

Raised troponin tied strongly to confirmed inflammation, with a pooled log odds value of 4.14 and no clear split among studies in the combined fit. False alarms were common, though, leaving weak rule-in power from a raised value alone, so the authors frame troponin as a watch tool needing partner checks for safe calls.
pmc-13349952:
Xijun Luo and co-authors examined the protein TAZ in gastric cancer tissue in a 2026 clinicopathological study. TAZ helps drive the Hippo pathway, which controls organ size and can fuel cancer when misregulated, but its link with the adhesion protein E-cadherin was unclear.

TAZ message and protein were higher in cancer than in nearby healthy tissue in fresh samples. Staining of stored tissue from 98 patients found TAZ in 67.3 percent of cancers versus 32.0 percent of normal lining, and high TAZ tracked with bigger tumours, lymph node spread, and later stage. Where TAZ rose, E-cadherin tended to fall, hinting TAZ could serve as a warning marker.
pmc-13350252:
Peng Chen and colleagues pooled trial evidence in 2026 on immune checkpoint drugs for advanced nasopharyngeal cancer. This tumour of the upper throat is common in parts of Asia. Seven prospective trials with 1,788 patients were combined.

Regimens with these drugs produced high survival estimates. Three-year overall survival reached 96.4 percent. Failure-free survival reached 88.2 percent in the pooled data. Comparisons across strategies probed timing and chemotherapy partners. They also weighed treatment length and which drug was used. The main question has shifted. It is no longer whether these drugs work, but how best to weave them into combined therapy. The synthesis maps those choices.
pmc-13350352:
Tom Heinekamp and colleagues linked grape genes to wine flavour in a 2026 breeding study. Judging wine quality is the slowest step in grape breeding, so finding DNA markers for flavour would speed selection of new vines.

A cross between two varieties produced 147 offspring grown at two sites over six vintages, yielding 1,635 small-batch wines and 25,284 sensory evaluations. Statistical models separated vine genetics, growing conditions, and each taster's quirks across eight flavour traits and a total quality score. Gene mapping then tied aroma chemicals to the DNA regions behind them, giving breeders a shortcut toward vines bred for taste as well as hardiness.
pmc-13350552:
Karen D Könings and Subha Ramani wrote a 2026 commentary asking who coaches the coaches in health professions education. Supervisors coach learners toward goals, mixing attention to weaknesses, strengths, and personal meaning, yet coaches themselves rarely get coached.

The authors propose upward coaching, where learners help educators refine their coaching through safe, dialogue-based feedback. Just as learners are expected to build feedback skills and own their action plans, teachers could build their own feedback literacy with learner input. As learners, teaching methods, and AI tools change, such mutual coaching could keep supervision honest and current.
pmc-13351452:
C Lombardo and colleagues published a dataset in 2026 of sound-wave speeds in rock layers beneath the middle and southern Adriatic Sea off Italy. The values come from twelve exploration wells drilled offshore between 1969 and 2000 under a national archive project.

Old paper well logs were digitised into standard files, rock units identified in specialist software, and average wave speeds calculated for each unit. Such velocities let geophysicists convert echo timing from seismic surveys into true depths. Rescuing legacy oil exploration data into reusable form serves geology and hazard research long after the wells themselves are gone.
pmc-13353152:
Yu Liu leads a 2026 year-long study of how movement skill and physical fitness shape each other in preschoolers. Both traits matter early, but single snapshots cannot show which drives which. A total of 202 children in Chongqing, China, with mean age of 4.65 years, were tested at baseline and after 12 months, and 194 finished, for a retention rate of 96.1 percent.

Eye-hand integration used the Beery VMI-6 short form, and fitness used a five-item national battery. Each trait proved stable over time, with fitness holding a stability value of 0.88. Cross-lagged models, adjusted for age and sex, fitted well. Results clarify direction of influence for planning early movement programmes.
pmc-13353352:
Gutthi Rishitha Reddy and colleagues track oral Candida colonisation during radiotherapy for head and neck cancer in a 2026 prospective study. Mouth soreness from radiation is common and cuts treatment tolerance, while damaged lining invites Candida growth that may worsen soreness. Seventy patients aged 40 to 80 years receiving curative radiotherapy gave swabs from several mouth sites.

Swabs were taken before treatment, in week three, and at the end, then grown to identify Candida species. Soreness was graded weekly on WHO and CTCAE scales. Analysis weighed age, other illnesses, and treatment factors alongside colonisation. Knowing when colonisation peaks may help time preventive mouth care.
pmc-13354952: Beth M Harvey and co-authors published a 2026 correction to their study of a glial cell path that guides regrowing optic nerve fibers in fish. The note fixes one mutant line name in the methods list of fish lines, swapping a wrong code for the right one. The full corrected list is given next to the first list. The authors state that results and findings do not change.
pmc-13355852:
Kohei Hashida and co-authors report a 2026 case of a 43-year-old woman who lost taste on both sides after a small bleed in one part of her brain, the left putamen. Taste loss after stroke is common but often missed, and this bleed site had rarely been linked to it. Her sense of smell stayed intact and her other symptoms were mild.

Scans showed the bleed with swelling reaching toward the thalamus, a relay for taste signals. A taste test on day eleven confirmed loss on both sides, worse on one. Other causes were judged unlikely. Her taste slowly returned and was fully back within two months, and the authors urge asking stroke patients about taste.
pmc-13358752:
Yan Ye and co-authors compare drug plans for squamous lung cancer in a 2026 review. This form of non-small cell lung cancer has fewer targeted options than others, so care leans on immune drugs, chemotherapy, or both together. Trials have tested each plan against some rivals but never all at once. The team joined the trials into one network.

They gathered 32 randomized trials with 9,652 patients and compared survival, time without the cancer growing, tumor shrinkage, and severe side effects. A network ranking can show which plan gives the best balance of benefit and harm. Such guidance helps doctors tailor first treatment to each patient's strength and wishes.
pmc-13358852:
Andres Zorrilla-Vaca and co-authors appraise breathing strategies in chest surgery in a 2026 paper. About a third of patients who lose part of a lung suffer lung complications afterward, the leading cause of death in this group. One-lung breathing during surgery adds its own strain. A strategy called open-lung ventilation uses pressure and reopening maneuvers to keep tiny air sacs from collapsing.

The authors weigh the PROTHOR trial, a large randomized test of higher pressure with reopening maneuvers against standard care. Better lung mechanics on the table may not always mean better recovery afterward. Their appraisal helps anesthesia teams set the ventilator with proof, not habit.
pmc-13359752:
Emelia A. M. Hinton and co-authors describe a twist in gut inflammation in a 2026 review. In inflammatory bowel disease, the gut lining tries to repair itself while under immune attack. The signal TNF drives both the attack and, surprisingly, part of the repair, pushing lining stem cells to expand and change. A second signal family, type I interferons, joins the cross-talk.

When both signals stay on for long, the repair program may freeze in place, creating what the authors call regenerative inflammation that keeps the disease going. This framing could explain why some patients never respond to anti-TNF drugs, and it points drug hunters toward the lining itself.
pmc-13359952:
Roberta Carvalho Cesário and co-authors test melatonin against breast cancer cells in a 2026 study. Melatonin, the night hormone, does more than set sleep timing. The team treated two cell types in the lab: a hormone-sensitive luminal type and triple-negative cells, the hardest kind to treat. They tracked growth, movement, and invasion alongside energy production and oxidative balance.

Melatonin slowed growth, migration, and invasion in both cell types and reshaped how the cells make energy and handle oxidation. The strength and shape of the effects differed by subtype. The results support further preclinical work on melatonin as a helper in breast cancer treatment.
pmc-13361452:
Hyeonbin Oh and co-authors used machine learning to predict how sound waves change rice flour in a 2026 study. Blasting gelatinized rice flour with ultrasound alters how it dissolves, thickens, and sets, traits that matter for drinks and ready foods. The team processed six rice varieties under nine sound settings and two thicknesses. They asked whether simple flour makeup, like starch, protein, and fiber content, could stand in for variety in the models.

Five model types were trained and compared, from simple regressions to boosted trees. Inputs ranged from process settings alone to settings plus flour makeup. A key test was whether a model trained on known varieties works on one it never saw. Such transfer would let makers predict results for new rice types without fresh trials.
pmc-13362452:
Alessia Brossa and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on tiny delivery bubbles that carry cancer drugs to tumors. It compares two kinds: liposomes, made in the lab and already used in clinics, and extracellular vesicles, small bubbles that cells shed on their own. Each kind has clear strengths and clear weak points, from targeting skill to ease of bulk production.

The review then covers hybrids that fuse the two, aiming to pair the natural targeting of cell bubbles with the control and load space of lab-made ones. Early results look good in lab work, yet bulk making and shared standards lag. The authors see hybrids as a strong next step for precise cancer care once those gaps close.
pmc-13363152:
Kohei Mitsui and colleagues present a 2026 study on how a lead-free solder ages at high heat and how that aging affects fatigue life. The solder, a tin alloy with antimony, silver, nickel, and a trace of germanium, is aimed at hot power electronics. The team aged samples, watched a silver-tin phase inside grow coarser over time, and ran repeated bending-style fatigue tests at room heat and at 175 degrees.

Antimony dissolved in the tin slowed the coarsening of the silver-tin grains, since it left less room for silver to move. At room heat both solders tired at the same rate, but at high heat the new alloy resisted the usual fall in hardening. The authors link the stable grains to the steadier hot performance.
pmc-13363252:
Xiaoying Xu and colleagues report a 2026 study on a light-responsive gel for infected bone defects. The gel builds on treated chitosan, a natural polymer, loaded with black phosphorus sheets and a calcium mineral coat formed in place. The phosphorus gives a heat effect under near-infrared light, while the mineral slowly frees calcium and phosphorus ions that bone cells use.

Strong light doses made the gel kill bacteria through heat and reactive oxygen. Gentle light instead nudged bone stem cells to grow and mature into bone-forming cells, with gene reads to match. In rat skull defects, the gel produced better new bone than controls. The dual mode, sterilize hard then heal gently, is the design's core appeal.
pmc-13363752:
Samikhshak Gupta and Vijaya V N Sriram Malladi present a 2026 study on soaking up bending waves in a beam with small passive dampers. Such wave control can quiet machines and structures without power-hungry active systems. They modeled a clamped aluminum beam with dashpot attachments, checked the model against laser vibration scans, and split the wave field into reflected and absorbed parts across a wide frequency band.

Absorption plotted against position, scaled by the local bending wavelength, fell into a repeating pattern with dips at half-wavelength spacing. That rule frees placement from tuning: spring and damping settings have their own best values per frequency, and several dampers placed by the wavelength rule can hold near-peak absorption anywhere. The team offers the pattern as a compact design guide.
pmc-13364252:
Bo Xu, Shuang Wang, and Xiaoyu Tang present a 2026 study on training AI across Internet of Things devices by blending federated and split learning without a single central server. In their semi-decentralized design, devices share the load of big models, split at points that fit each device's power and link, and several edge servers aggregate the shared parts. Since training delay is unknown ahead of time, they treat split and pairing choices as a learning problem in itself.

Their context-aware bandit algorithm reads each site's conditions to guess delays, then improves its choices round by round with provably small long-run regret. Experiments on several networks showed lower training latency and better test accuracy than the rival methods chosen. The work targets privacy-keeping training on weak devices.
pmc-13367552:
Yatin Dholakia reviews in 2026 India's new split tier plan for TB care, built to close gaps in a land that holds more than a fourth of world TB. Plain same care for all misses sick, poor, and high risk folks. The new plan sorts folks by ill weight and life need at first call.

Tiers span town, site, and state aid, with food, mind, and cash checks built in. Case finds turn from wait for signs to risk led hunts. Tech tools join the plan. The aim is care fit to the folk, not the form, as the land drives to end TB.
pmc-13377852:
Jun Zhao and co-authors list a key gene set in a cure herb in a 2026 study. The herb, a root used in Chinese care, owes its worth to bitter soap-like parts. A gate enzyme starts the chain that builds those parts, fed by a food path in the plant.

Four gate genes were found and split in two kin sets on two code strands. Their start zones hold stress and hormone cues. Reads in root, stem, and leaf plus spray tests tied gene acts to soap build. The list gives herb farms aims to breed roots with more cure parts.
pmc-13378152:
HuiMin Gao and colleagues published a 2026 study on faster quality checks for Relinqing granule, a product made from the plant Polygonum capitatum. The granule is used for urinary problems, but official checks have rested on just one plant compound. That narrow test cannot capture overall quality.

The researchers isolated twenty compounds from the plant and found that three of them reduced inflammation in tests. They then built a method using near-infrared light, which passes through a sample without destroying it, to predict the amounts of those three compounds. The method matched standard lab tests closely. It could give makers a quick, low-cost way to check each batch.
pmc-13379252:
Ikram Aluahabi and colleagues present a 2026 study on liver biopsy for a rare blood vessel disorder of the liver, shortened to PSVD. Diagnosis rests on biopsy tissue showing no cirrhosis but certain vessel changes, often alongside signs of high pressure in the liver's veins. Guidance calls for a fairly large, intact sample.

The team reviewed nine years of cases at a specialist department and asked whether smaller or broken samples still gave the answer. They gathered clinical, scan, and tissue details for each patient. The study tests whether strict sample rules are always needed, which matters because insisting on them can mean repeat procedures for patients.
pmc-13380452:
Tomohiro Shigematsu and co-authors present a 2026 study on whether a drug for anaemia helps a transplanted kidney work sooner. The drug, daprodustat, mimics low-oxygen signals and has shown kidney-protective effects in earlier lab work. Its value around the time of transplant was unknown.

The study reviewed living-donor kidney transplants at one centre between 2019 and 2023. Patients who received the drug from the day before surgery through the first week were matched with similar patients who did not. The treated group had better kidney function in the first two weeks after surgery. Fewer treated patients had slow-starting grafts, though the study was small and looked back at past records.
pmc-13380752:
Hyungwoo Lee and colleagues describe a 2026 computer method for measuring retinal blood vessels in mice bred to model a hereditary brain vessel disease. The disease, with a very long name shortened to CADASIL, also affects vessels in the eye, which offers a window for study. Precise measures of vessel narrowing are hard to obtain by eye.

The team trained image classifiers to tell normal mice from two mutant lines, using dye-based eye scans. Heat maps from the classifiers marked the vessel areas that drove each decision. A measurement pipeline then traced vessel centres and recorded width, variation, and winding. A further index captured regular bulging along vessels, offering a new way to track the disease.
pmc-13384252:
Abhijith Biji and colleagues fold social and life factors into disease risk models alongside genetic scores in 2026 work. Using the All of Us biobank, with 413,457 people, they compressed over 100 survey measures into a few summary axes. Six chronic diseases were modeled, from asthma and kidney disease to breast and prostate cancer.

Adding the social axes improved prediction for every disease, sometimes more than genetic scores did. Known risks like income and smoking surfaced, along with less expected ones like loneliness and spirituality. Genetic and social risks mostly added up rather than interacting, which supports using both in fairer, sharper risk tools.
pmc-13385652:
Chen and colleagues evaluate a four-level engineering curriculum at a Chinese automotive teaching center, in 2026 education research. The framework blends outcome-based education with the conceive-design-implement-operate model and a teaching-learning-competition loop, progressing students from experiments toward industry-style projects. The team tracked graduate employment, surveyed students' self-assessed competencies, and collected employer feedback to judge whether the structure works at a resource-constrained university rather than an elite school.

During implementation, the graduate employment rate held around 95 percent for four straight years. Job-major alignment, graduates working in their field, ran at about 80.0 percent across the period. The 2023 cohort's starting salary rose 42 percent compared with the 2020 cohort before the framework matured. Students reported high perceived problem-solving ability, and competition results trended positively. Chen argues the competition-driven closed loop gives ordinary universities a workable reform path without budgets.
pmc-13389752:
Efstathios T Detorakis and colleagues report, in 2026, results for a radioactive plaque treatment used after incomplete removal of eye surface cancers. They treated patients with conjunctival melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma whose tumours had not been fully cut out.

Eight patients, four with each cancer type, received ruthenium-106 plaque therapy at a hospital in Heraklion, with no other added treatment to the tumour bed. The plaque delivered a set dose at one millimetre depth, and local control reached three quarters of cases over follow-up ranging from 18 to 75 months. Two patients later needed removal of the eye socket contents after spread. Eye cancer specialists gain small but direct outcome data for a salvage option.
pmc-13390352:
Tahir and colleagues engineer a cumate-inducible switch for Burkholderia bacteria, in 2026 microbiology research. Such systems let scientists turn a gene on with a chemical signal, key for dissecting how these bacteria, dangerous pathogens, cause disease. Existing switches for Burkholderia are few and leaky. The team mutated the circuit and its regulator protein, CymR, to build a version with minimal background leak and tunable control. They verified it with glowing tags and with the cell's own sugar-tagging machinery.

Proteome-wide comparison showed cumate perturbs the cell differently from the rhamnose system, making the two complementary. Because cumate slips through membranes, the switch worked while they replicated inside eukaryotic cells, using chromosome-integration vectors. Running the glycosylation system inside cells showed that sugar tagging contributes to intracellular replication. Tahir offers the toolkit for virulence studies that switch genes mid-infection, when older systems stay silent.
pmc-13390752:
Julian Aguilar-Rosero and co-authors test, in 2026, whether coffee waste can clean dye from water in a sustainable way. About ninety percent of the coffee fruit's weight goes unused in the commercial cycle, creating a large residue problem for the industry.

Three wastes were tried as absorbents for methylene blue dye: coffee husk, spent coffee, and expired coffee. Tests of crystal structure, heat stability, and chemical groups showed that removing fat aligned the material's structure, while charged carboxyl and hydroxyl groups did the dye binding. Water treatment researchers gain a waste-to-resource option with a stated binding mechanism, plus a comparison across three waste streams from the same industry.
pmc-13392152:
Hannah Merrick and a large team evaluate, in 2026, a primary care health check designed with and for autistic adults. Autistic people face more illness of body and mind than most. They also meet steady barriers when they seek care.

The check ran inside a trial in northern England. That trial tests if the check helps health and if it is worth its cost. Forms and talks with autistic people, carers, and staff judged how the check felt and how it ran in real clinics. Care planners gain proof judged by users. It shows what makes a check truly fit for autistic adults. Just putting the check on a list is not enough.
pmc-13392452:
Réka Csáki and a large group of collaborators examined rare changes in KCNA5, the gene for a potassium channel called Kv1.5, in people with pulmonary arterial hypertension. Most such changes sit in a class labelled uncertain, because nobody had tested what they do to the channel. The team drew patients from eight expert centres in Germany and Austria.

Sequencing covered 540 patients and found eleven rare variants, eight of them previously unreported. Six new protein-changing variants went forward for lab testing in frog egg cells, structural work, and cell studies. One variant, noted as G435R in the data, carried far less current than the normal channel. Findings of that kind help clinics judge whether a rare change truly drives disease or is harmless background variation.
pmc-13393652:
Maxine Fogarty and six colleagues measured fearfulness and willingness to explore in laying hens across sixty-four flocks on Australian free-range egg farms, then hunted for farm features that track those temperaments. Each flock faced a novel object and an unfamiliar person, indoors and out on the range, at thirty to forty-six weeks of age. Records, manager interviews, and weather data supplied the farm-side variables, modelled together.

Hyline Brown flocks showed less fear of people and of the novel object outdoors than ISA Brown flocks, despite the strains being marketed as near-identical. Aviary housing made hens bolder around people than flat-deck housing did. Tight feeder space per hen strongly predicted fear of the novel object. Unexplained flock-to-flock variation hinted at stockperson culture mattering too. The authors suggest management tweaks that could lift both welfare and productivity.
pmc-13393952:
Krishna Nanaware and four colleagues ran a double-blind randomised trial comparing two enzyme-based toothpastes against a control in fifty-four patients wearing fixed braces, whose brackets trap plaque and inflame gums. Both test pastes harness natural salivary enzymes. Plaque, gum inflammation, and bleeding on probing were scored over twenty-four weeks, and saliva was assayed for two biochemical markers of oxidative and inflammatory activity.

Both enzyme pastes beat the control on all three clinical measures across the follow-up visits. One saliva marker, reflecting oxidative protein damage, fell significantly in both enzyme groups and correlated strongly with the clinical scores, while the second marker showed no meaningful correlation with anything. The authors conclude enzyme dentifrices offer real anti-plaque and gum benefit for orthodontic patients, a group whose cleaning is mechanically harder.
pmc-13394452:
Yan Sun and co-authors present, in 2026, a colour-changing switch that force must unlock before light can flip it. Stress pulls the starting molecule apart and frees a yellow light switch built on an anthrapyran frame. Only then can ultraviolet light open a ring and turn the dye orange-red. Older designs gave just one colour change, from clear to coloured.

Three stages now mark what a plastic part has been through. Force alone leaves it yellow, and force plus light turns it orange-red. The authors say such parts could sense strain, print patterns in colour, or act as tiny logic gates. The work widens the kit for smart plastics.
pmc-13394852:
Gun Ahn leads a 2026 study that tries to predict who gains from a phone-based mindfulness course. The course aimed at anxiety in autistic adults, who face high anxiety rates. The team reused data from a trial with 73 adults who finished six weeks of app training. They trained six machine learning models and also tested a large language model given a few examples.

A random forest model guessed best who would feel calmer. People who began with higher anxiety tended to gain most. Standard maths models ran close behind the forest. Language model guesses added a low-data option worth more study. The authors see a path to matching patients with care that fits.
pmc-13395352:
Yangji Jia and co-authors test, in 2026, three forage oat types for salty, high land in the Qaidam Basin. The basin's cold, salty soils strain most crops. A two-year field trial weighed yield, feed quality, and steadiness across years. Each type took a different path to success.

One type gave the most fresh yield but swung with the weather. A second gave the best protein and the steadiest quality. The third was the most even all round and used water best. Yield traits traded against feed value across the set. The authors frame the pick by farm goal: bulk, quality, or reliability. Their guide targets salty highland regions alike.
pmc-13395452:
Belina-Anne William M. Thomas leads a 2026 study of behaviour in Malaysian teen boys who cannot tell some colours apart. Colour vision faults can hamper school, play, and friendships. The team screened schools and matched 44 boys with the fault to 44 peers with normal sight, aged 13 to 16. Parents filled a standard behaviour checklist for each boy.

Boys with the fault scored worse on most scales, from anxiety to rule breaking. Attention trouble showed the strongest link. More of them fell in the borderline or clinical range on several scales. Low household income tied to worse scores on some scales. Findings on parent schooling were less sure. The authors urge support that fits family means.
pmc-13395752:
Keuntak Yuk, Hyunjeong Hwang, and Seungho Kim recount, in 2026, a rescue airway trick during windpipe surgery. Their patient, a 33-year-old woman, had a windpipe narrowed by up to ninety percent after past tube care. She needed the tight segment cut out. Small breathing tubes failed to pass at the start of anaesthesia.

A laryngeal mask, seated above the tight zone, kept her oxygen up without crossing the narrowing. Carbon dioxide rose for a while, then eased during surgery. After the segment was cut, a tube across the field took over and the join was finished. She left hospital on day seven. The authors back the mask as a planned backup.
pmc-13395952:
Barbara Barreto Oliveira and co-authors charted drug resistance in bacteria from cat urinary infections in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in a 2026 report. They examined 448 isolates from urine cultures collected between 2020 and 2024 and tested each against a panel of antibiotics.

Escherichia coli caused the largest share at 45.1 percent, followed by Proteus and Klebsiella species. Resistance to first-choice drugs was common, passing 50 percent for some, and 55.8 percent of all isolates resisted several drug classes at once. Meropenem still worked against every isolate tested. The pattern gives local vets a firmer base for choosing first treatments and for watching resistance trends.
pmc-13396052:
Jiemin Fan and colleagues ran a controlled feeding trial in 2026 on two kinds of fiber and bile acids. Bile acids are gut-made chemicals that help digest fat and signal to the body, and each fiber might change them differently. Resistant starch and polydextrose ferment in the gut in different ways, so their effects might differ too.

Healthy volunteers took 23 grams a day of resistant starch, 12 grams a day of polydextrose, both, or a placebo, for 50 days, in a blinded design. Bile acids were measured in blood from 74 people and stool from 50, and gut bacteria were profiled from gene sequencing. The results separate what each fiber does on its own from what they do together.
pmc-13399252:
Phoebe R Darlison and co-authors pooled randomized trials to test whether giving albumin fluid around heart surgery protects the kidneys, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Kidney injury after cardiac surgery is common and serious. Albumin is widely used in operating rooms despite uncertainty about whether it prevents that injury. The team searched major databases and trial registries for trials in adults having on-bypass surgery.

Fourteen trials with 3,304 patients qualified, and seven reported the main kidney outcome. The pooled risk ratio for kidney injury with albumin was 1.09, with a credible interval from 0.86 to 1.34 in the Bayesian analysis, meaning albumin looked no better than other fluids. Only four trials scored low risk of bias. Intensive care and hospital stays, dialysis need, and death rates also showed no clear differences. The authors conclude albumin is unlikely to prevent kidney injury here, and other preventive strategies deserve attention.
pmc-13399452:
Francesca Baratta and colleagues surveyed adults in community pharmacies across north-western Italy about oral cancer, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Interviewers administered a structured questionnaire to pharmacy customers between July 2023 and June 2024, collecting 914 completed responses from people averaging 54 years old.

Overall, about seven in ten respondents (70.4 percent) had heard of the disease, mostly through family and friends at 51.8 percent or through media at 43.2 percent, as the survey reports. Knowledge of causes was lopsided. While nearly all respondents, 97.9 percent, named smoking, only 63.9 percent named alcohol and just 18.6 percent named sunlight exposure, which matters for lip cancer. Nearly everyone surveyed, 92.2 percent, wanted more information, and two thirds picked the community pharmacy as their preferred source. The authors propose pharmacies, with their walk-in reach, as a practical channel for awareness campaigns.
pmc-13399652:
Huicong Yang and colleagues report a laboratory detective story in 2026: a heart failure blood test that screamed emergency in a man whose heart was fine. The 53-year-old patient had B-type natriuretic peptide readings of 4394 to 4419 picograms per milliliter. That is more than forty times the reference limit. Yet he had no heart failure symptoms and a normal ejection fraction of 62 percent.

The mismatch pointed at the assay itself. Diluting the sample behaved linearly, ruling out a hook effect. Adding mouse immunoglobulin, a standard blocking trick, trimmed the apparent BNP by only 15.7 percent. Even a heavy 600 microgram per milliliter dose left a residual reading of 2240. That was evidence of unusually strong human anti-mouse antibodies bridging the test's capture and detection antibodies. Their practical rule: when BNP clashes with the clinical picture and NT-proBNP, suspect the test before treating the patient.
pmc-13399852:
Hanting Yi and colleagues describe a modified double-bundle reconstruction of the anterior cruciate ligament that borrows the bone-saving tricks of the all-inside method, in a 2026 technique paper. The native ligament works as two bundles, and rebuilding both reproduces its anatomy and rotational control better than a single bundle. All-inside surgery instead uses short sockets with cortical button fixation.

Their hybrid keeps the two hamstring graft bundles but seats each in a socket rather than a through-tunnel: four sockets in total, with suspensory fixation at the cortex. Each bundle is tensioned separately so the anteromedial and posterolateral parts can mimic their different working ranges. Less bone is removed and each bundle can be made thicker than in the tunnel version. Their goal is less residual looseness and a better return-to-sport rate for high-demand patients.
pmc-13400552:
Yuanxin Sun and team build, in 2026, imaging models to predict whether small lung adenocarcinomas have invaded the membrane wrapping the lung. That invasion changes staging and surgery choices, yet it is hard to judge before operation. The team used detailed CT scans from patients whose cancers measured 30 mm or less.

Records from 816 surgical patients at two centers fed three model types: classic image features, a deep learning vision model and a combined version. Image regions were split into solid, hazy and surrounding zones to enrich the signal. The combined model scored best in training, while simpler models held up similarly in outside testing. The hybrid pipeline, the authors say, can flag invasion risk before surgery.
pmc-13400652:
Philipp Rieche and colleagues challenge, in 2026, a textbook dividing line in membrane chemistry. Bacterial membrane fats were thought to use one mirror form of a glycerol phosphate backbone, while archaea used the other. Recent finds of both forms in some bacteria raised a question: can ordinary bacterial enzymes make both?

The team tested the three enzymes that build the backbone in a Gram-positive and a Gram-negative bacterium. One enzyme, PlsB, accepted only the standard form. The other two, PlsY and PlsC, used both mirror forms readily. Mixed backbones, then, are a normal product of bacterial fat making, and the supposed strict divide between bacterial and archaeal membranes looks softer.
pmc-13401152:
Xinyuan Wu and a large team review, in 2026, human-robot teamwork as the realistic path toward more autonomous clinics. Robots are entering care. But patient variability, safety demands and shifting clinical settings block full autonomy. The review takes a systems view of recent progress, from architecture and learning to safety and deployment.

The authors propose a dual-brain design. One brain handles clinical reasoning and decision support. The other handles sensing, planning and physical tasks. Examples span imaging, rehab, surgery and outpatient care. Autonomy, they argue, is arriving in stages. It moves from supervised aid to bounded subtasks and coordinated workflows, not by replacing clinicians. Safe adoption, they add, rests on trust, accountability and attention to human factors.
pmc-13401552:
Richard Bui and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of liposomal bupivacaine, a long-acting local anaesthetic that releases its drug slowly from fat-based particles, for pain control around surgery. Good postoperative pain care more and more aims to spare opioids through combined techniques.

Since its first FDA approval, the DepoFoam-based product has spread across surgical specialties and nerve block methods. The review covers its pharmacology, how well it works, its safety profile, and its cost. Current evidence suggests it can cut opioid use after surgery and improve recovery in selected patients and procedures. Its edge over standard local anaesthetics is inconsistent, though, above all against well-optimized multimodal regimens using plain bupivacaine with additives or continuous nerve catheters. The authors weigh where the pricier product earns its place.
pmc-13401652:
In-Uk Song, Byungseok Kim, and Yong An Chung present a 2026 case report of deep magnetic brain stimulation for levodopa-induced dyskinesia, the involuntary movements that long-term Parkinson's treatment often causes. Usual options, such as changing levodopa dose, amantadine, or deep brain stimulation surgery, can fail, be hard to take, or be refused.

Two patients with Parkinson's disease and severe dyskinesia got low-rate deep repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation over the supplementary motor area for two weeks, with no drug changes. Both stuck to the plan and showed short-term drops in how bad the dyskinesia was, on the Unified Dyskinesia Rating Scale and related motor scores. No serious adverse events happened. The authors call the approach feasible for chosen patients, while stressing that two cases without a control group or sham treatment cannot prove it works.
pmc-13401752:
Shinjie Choi, Hyoungmin Kim, Tae-Joon Cho, and Jung Min Ko compare two Korean siblings with Morquio A syndrome treated with enzyme replacement therapy at different ages, in a 2026 case report. The drug, elosulfase alfa, is the only approved treatment for this mucopolysaccharidosis, and the siblings offer a rare natural experiment on timing.

Both children received five years of therapy: the younger started at under one year of age, the older at about five years. Both lost ground on height relative to healthy curves, tracking the disease's natural history, and both showed persistent skeletal deformity by age five. The younger sibling, though, escaped the severe spinal problems of the older pattern, needing no neck surgery for cord compression. Heart measures normalised in both, with stable pumping function and healthy valves. The authors conclude early treatment softens spinal and upper body disease but cannot stop lower limb progression.
pmc-13402652:
Wenyang Xu and co-authors review secondary debilitation, the downward spiral of weakness that follows hip fracture in older adults and often outlasts the broken bone itself. A fracture can trigger muscle loss, poor nutrition, and fresh illness, each feeding the next in a cycle that steals independence. Their narrative review sorts the problem by phase and by the biology underneath, including sarcopenia, the age-linked loss of muscle.

Early care, they argue, should weigh risk carefully and prevent complications before they start. The middle phase calls for combined teams: comanaged wards, fracture liaison services, and systematic rehabilitation running together rather than in turns. Late care may add emerging drug therapies still under study. The authors offer the framework as an evidence base for sharper risk scoring and better-targeted intervention after hip fracture.
pmc-13402852:
Shin-ichi Taniguchi and co-authors interview Japanese doctors about the strain of caring for older patients who carry both type 2 diabetes and dementia. Dementia erodes the daily self-care diabetes demands, forcing hard calls on goals, family roles, and fairness. Six primary care physicians and six diabetes specialists gave semi-structured interviews, coded with the SCAT method for comparing themes.

Both groups described a gap between ideal and feasible care, family friction, emotional burden, and constant practical adjustment of treatment. Primary care doctors dwelt on dignity, life context, long relationships, and coordinating other professionals. Specialists dwelt on disease uncertainty, resetting glucose goals, and the ethics of naming dementia itself. The authors ask for training and organizational backing so doctors can tailor goals without carrying the burden alone.
pmc-13402952:
Izzy C Tiddy and colleagues show that artificial light at night rewires how a coral reef fish answers a predator, flipping its metabolic response upside down. Coastal light pollution keeps spreading, yet its reach into predator-prey encounters was untested. Using virtual reality to flash a standardized predator at wild-caught Polynesian anemonefish while measuring oxygen use, the team compared fish with ambient night histories against fish raised under artificial light.

Normally lit fish did what prey should: they suppressed metabolic rate when the predator appeared, a classic freeze-and-hide economy. Chronically lit fish did the opposite and raised metabolic rate to the same threat. The authors warn that scrambled energy budgeting under light pollution could cascade into survival and population effects on lit reefs, and urge managers to count night light among reef stressors.
pmc-13403152:
The European Food Safety Authority, with Giulia Bellisai among the listed contributors, assesses a request to raise residue limits for the pesticide acequinocyl on celery, Florence fennel, and rhubarb. Agro-Kanesho applied through Germany under the European residue law, proposing a jump from the quantification limit of 0.01 milligrams per kilogram to 3 milligrams per kilogram for northern European use. A public consultation in 2025 drew no extra data or comments.

Germany evaluation report reached the European Commission and EFSA in February 2026, and the Commission mandated EFSA assessment that March. EFSA found data gaps, sent questions back, and received the evaluating state replies in May 2026. The opinion walks the regulatory chain step by step, showing how a residue change is evidenced, consulted on, and judged before any limit moves.
pmc-13403452:
Jiaxin Li and colleagues studied in 2026 whether a simple blood ratio could flag risk after a sudden heart event. The ratio joins platelet count to albumin level, a sign tied to swelling and poor nutrition. Their group held 1,326 patients treated during 2022 and 2023, all followed for one year.

Over that year, 137 people died and 280 people had a major heart or brain event. Risk did not rise in a straight line with the ratio. Both very low and very high values tied to worse outcomes, with a turn point near a ratio of 5.3 in their models. Such a U shape matters when doctors sort patients by risk.
pmc-13403552:
Hugo J Leme and co-authors described in 2026 a woman whose itchy hive-like skin disease resisted years of standard drugs. The 78-year-old had lived with the rash for 12 years across her trunk, back, and legs. Steroids, cyclosporine, methotrexate, and two other immune drugs had all failed her.

A fresh biopsy helped pin down the rare diagnosis, which mixes hive-like bumps with eczema patches. The team then tried mycophenolate mofetil, a drug that quiets immune cells. Her skin improved a great deal on that drug. The report backs it as an option when common choices fail, and it notes how hard the diagnosis can be.
pmc-13403652:
Rukuang Huang and co-authors built a large brain model in 2026 that learns from magnetic brain scans, much as chat models learn from text. Such scans track fast brain activity with fine timing, yet their rich patterns strain older tools. The team trained the model on rest scans from 612 people.

A new coding step turned steady brain signals into tokens without losing timing detail. The trained model could then make fresh data with lifelike traits, from brief bursts to person-to-person spread. It also beat a standard baseline on reading tasks with new people and sessions. Small fine-tuning rounds lifted its scores further.
pmc-13403852:
Max C. Pensel and colleagues followed mental health patients in 2026 through the first year of the COVID pandemic to track dissociative symptoms. Such symptoms, like feeling detached from self or world, often ride along with trauma stress. Records from 93 people at a Bonn hospital covered up to three points in time.

Patients with strong trauma symptoms at the start kept the most intense dissociation all year. Healthy controls sat lowest on the scale. Local virus case counts had no clear sway on symptoms. The strictness of public control steps did sway them, most of all in the trauma group. Social and policy strain weighs on these patients, the authors note.
pmc-13403952:
Onur Aslan and colleagues measured three calcium-linked markers in 2026 across healthy people and patients with clogged heart arteries. Groups held 50 controls, 46 artery patients, and 40 patients who also had type 2 diabetes. Blood tests read gene activity and protein levels for each marker.

Levels of adropin and its gene ran low in artery patients and fell further as artery scores worsened. The other two markers also dropped, with one gene lowest in the diabetes group. Computer network checks tied all three to calcium signaling and heart muscle work. The team calls the links early and in need of larger checks.
pmc-13404352:
Shuyuan Tan and a large team split trial results by sex in 2026 to see who gains from rehab around heart valve surgery. The parent trial held 818 adults having planned valve operations at one center. Rehab added coaching, breathing muscle drills, airway clearing steps, and early walking.

In women, rehab tied to lower risk of lung problems after surgery and of pneumonia in particular. Risk of a collapsed lung pocket also fell in that group. In men, no clear gains showed on any of those measures. The main combined outcome did not budge for either sex. A sex-by-care link for pneumonia reached firm levels, so fresh multi-center trials should test the split.
pmc-13405052:
Becca Freeden and colleagues survey women in the United Kingdom about bladder leakage and exercise, in 2026 work. Leaking urine during activity can push women away from sport, with lasting effects on health. Evidence on how strongly the two connect has been thin.

An online survey drew 413 respondents through social media and university channels, with 410 kept in the analysis. Most were aged 25 to 44, the largest group in the reported sample. Leakage severity was scored with the ICIQ-UI short form and activity with the IPAQ short form. Free-text answers added personal accounts of how leakage changes participation, letting the team link measured activity levels with lived experience.
pmc-13405552:
Rafael da Silveira Moreira and co-authors analyse tooth loss in older Brazilians using the SB Brasil 2023 survey, in 2026 work. Nearly ten thousand people aged 65 to 74 were examined across all 27 federal units. Complete tooth loss, edentulism, affected 36.5 percent of them in the reported figures.

Places with more dentists per head showed slightly lower odds of tooth loss, a protective pattern. Deprivation raised risk steeply, with the poorest fifth facing odds of 1.92 against the reference group. Missing specialist dental centres and prosthesis laboratories also tracked with more tooth loss. Women and those aged 69 or older carried higher odds, combining town-level and personal influences.
pmc-13407152:
Fernando A. Arosa and Elsa M. Cardoso offer, in 2026, a fresh way to think about the tail end of MHC class I molecules, the display structures that show cell contents to killer T cells. Textbook accounts treat these molecules as steady presenters, yet on the cell surface they actually occur in several shapes, some loaded with fragments and some empty.

The authors propose that the short inner tail acts like a switch linking shape changes to internal regulation, including chemical edits to conserved motifs, movement through the cell, and signalling. Computer predictions of flexible, disordered stretches in the tail support the scheme. Direct evidence remains thin, they concede, so the piece is framed as a working model to steer experiments on immune and non-immune cell communication.
pmc-13407452:
Mark Ryan writes, in 2026, about the hidden workers who screen violent material so that AI systems and social platforms stay clean. These data workers must view and hear content that includes torture, sexual abuse, and murder, labour that stays invisible behind secrecy agreements, outsourcing to poorer countries, and responsible-AI branding.

Ryan uses phenomenological analysis, the close study of lived experience. He argues the exposure wounds workers in ways unlike other jobs that face violent material. The volume, speed, and accumulation are unmatched. Workers describe trauma from doubting whether what they saw was real, exhaustion from being unable to help victims, and a spread of physical, psychological, and relationship problems. The piece demands the profession be recognised rather than concealed.
pmc-13407652:
Ravi Gupta and co-authors ran, in 2026, a randomised trial comparing two dissection orders for keyhole gallbladder removal. Bile duct injury is the operation's feared complication. It usually follows misread anatomy. A standard safe view of the anatomy prevents it. The body-first technique claims to reach that view more reliably than the standard approach.

Eighty patients were randomised evenly. The body-first group reached a satisfactory safe view in 92.5 percent of cases against 75 percent with the standard method. That gap missed significance on a simple test. It held after adjustment, though. The standard method carried far lower odds of success. Operating time was similar, driven mainly by case difficulty rather than technique. Recovery and satisfaction measures were also collected through three months.
pmc-13408052:
Ji-Yang Song and co-authors present, in 2026, a child whose racing heart slowly weakened the heart itself. Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy arises when a persistent fast rhythm enlarges the heart and breeds failure, yet it reverses when the rhythm is fixed. The reported child had endured a year of intermittent breathlessness and palpitations. Only then was the cause pinned down.

Electrical mapping inside the heart, guided by a three-dimensional navigation system, located the rogue focus driving paroxysmal atrial tachycardia to the rim of the right upper pulmonary vein. Radiofrequency ablation burned the spot successfully. Symptoms improved markedly, the child went home uneventfully, and eight months on there was no recurrence, with ultrasound confirming heart size and function back to normal. Early rhythm treatment is the case's lesson.
pmc-13408152:
Huiyu Dan and co-authors separate, in 2026, two effects that have been boosting claims for heat-to-power films. Pyroelectric films generate charge when heat changes, but part of the signal comes from the contact interface rather than the film itself. Ignoring that interfacial share overstates the intrinsic effect. The team exploits the fact that only the intrinsic part flips when polarisation is reversed.

Polarity-reversal measurements split the contributions film by film. In lead titanate films with Schottky contacts the intrinsic effect dominated, while in barium titanate films the interfacial effect ruled. Correcting the split changed the energy figure of merit used to rank films. A machine-learning model then predicted each effect's share for new candidates, offering a rapid screening strategy for high-performance pyroelectric devices.
pmc-13408452:
Nina Marsh and co-authors ask in 2026 whether a hard childhood changes how the hormone oxytocin steers giving in adults. Oxytocin is known to shape social behaviour. Early hardship can also blunt the will to help strangers. Volunteers played a donation task inside a brain scanner. Each had first received oxytocin or a placebo.

The hormone pushed the two groups in opposed directions. Adults reporting more childhood hardship donated more under oxytocin. Those with gentler childhoods donated less. Brain recordings matched the behaviour. Links between two brain areas tied to social judgement and empathy shifted in step. The team reads this as early life tuning the social circuits of the brain. The same chemical signal then lands in unlike ways, depending on a person's past.
pmc-13408652:
Ji-Yoon Kim, Un-Bong Baik, Dawoon Jeong, and Yoon-Ji Kim compare in 2026 two ways of widening a narrow upper jaw in growing children: clear aligners versus conventional slow expanders. Forty-eight patients around nine years old took part across several centres, half in each group, with jaw measurements taken before treatment, after expansion, and after a retention period.

Both approaches widened the arch significantly and the gains held through retention. The expander group showed slightly more whole-tooth movement at the molars, though not significantly, while aligners produced greater widening at the canine tips. Older children gained less at the canines. Against a preset non-inferiority margin, aligners matched the conventional appliance overall. Orthodontists gain prospective evidence that a removable, discreet option can do the widening job in suitable growing patients.
pmc-13410452:
Alexandra Gruzdenko and co-workers show in 2026 that liquid crystal polymers can move under magnets without any added magnetic filler. Tiny robots for medicine usually need composite mixes, which complicates making them. A single soft material that answers to a magnet would simplify design.

Flat microdisks of the polymer turned in a rotating magnetic field, driven by the material's own uneven magnetic response. They kept pace with the field up to a step-out rate near that of swimming microbes, using modest field strengths. Light-based patterning set each disk's inner alignment, which tuned how it sat in the field and when it slipped. Shape-changing tricks known for these polymers could later add gripping or crawling.
pmc-13410852:
Chantal Kopecky and colleagues show in 2026 that the stiffness of the gel around breast cancer cells steers how stem-like those cells become. Flexible cells that can change type help tumors spread and resist drugs. Surroundings are part of that story, since tissue stiffness varies across a tumor.

Flat patterned gels and printed three-dimensional matrices let the team set stiffness precisely. Soft matrices pushed cells toward stem-like traits, raised a marker called ALDH1, and made them harder to kill with two drugs. Stiff matrices kept cells in a more settled, mature state. A surface marker also switched form with stiffness. Printed matrices copied the flat results, offering a lifelike test bed.
pmc-13411052:
Ji-Yoon Jung and colleagues compare in 2026 two anesthesia starting drugs for agitation as patients wake after bladder surgery done through the urethra. Waking agitation can distress patients and staff, and drug choice may sway its odds. Records came from adults having planned endoscopic urologic surgery.

From 239 patients, matching formed 99 pairs with similar profiles. Agitation struck about 13 percent of the remimazolam group versus about 36 percent with propofol. Agitation also ran milder with remimazolam, while tube removal time, pain scores, and recovery room medicines matched between groups. Younger age and male sex raised agitation risk on their own. The gentler wake-up came at no cost to recovery speed.
pmc-13411152:
John Ku, Kailey Flora, Stefanie Steiger, and Hans-Joachim Anders review in 2026 the double life of neutrophils, the most common white blood cells, in kidney disease. These cells defend the urinary tract by swallowing germs and casting DNA nets. Turned loose wrongly, the same weapons scar the kidney itself.

Misdirected neutrophil attack drives injury in vessel inflammation, blocked blood flow, cholesterol crystal showers, and steady decline toward kidney failure. Local chemistry decides which face the cells show, and kidney toxins in chronic disease warp them further. New imaging and single-cell tools are redrawing the map of their behavior. Drugs that calm specific neutrophil pathways form the hopeful frontier the review lays out.
pmc-13411252:
Fernanda Karla Metelski and colleagues examine in 2026, in Portuguese, how health workers in a priority Brazilian city care for people living with HIV. Global pledges aim to end the AIDS epidemic by 2030, and local practice decides whether those pledges land. Interviews covered 45 people: care staff, managers, and patients.

Seven themes emerged around quick testing with counseling, early diagnosis, and prompt start of antiretroviral therapy. Nurses carried much of the preventive and clinical load. Engagement with treatment showed strains, and information systems had clear limits. Tackling stigma, which patients met from family, staff, and society alike, lagged furthest behind. Fair, joined-up strategies that face social conditions head-on are the study's closing plea.
pmc-13411352:
Laith Al-Eitan and colleagues test in 2026 whether variants in two genes raise the odds of high blood pressure. Pressure control involves many genes and habits, and most mechanisms remain murky. Blood DNA came from 220 patients with hypertension and 220 people with normal pressure.

Three variants were typed across the folate-handling gene MTHFR and the salt-regulating gene WNK1. One MTHFR variant, rs1801131, linked significantly to hypertension under several inheritance models. A paired-letter pattern in the same gene doubled the odds in carriers. No headline claim is made for the WNK1 variant in the report. The MTHFR marker may join future gene-based risk checks, pending confirmation in larger groups.
pmc-13412252:
Andrea Giovanni Parato and co-authors pool trials in 2026 on devices that seal the vein after heart catheter procedures done through the groin. The reviewers searched three databases through April 2025 for randomized trials making that comparison.

Seven trials with 948 patients met the criteria. Device closure clearly shortened the time to stop bleeding and the time until patients could walk. Discharge eligibility also came sooner, while major complications stayed rare and similar between groups. Minor vascular complications fell by more than half with devices, supporting their wider use.
pmc-13412552:

Combining tumour data from a major cancer atlas with seven independent datasets, the analysis found eight RGS genes consistently altered in breast cancer. Two genes acted as independent risk factors, while two others tracked immune activity; one, RGS18, came mainly from the tumour surroundings rather than cancer cells. The authors link the changes to gene amplification and methylation and propose the family as a stratification framework.
pmc-13414052:

The strain, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei Yb, first showed immune-stirring effects in cell dishes. Antibody levels and airway twitchiness, though, barely moved, and eosinophil counts in lung fluid showed no clear gain. Freeze-dried yogurt lagged behind both. The authors caution that matching doses and adding yogurt-only controls must come before asthma claims.
pmc-13416752:
Xiaohang Lu, Nana Ma, and Yuan Wang test whether adding monosodium glutamate lifts a health linked compound in black highland barley, in a 2026 study. The compound is GABA, an amino acid valued for its effects in the body. Germination conditions and precursor choice were tuned first with single factor trials.

Glutamate salt beat plain glutamic acid, and GABA peaked near 2.55 milligrams per gram of grain. Three lab methods profiled 1,248 metabolites, covering amino acids, fatty acids, and flavour compounds. The added precursor feeds an enzyme that makes GABA, which may also support energy pathways. Results offer a route to richer barley foods.
pmc-13418052:

The team used tin oxide films in electrolyte-gated transistors, where a liquid gate drives chemical change.

Electrochemical doping converted the material from p-type tin oxide to n-type tin dioxide by oxidising its tin atoms. Both forms showed low-voltage operation, sharp switching, high on-off current ratios, and long-term stability. By doping only chosen areas of a single tin oxide layer, the team built working inverter, NAND, and NOR gates, the building blocks of logic circuits. They present it as a path to programmable oxide circuits that sidestep the fragility of two-dimensional materials.
pmc-13418152:
Lotte Habermann-Horstmeier and Lukas M Horstmeier analyse how immune and gut symptoms cluster in ME/CFS by sex and menopause, in a 2026 study. Data covered 748 adults with a medical diagnosis, mostly women. Symptoms were coded simply as present or absent, and a battery of statistical models searched for underlying groupings in each sex.

In women, immune symptoms and gut symptoms formed two related but separate clusters. In men, all four symptoms merged into one combined cluster. Infection susceptibility was the strongest single predictor overall. Among women, flu like symptoms were commoner before menopause, while gut symptoms stayed stable across menopause groups.
pmc-13418852:

The measure is the level of erythropoietin, a hormone that drives red blood cell growth. Their data come from a large European registry study that follows patients with these bone marrow disorders over time.

Levels were on hand for 672 of the 1610 patients who had at least a year of follow-up in the registry. The team linked the hormone levels to later outcomes, adjusting for blood counts, marrow findings, and genetic risk groups. A cheap test with real forecast value could help doctors choose who should get growth-factor drugs early. The pooled registry scale gives the estimates a firmer base than single-clinic work.
pmc-13419952:
Cheng Chen and colleagues survey fresh progress in cardiac intensive care, the specialty units for the sickest heart patients. Treatment approaches and team organization receive the same treatment in turn. Care this complex demands many specialties working as one team, a theme the authors stress throughout. Unit leaders get a single map of where the field is moving and what to adopt next.
pmc-13421052:

In computer tests on a phantom, LOTUS cut the g-factor by 20 to 31 percent. The g-factor gauges how much noise grows when a scan is sped up. The comparison was against rival paths at the highest rate of skipped data. LOTUS also rebuilt images more faithfully on error and likeness measures in those tests. Brain scans from two volunteers, at two and four times the speed, showed the same pattern. Gains grew as more slices were combined. pmc-13421152:

Higher drug levels in the blood modestly raised the risk. Why the combination behaves this way remains unclear.
pmc-13421352:

That swap resists breakdown in the body. Several frontline diabetes drugs, the SGLT2 inhibitors, are built this way because of it. Their method starts from unprotected natural sugars, converts them into hydrazide reagents, and releases sugar radicals under mild conditions for coupling to aromatic partners. The route produced all approved SGLT2 inhibitors, natural products and medicinal probes, and it forms carbon bonds at positions beyond the usual attachment point. The authors offer it as a shorter platform for sugar-based chemistry.
pmc-13421452:

Instead of comparing single connections, they computed brain gradients — maps that order cortex from sensory areas to higher-order regions — in 1,071 participants.

The sample covered people at clinical high risk for psychosis, recent-onset psychosis, recent-onset depression and healthy controls. Every clinical group showed changes in the visual-to-sensorimotor gradient, while only recent psychosis altered the sensory-to-association gradient. High-risk and psychosis groups scored lower in the ventral attention network, and clinical groups overall showed a compressed gradient range. Linking differences to receptor maps, the authors probe the chemistry beneath the disorder.
pmc-13421652:
Karthik Shree Harini and Devaraj Ezhilarasan write, in a 2026 commentary, about fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction as it presents in India. The condition, now called MASLD, is the world's commonest chronic liver disease, and the Indian picture has features that global averages hide.

Population-specific genetic influences add another regional layer, and the tight link with type 2 diabetes shapes risk. The authors argue for region-specific prevention, earlier risk assessment and care that treats liver and metabolism together rather than in separate clinics.
pmc-13422352:

Nearly half of those isolates formed biofilms, in strengths from weak to strong. Eight antifungal drugs were tested by disk diffusion, and two biofilm genes, ALS1 and HWP1, were checked by PCR. The authors tie biofilm formation to the resistance picture their susceptibility results draw.
pmc-13422652:

Seventeen women completed the diet, a month of gradual carbohydrate return, then a balanced lower-calorie diet, with body scans and a day sealed in a whole-room calorimeter at each stage.

The authors read the pattern as physiology recovering, not fighting back.
pmc-13422752:

pmc-13423052:

A credit-risk scenario shows profiles being rescored as economic conditions move, sharpening judgement without discarding the fuzzy base.
pmc-13423152:

Both groups get the same 50 hours spread over two weeks. Outcomes centre on motor function and daily independence. Showing that parents can deliver the therapy at home could widen access where specialist services are scarce.
pmc-13423352:

pmc-13424152:

Services themselves were judged imperfect, with narrow scope, scarce resources, and variable caregiver quality. The cost burden of care formed a further theme. The authors use the accounts to mark where the young scheme needs repair.
pmc-13424552:

pmc-13424952:

pmc-13425652:

pmc-13425752:

pmc-13426352:
Weite Liu and colleagues review advances in using intraocular fluid to diagnose and treat uveitis in a 2026 article. pmc-13426452:
Sofia Leonardo and a large international team evaluated a global nutrition program for childhood cancer in resource-limited settings in a 2026 article. pmc-13426952:

pmc-13427752:

pmc-13428252:

pmc-13428452:

pmc-13429252:

The authors argue brain health policy should look beyond the person to the neighborhood and its social ties.
pmc-13430652:

The authors say the approach sidesteps several limits of the technique, including weak statistical power from small samples. Code and a worked guide are freely available on GitHub and Zenodo.
pmc-13430952:

A model built only from upstream factors separated those with care needs from those without with strong accuracy. Age, nutrition risk, work status, mood, self-rated health, income, and home changes ranked as the top drivers.
pmc-13432152:

pmc-13432352:
Vienna Man Wah Ng and co-authors followed patients in 2026 who had early bowel cancer snipped out through the bowel wall, asking whether a follow-up salvage operation truly lifts long-term survival. The authors back snip-only care as a safe pick when risk reads stay low.
pmc-13432852:

pmc-13433152:
Yang Wen and co-authors built a fair test frame in 2026 for grading chat model advice on diabetic foot care. Fast action on nerve risk, sores, and blood flow can save limbs in that field. One model topped most worth scales, while a rival read easiest yet scored low on worth for some scales. A harm flag sweep screened for plain danger signs. Deep fact checks sat outside the frame's scope.
pmc-13433252:

When the rule stretched to new sights, patterns grew still more spare and sight-free. The arc heals the clash, since both views catch true phases of one road. Crowd codes shed bulk as rules firm up, then shed ties to sights as rules go wide.
pmc-13433952:

The gate pours calcium from cell stores when a sugar note calls, which shapes signals for life acts from cell death to muscle pull. Kind two had lacked frames while its kin stood mapped.
