pmc-13434052:
Zechang Wei and co-authors cast a fluid metal mix in 2026 as a dual-use skin for war gear. It hides heat glow from heat eyes. It also turns heat gaps into power and signals. Stock hide goods do one job, which falls short of mixed field needs. The mix of gallium and indium stays fluid at room heat.

Small heat gaps across the film stir up voltage, since the mix rides the heat-to-charge effect well. That free power feeds live reads of body heat and breath pace. pmc-13434152:

pmc-13436352:

pmc-13436552:

That signal did not come with the same support in men or overall. The authors urge caution, since the sex-specific result could be a chance finding, and they call for validation in larger independent groups before any clinical meaning is attached.
pmc-13436652:

Overdose visits kept their prior slope without a step jump. Appendicitis visits serve as a control for ward wide swings. pmc-13436952:

pmc-13437352:

pmc-13439552:

pmc-13440152:

pmc-13440452:

pmc-13443052:

pmc-13446352:

pmc-13447152:

pmc-13448252:

pmc-13449652:

pmc-13449952:

pmc-13450252:

pmc-13452252:

pmc-13452352:

pmc-13453752:

pmc-13454252:

pmc-13454452:

pmc-13454552:

pmc-13454952:

pmc-13455352:

pmc-13455452:

pmc-13455552:

Thomas Vaughan put the Fama and Confessio into English in 1652, the first English Rosicrucian texts. The two manifestos first came out in German lands in 1614 and 1615. They claimed a hidden brotherhood held deep lore and sought to reform the world.

The Fama tells of Christian Rosenkreuz, his travels, and his vault tomb. The Confessio calls scholars to join the work and share their finds. No proof of the brotherhood ever surfaced, yet the call stirred Europe. Vaughan's version spread the Rosy Cross myth across England in time. Alchemists and seekers mined these pages for secret lore.
self-culture-and-perfection-of-character: Self-Culture and Perfection of Character, 1852. The self-culture. This book preserves that work. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
stowe-uncle-toms-cabin-1852:
Harriet Beecher Stowe published Uncle Tom's Cabin in 1852, with the subtitle Life Among the Lowly. The contents alone map a wide cast, from an evening in Tom's cabin to a Quaker settlement. Early chapters show Eliza learning she may lose her child and choosing flight.

Eliza's escape across the ice, little Eva, Topsy, and the cruel Simon Legree became known to millions. Tom's faith under harsh masters forms the moral core of the long tale. The novel sold hundreds of thousands of copies in its first year. It turned broad feeling against slavery and became the best-selling novel of its century.
the-lock-and-key-library-the-most-intere: Julian Hawthorne's "most interesting stories" collection: the world's best short fiction gathered for American readers. Mystery, adventure, and romance from many lands fill a rich and varied anthology. This complete edition shows his sure editorial taste, and every story earns its place.
the-philosophy-of-phrenology-1852: The Philosophy of Phrenology, 1852. The phrenological philosophy. This book preserves that work. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It retains its place in time. The paper lasts as a quiet witness to its time.
theatrum-chemicum-britannicum-containing: Theatrum chemicum britannicum, 1652. The British chemical theatre. This book preserves that collection. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
theatrvm-chemicvm-britannicum-containing: Theatrum chemicum britannicum, 1652. Another edition. This book preserves that collection. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
tob-0152:
Crowley's Vision and the Voice records his workings of 1909 in Algeria, where he scryed the thirty Aethyrs of the Enochian system. Vision by vision, angels, abysses, and terrible splendors pass before him. The notebooks became one of Thelema's central records of attainment.

Volume four of the notebook edition continues the transcribed series. Crowley crosses the Abyss in the visions and claims the grade of Magister Templi, master of the temple. The text is dense, symbolic, and meant for initiates. The material remains under copyright, with no public-domain text distributed here. Students of Crowley treat the work as his spiritual diary at its most intense.
tob-13152:
A. E. Waite devoted his late work The Holy Grail to the legends of the Grail, the vessel of the Last Supper and the Crucifixion. Waite was both occultist and scholar of Christian mysticism. He had chased the Grail's meaning through years of study.

He traces the tales from early romances onward, asks how they took Christian shape, and argues the Grail hides a secret tradition of the church. The book is dense, learned, and fully Waite's own in its claims. Readers of Arthurian romance and of occult history alike treat it as the mature sum of his Grail research.
turgenev-sportsmans-sketches-1852:
Ivan Turgenev published A Sportsman's Sketches in 1852, his twenty-five sketches of peasant life under serfdom. The sketches exposed serfdom's cruelty so tellingly that the book is credited with helping free the serfs. Turgenev, hunting with his spaniel, listens more than he shoots, and Russia heard its peasants speak.

Khor and Kalinych, the first sketch, pairs a shrewd, practical serf with a dreamy, gentle one in Orel province. Bezhin Meadow gives peasant boys telling ghost tales by a night fire, in pages of famous beauty and dread. Landowners, overseers, and serf actors and singers fill out a survey no statistics could match for truth of life. The sportsman's mild voice let radical matter past the censor into the conscience of the reading class of Russia. Alexander II kept the book by him, it was said, when he signed emancipation.
un-ga-res-1752: West New Guinea passed from Dutch hands toward Indonesia under a deal noted in Resolution 1752, adopted on 21 September 1962. Indonesia and the Netherlands had settled their long fight over the land. The Assembly thanks the Acting Secretary-General for his work in bringing the peace about. It takes note of the deal, accepts the role the deal gives the Secretary-General, and grants him power to carry out the tasks laid on him.
un-ga-res-1952:
Hope and pressure mix in Resolution 1952, adopted by the General Assembly on 11 December 1963, on the question of Northern Rhodesia. The British-run land, soon to become Zambia, stood near the end of colonial rule. The Assembly had read the report of its decolonization team and heard the ruling power report fresh steps toward a new constitution that same month.

The text states again the fixed right of the people of Northern Rhodesia to rule themselves and stand free. It notes with pleasure that votes for a new law-making council will be held in January 1964. Britain is asked to fix, with the new elected rulers, a date for freedom, and as soon as can be. The hope is voiced that no new block will bar the way.
un-ga-res-a-69-52:
United action toward a world free of nuclear arms is urged in Resolution A/69/52, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. All states, it holds, must take fresh, workable steps toward the total end of such arms. The end goal of all arms work is named: full disarmament under strict and sound world check.

Deep worry at the ruinous toll of any use of nuclear arms runs through the text. All states must keep to world law at all times, the law of war among it. Every effort must be made, it holds, to shun the use of such arms at all. The vote stands in a yearly chain that keeps the end goal in sight.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 1752 (XVII) was adopted on 21 September 1962. It welcomed the settlement of the dispute over West New Guinea, also called West Irian. The dispute was between Indonesia and the Netherlands. The Assembly took note of their agreement. It praised the Acting Secretary-General's part in reaching a peaceful deal. It gave the Secretary-General power to carry out the tasks the agreement gave him.

General Assembly Resolution 1952 (XVIII), adopted on 11 December 1963, concerned Northern Rhodesia, the British-ruled territory that soon became Zambia. The Assembly restated the people's firm right to self-rule and independence, in line with the 1960 declaration on ending colonial rule.

The text welcomed word that voting for a new Legislative Council would take place in January 1964. It voiced the hope that independence would come at the nearest possible date. It asked the ruling power to fix that date, working with the newly elected government. It asked that nothing block the territory's move to statehood.

General Assembly resolution 69/52 (2014), 'United action towards the total elimination of nuclear weapons,' strings together the practical agenda of the Non-Proliferation Treaty system. It condemns the Democratic People's Republic of Korea's nuclear tests and missile launches in the strongest terms. It demands it abandon its programmes. It stresses that it can never hold nuclear-weapon state status. For the recognized nuclear powers it urges deeper cuts, test-ban ratification, and a fissile material treaty. It urges security assurances and universal safeguards. This comes ahead of the 2015 treaty review conference.
un-sc-res-1352:
Iraq's oil-for-food program let a sanctioned state sell oil to buy civilian goods, and it needed a short renewal in 2001. The Iraqi people had lived under sanctions for more than a decade. The program was a temporary measure, meant to cover civilian needs until Iraq met the Council's terms. Resolution 1352 was adopted unanimously on 1 June 2001.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the terms of Resolution 1330, the previous oil-for-food decision. Those terms would now run until 3 July 2001. That short span is the whole grant the resolution makes. The Council also stated what it intended next. New arrangements would be considered, to speed the flow of civilian goods into Iraq. At the same time, controls on goods banned under the sanctions had to grow tighter.
un-sc-res-1452:
Sanctions on the Taliban and Al-Qaida froze bank accounts around the world. Some frozen funds covered food, rent, and medicine for listed people. On 20 December 2002 the Security Council carved out a humanitarian exception. It acted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The text amended how the asset freeze in resolutions 1267 and 1390 would work. States gained a way to release money for basic needs.

Funds could be freed when a state judged them necessary for basic expenses. Interest and contract payments could still be added to frozen accounts. The sanctions committee had to track which states used the exception. It would keep and update a list of them. The change softened a blunt tool without lifting the freeze.
un-sc-res-1552: In 2005 the Security Council added Resolution 1552 to its record, and the text is kept here through a Wikisource transcription. Formal resolutions like this one often extend or adjust an existing course of action rather than start one. Whatever its subject, the entry's worth lies in the exact official wording, preserved end to end.
un-sc-res-1652:
Côte d'Ivoire's peacekeeping operation was renewed by the Security Council on 24 January 2006. The International Working Group had issued a communiqué on 15 January backing the prime minister's road map to elections. The Secretary-General's report of 3 January 2006 was before the Council. The crisis and the blocks on reconciliation persisted from all sides, the Council said.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the mandates of the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire and of the French forces supporting it to 15 December 2006. The troop movement provisions of resolution 1609 (2005) ran for the same period. The Council said it would review the mission's tasks and troop levels alongside the coming report on Liberia. The aim was free, fair, open elections no later than 31 October 2006. Progress on the road map would guide any change to the force.
un-sc-res-1752:
Georgia's observer mission was renewed after an attack in the Kodori valley on 13 April 2007. The Secretary-General had reported on 11 January and 3 April. UNOMIG and the CIS peacekeeping force shared the work of steadying the zone. Talks on documents covering the non-use of violence and the return of refugees were near completion. Economic recovery in Abkhazia was judged badly needed.

The Council condemned the attack on villages in the upper Kodori valley and called for those behind it to be found. Both sides were told to resume dialogue and to honor the ceasefire and non-violence deals in full. The package of documents on non-violence and refugee return had to be finished without delay. The Council backed the confidence-building proposals put forward by the Group of Friends. It extended UNOMIG's mandate to 15 October 2007. Georgia's sovereignty and territorial integrity inside its recognized borders were restated.
un-sc-res-1852:
The inquiry into the Beirut bombing that killed former prime minister Rafiq Hariri gained a final extension on 17 December 2008. The International Independent Investigation Commission had sent its latest report. The Special Tribunal for Lebanon was on track to start work on 1 March 2009 at The Hague. The commission asked to run to 28 February 2009 so it could hand over without a break.

The Council welcomed the commission's report and praised the progress made on all the cases in its mandate. It extended the commission's mandate to 28 February 2009. The commission would keep investigating while shifting its operations, staff, and files to The Hague. Lebanon's prime minister had written on 4 December 2008 in support of the request. Once the tribunal opened, its prosecutor would take over the inquiry into the 14 February 2005 attack and any linked cases.
un-sc-res-1952: Adopted in 2010, Resolution 1952 is preserved in this collection as a Security Council act in record form. The transcription is English Wikisource's. Inside, the members state the situation in their shared diplomatic language, then convert it into instructions in numbered paragraphs. The entry keeps the conversion whole, which is where the Council's power lives.
un-sc-res-252:
Jerusalem's status brought Jordan's complaint before the Council in 1968. On 21 May 1968 the Council took up measures Israel had adopted in the city. The General Assembly had already told Israel to cancel such steps. Israel had instead taken more of them. The Council restated that land cannot be gained by military conquest.

It deplored Israel's failure to obey the Assembly resolutions. It held that all Israeli laws and acts meant to change Jerusalem's status are invalid. Taking land and property for that purpose cannot change the city's standing. Israel had to cancel the measures already taken. It also had to stop any further steps of that kind.
un-sc-res-452: For the year 1979, the catalog lists Resolution 452 among the Security Council's formal decisions. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-52: Three years of atomic work went on the record in Security Council Resolution 52, passed on 22 June 1948. The Atomic Energy Commission, set up by the Assembly's first vote in 1946, had sent the Council its first, second, and third reports. The Council rules that the Secretary-General send all three reports to the General Assembly and to all member states. The record of the Council's own talks on the reports goes with them, as a matter of special weight.
un-sc-res-652: Among the formal acts of the United Nations Security Council sits Resolution 652, which the catalog dates to 1990. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Iraq's oil-for-food program gained a short bridge in the spring of 2001. On 1 June, the Council adopted Resolution 1352 without dissent. It acted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The program let Iraq sell oil under UN control to buy civilian goods. Broad sanctions from the 1990 invasion of Kuwait stayed in place.

The text extends the current rules by about a month, to 3 July 2001. It then announces a plan for new rules. A Goods Review List would speed civilian trade. Controls on banned items would grow tighter. Oil cash would be kept inside the UN escrow account. The step led toward the revised sanctions of later months.

Frozen bank accounts can also freeze ordinary life. Resolution 1452, adopted unanimously on 20 December 2002, carved humanitarian room into the Taliban and Al-Qaida sanctions. People on the blacklist could not touch their money at all. That blocked rent, food, medicine, and legal bills, even where no terror link existed.

The text lets states release funds for basic expenses. Food, housing, medical care, taxes, utilities, and lawyers qualify. States must notify the sanctions committee first. Silence for forty-eight hours means consent. Larger extraordinary expenses need the committee's approval. Interest earned on frozen accounts stays frozen. The change kept pressure on listed terrorists while easing pointless hardship around them.

The year 1960 brought a wave of new African states to the UN. Congo won independence from Belgium that summer. Its freedom quickly slid into crisis and foreign meddling. Still, the new republic applied for membership at once. Resolution 152 was adopted unanimously on 23 August 1960.

Members recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of the Congo. The Assembly soon did. A UN seat gave Congo legal standing during its turmoil. It also strengthened the case for the huge UN operation then deploying there. That mission tried to hold the country together. Congo's admission remains a marker of the great decolonization wave that reshaped the UN.

Weapons kept flowing to militias in Ituri and the Kivus, and on 27 July 2004 the arms embargo on armed groups in eastern Congo is renewed. A group of experts had reported on the flow. The parties, the Council found, had failed to meet its demands, and the inflow of arms kept the whole region insecure.

Acting under Chapter VII, the embargo measures are renewed until 31 July 2005. The measures would be reviewed by 1 October 2004 and regularly after that. The group of experts is re-established until 31 January 2005 to track compliance, with a written report due through the sanctions committee before 15 December 2004.

Resolution 1652, adopted on 24 January 2006, extends the UN operation in Côte d'Ivoire through most of that year. The Council had endorsed the international working group's January communiqué and the roadmap for ending the country's division. The Secretary-General's report of 3 January described a peace process still blocked by obstacles from all sides.

Under Chapter VII, the mandates of the UN operation, UNOCI, and the French forces supporting it were extended until 15 December 2006. The special arrangements for reinforcing UNOCI, set the previous June, were extended for the same period. The Council voiced deep worry that the crisis dragged on, a judgment repeated so often in these renewals that it reads as the era's refrain.

Resolution 1752, passed on 13 April 2007, keeps the UN watch team in Georgia for six more months. Two UN reports, in January and April, set out the team's work in Abkhazia. The Council praised the UN chief and his envoy for their steady push. A friends group, Russia as go-between, and a European security body all lent a hand. The team worked hand in glove with a peace force from the post-Soviet bloc, and both held the zone calm.

The team's term ran to October 2007. The Council restated its faith in Georgia's unity and its borders, as the world knows them. A pact could come by calm means alone, it said. Both sides were called back to talks. Trade and jobs in Abkhazia were named a dire need for the folk the war had hurt.

Resolution 1852, adopted on 17 December 2008, covers the final handover in the Hariri murder investigation. The independent commission investigating the 2005 bombing that killed Lebanon's former prime minister had asked for more time. The new Special Tribunal for Lebanon was on track to open at The Hague on 1 March 2009, and Lebanon's prime minister supported the request in a December letter.

The Council extended the commission's mandate until 28 February 2009. The point was continuity: investigators would keep working without a gap while gradually moving operations, staff, and files to The Hague, so the transition finished as the tribunal began. The commission's work on the bombing and other attacks since October 2004 was commended.

Armed groups in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo were still attacking civilians in late 2010. Resolution 1952, adopted on 29 November 2010, renews the sanctions aimed at those groups. The text names the FDLR and the Lord's Resistance Army. Money from illegal mining helped keep such groups armed.

The Council renewed the arms embargo, transport controls, travel bans, and asset freezes until 30 November 2011. It extended the group of experts that monitors the measures. A sixth expert was added to cover natural resources. The text also backed guidelines for companies that buy minerals from Congo. Firms were expected to check their supply chains with care. The aim was to stop the mineral trade from paying for armed groups and abuses.

Resolution 2052, adopted on 27 June 2012, renews the UN Disengagement Observer Force on the Golan Heights. UNDOF watches the area of separation between Israeli and Syrian forces under a 1974 agreement. The Secretary-General reported breaches of that deal, including Syrian troops entering the area in March and shots fired at UN observer teams. Events in Syria's own conflict were starting to spill into UNDOF's zone.

The Council renews UNDOF for six months, until 31 December 2012. It calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338, respect the 1974 agreement in full, show the greatest restraint, and guard UN staff safety and access. It welcomes work to upgrade the force's gear and sites. A report on events and on steps toward Resolution 338 is due at the end of the period.

Jerusalem's status drew a firm Council line in the spring of 1968. On 21 May, it adopted Resolution 252. Thirteen members voted yes and none voted no. Canada and the United States held back. Israel had seized East Jerusalem in the 1967 war. It was now passing laws the Assembly had already called invalid. Jordan brought the matter back to the Council.

The text restates a core rule: land taken by war cannot be kept. It deplores Israel's failure to heed the Assembly. All Israeli steps that tend to change the city's legal status are declared invalid. Land seizures count among them. Israel must undo such steps and take no more. The Council held this line for decades.

Grenada's application for United Nations membership is the subject of Resolution 352, adopted unanimously on 21 June 1974. The Council had examined the Caribbean island's request, filed as document S/11311. Grenada had become independent from Britain in February of that year, under Prime Minister Eric Gairy.

In its only operative line, the Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Grenada to membership. Admission resolutions follow a fixed pattern because the Charter allows the Assembly to seat a state only after the Council recommends it. The entry in the record is brief, but it documents the small spice-growing island's formal entry into the community of nations in the mid-1970s.

Israeli settlements in the Arab territories occupied since 1967, including Jerusalem, are taken up in Resolution 452. A commission of the Council had examined the settlements and reported with recommendations. Israel had refused to cooperate with the commission. The resolution was adopted in 1979.

The Council praised the commission's work and accepted its proposals. It said that Israel's policy of building settlements in the occupied lands has no legal validity. The policy breaks the Fourth Geneva Convention, the text holds. The government and people of Israel were called on to stop at once. The building and planning of settlements in those lands, Jerusalem included, had to end. The commission was told to keep watching the situation and report back, given the size of the problem.

Early reports of the United Nations Atomic Energy Commission reached the Council in 1948. The commission had been set up after the Second World War to work on control of atomic energy. It sent its first three reports to the Council. Resolution 52, adopted on 22 June 1948, does one thing with them. It tells the Secretary-General to pass the reports to the General Assembly and to all member states. The record of the Council's own talks on the subject went with them, as a matter of special concern.

Namibia won its independence in March 1990, after decades under South African rule, and it applied to join the United Nations within weeks. Resolution 652 was adopted on 17 April 1990, without a vote against it. The Council examined Namibia's application. It then recommended to the General Assembly that the Republic of Namibia be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The recommendation crowned a long campaign, backed by the United Nations for many years, to free the country.
voltaire-micromegas-1752:
Voltaire wrote Micromegas in 1752 as a tale with a sharp point. A giant from a star of Sirius, eight leagues tall, roams the sky. He picks up a small friend from Saturn on his way. The pair come to Earth and at first miss the folk who live here.

With a lens of cut gems they spot a ship full of men of thought. Talk with the small crew shows both pride and true wit in men. The giant laughs at wars fought for specks of mud. The tale is a root work of tales of guests from the stars.
wapping-witch-answer-1652:
Rival prints of the Wapping witch case drew a sharp reply in 1652. A Declaration in Answer to Pamphlets concerning the Witch of Wapping takes the other accounts apart point by point. Such print fights were common, but few over witch cases survive so fully.

The writer charges the first pamphlets with false reports and works to set the record straight. Readers watch two camps argue over what was said, done, and proved. The quarrel shows the witch panic fought out in the press as much as in court. It is a rare, clear look at how trial news was made and unmade.
wapping-witch-relation-1652:
London itself had a witch case in 1652, told in The Witch of Wapping. The pamphlet gives the full relation of the charge and trial in the riverside parish of Wapping. A city case drew eyes that county trials could not.

The text walks readers through the claims, the court work, and the fate of the accused. It brings the hunt for witches to the crowded streets and docks of the capital. Country fears look strange in town dress, and the print knows it. The case shows the panic could touch even the heart of London.
zoist-vol-10-1852:
The Zoist's tenth volume runs from April 1852 to January 1853. A decade of Elliotson's journal now stands in print. Mesmeric practice reports arrive from a loyal band of doctors and amateurs. Trance surgery, once the headline, now shares space with subtler mental cases.

Cerebral physiology still names half the journal's mission on its cover. Somnambulists and their feats draw the curious, as ever. The movement's complete record would fill thirteen volumes by 1856. Volume ten shows a cause grown older, its hopes and habits fixed. What the medical world dismissed, these pages preserved. That preservation is the set's lasting service.
